1. Majilio: Kipindi cha Faraja, Tumaini na Kujiandaa kwa Amani

Juma la pili la Majilio linatualika kuwa watu wa tumaini. Nabii Isaya leo anatupa ujumbe wenye nguvu:
“Farijieni watu wangu… mpeni habari njema, mpeni moyo.”

Majilio ni kipindi cha kumkaribisha Kristo anayekuja kuponya, kutuliza mioyo, na kutuweka huru na hofu. Ni kipindi cha kuangalia ndani ya maisha yetu na kuuliza:
 • Je, Kristo atanikuta wapi?
 • Je, nimekuwa chanzo cha faraja au chanzo cha majeraha kwa wengine?
 • Je, ninaishi kama mtu anayengoja Mungu kwa moyo wa amani?

2. Tanzania: Neema ya Uhuru na Wito wa Kutunza Amani

Leo ni Siku ya Uhuru wa Tanzania – siku ya kukumbuka zawadi kubwa tuliyopewa na Mungu:
AMANI.

Amani yetu si bahati mbaya; ni baraka na urithi wa waasisi wetu. Lakini pia ni jukumu letu. Kwa sababu:

1989 (MCMLXXXIX) was a common year starting on Sunday of the Gregorian calendar, the 1989th year of the Common Era (CE) and Anno Domini (AD) designations, the 989th year of the 2nd millennium, the 89th year of the 20th century, and the 10th and last year of the 1980s decade.

1989 was a turning point in political history with the "Revolutions of 1989" which ended communism in Eastern Bloc of Europe, starting in Poland and Hungary, with experiments in power-sharing coming to a head with the opening of the Berlin Wall in November, the Velvet Revolution in Czechoslovakia and the overthrow of the communist dictatorship in Romania in December; the movement ended in December 1991 with the dissolution of the Soviet Union. Revolutions against communist governments in Eastern Europe mainly succeeded, but the year also saw the suppression by the Chinese government of the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests in Beijing.

It was the year of the first Brazilian direct presidential election in 29 years, since the end of the military government in 1985 that ruled the country for more than twenty years, and marked the redemocratization process's final point.

F. W. de Klerk was elected as State President of South Africa, and his regime gradually dismantled the apartheid system over the next five years, culminating with the 1994 election that brought jailed African National Congress leader Nelson Mandela to power.

The first commercial Internet service providers surfaced in this year,[1][2] as well as the first written proposal for the World Wide Web and New Zealand, Japan and Australia's first Internet connections. The first babies born after preimplantation genetic diagnosis were conceived in late 1989.[3]

The other 9/11: George H.W. Bush's 1990 New World Order speech
Out of these troubled times, a new world order can emerge.
By George H.W. Bush|Contributor

12:41 PM on Sep 8, 2017 CDT

Editor's note: The following is an excerpt of George H.W. Bush's speech before a joint session of Congress on Sept. 11, 1990, in which he describes his vision of a new world order amid the Persian Gulf crisis. Read the full speech here.

We stand today at a unique and extraordinary moment. The crisis in the Persian Gulf, as grave as it is, also offers a rare opportunity to move toward an historic period of cooperation. Out of these troubled times, our fifth objective — a new world order — can emerge: a new era — freer from the threat of terror, stronger in the pursuit of justice, and more secure in the quest for peace. An era in which the nations of the world, East and West, North and South, can prosper and live in harmony.

A hundred generations have searched for this elusive path to peace, while a thousand wars raged across the span of human endeavor. Today that new world is struggling to be born, a world quite different from the one we've known. A world where the rule of law supplants the rule of the jungle. A world in which nations recognize the shared responsibility for freedom and justice. A world where the strong respect the rights of the weak. This is the vision that I shared with President Gorbachev in Helsinki. He and other leaders from Europe, the Gulf, and around the world understand that how we manage this crisis today could shape the future for generations to come.

The test we face is great, and so are the stakes. This is the first assault on the new world that we seek, the first test of our mettle. Had we not responded to this first provocation with clarity of purpose, if we do not continue to demonstrate our determination, it would be a signal to actual and potential despots around the world. America and the world must defend common vital interests — and we will. America and the world must support the rule of law — and we will. America and the world must stand up to aggression — and we will. And one thing more: In the pursuit of these goals, America will not be intimidated.

President George Bush and first lady Barbara Bush welcomed Soviet President Mikhail...
President George Bush and first lady Barbara Bush welcomed Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev and his wife, Raisa, for a state dinner at the White House in May 1990. (File Photo/The Associated Press)
Vital issues of principle are at stake. Saddam Hussein is literally trying to wipe a country off the face of the Earth. We do not exaggerate. Nor do we exaggerate when we say Saddam Hussein will fail. Vital economic interests are at risk as well. Iraq itself controls some 10 percent of the world's proven oil reserves. Iraq plus Kuwait controls twice that. An Iraq permitted to swallow Kuwait would have the economic and military power, as well as the arrogance, to intimidate and coerce its neighbors — neighbors who control the lion's share of the world's remaining oil reserves. We cannot permit a resource so vital to be dominated by one so ruthless. And we won't.

Recent events have surely proven that there is no substitute for American leadership. In the face of tyranny, let no one doubt American credibility and reliability. Let no one doubt our staying power. We will stand by our friends. One way or another, the leader of Iraq must learn this fundamental truth. From the outset, acting hand in hand with others, we've sought to fashion the broadest possible international response to Iraq's aggression. The level of world cooperation and condemnation of Iraq is unprecedented. Armed forces from countries spanning four continents are there at the request of King Fahd of Saudi Arabia to deter and, if need be, to defend against attack. Moslems and non-Moslems, Arabs and non-Arabs, soldiers from many nations stand shoulder to shoulder, resolute against Saddam Hussein's ambitions. ...

I cannot predict just how long it will take to convince Iraq to withdraw from Kuwait. Sanctions will take time to have their full intended effect. We will continue to review all options with our allies, but let it be clear: We will not let this aggression stand.

George H.W. Bush was the 41st president of the United States.

The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, adopted by all United Nations (UN) members in 2015, created 17 world Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The aim of these global goals is "peace and prosperity for people and the planet"[1][2] – while tackling climate change and working to preserve oceans and forests. The SDGs highlight the connections between the environmental, social and economic aspects of sustainable development. Sustainability is at the center of the SDGs, as the term sustainable development implies.

These goals are ambitious,[according to whom?] and the reports and outcomes to date indicate a challenging path. Most, if not all, of the goals are unlikely to be met by 2030. Rising inequalities, climate change, and biodiversity loss are topics of concerns threatening progress. The COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 to 2023 made these challenges worse, and some regions, such as Asia, have experienced significant setbacks during that time.

There are cross-cutting issues and synergies between the different goals; for example, for SDG 13 on climate action, the IPCC sees robust synergies with SDGs 3 (health), 7 (clean energy), 11 (cities and communities), 12 (responsible consumption and production) and 14 (oceans).[3][4]: 70  On the other hand, critics and observers have also identified trade-offs between the goals,[4]: 67  such as between ending hunger and promoting environmental sustainability.[5]: 26  Furthermore, concerns have arisen over the high number of goals (compared to the eight Millennium Development Goals), leading to compounded trade-offs, a weak emphasis on environmental sustainability, and difficulties tracking qualitative indicators.

The political impact of the SDGs has been rather limited, and the SDGs have struggled to achieve transformative changes in policy and institutional structures.[6] Also, funding remains a critical issue for achieving the SDGs. Significant financial resources would be required worldwide. The role of private investment and a shift towards sustainable financing are also essential for realizing the SDGs. Examples of progress from some countries demonstrate that achieving sustainable development through concerted global action is possible. The global effort for the SDGs calls for prioritizing environmental sustainability, understanding the indivisible nature of the goals, and seeking synergies across sectors.

The short titles of the 17 SDGs are: No poverty (SDG 1), Zero hunger (SDG 2), Good health and well-being (SDG 3), Quality education (SDG 4), Gender equality (SDG 5), Clean water and sanitation (SDG 6), Affordable and clean energy (SDG 7), Decent work and economic growth (SDG 8), Industry, innovation and infrastructure (SDG 9), Reduced inequalities (SDG 10), Sustainable cities and communities (SDG 11), Responsible consumption and production (SDG 12), Climate action (SDG 13), Life below water (SDG 14), Life on land (SDG 15), Peace, justice, and strong institutions (SDG 16), and Partnerships for the goals (SDG 17).

Another general rule for predicting oppositions of Mars is from the following: the planet has an approximate 15.8-year periodic opposition cycle, which consists of three or four Aphelic oppositions and three consecutive Perihelic oppositions. Perihelic oppositions are also called "favorable" because the Earth and Mars come closest to each other on those occasions. We sometimes refer to this as the seven Martian synodic periods. This cycle is repeated every 79 years (± 4 to 5 days) and, if one were to live long enough, one would see this cycle nearly replicated in approximately 284 years. The 2031 Mars apparition is considered Transitional (between Aphelic and Perihelic) because the orbital longitude at opposition will be 68.4° from the aphelion longitude of 70° Ls and 111.6° Ls from perihelion (250° Ls).

NOTE: Ls is the planetocentric longitude of the Sun along the ecliptic of Mars’ sky. 0° Ls is defined as that point where the Sun crosses the Martian celestial equator from south to north, that is the planet’s northern hemisphere vernal equinox. The other Ls values that define the beginnings of Martian northern hemisphere seasons are: summer, 90° Ls; autumn, 180° Ls; and winter, 270° Ls. For Mars’ southern hemisphere these values represent the opposite seasons. Distance (A.U.) - Distance from Earth to Mars in astronomical units, where one (1) A.U. equals 92,955,807.267 miles or 149,597,870.691 km.
Opposition occurs 11 months after conjunction when Mars is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun. Mars will remain visible for more than twelve months after opposition and then become lost in the glare of the Sun around May 31, 2032 as it approaches the next conjunction (July 11, 2032). Presidential elections are scheduled to be held in the United States on November 7, 2028, to elect the president and vice president of the United States for a term of four years.

In the 2024 elections, the Republican Party gained a majority of seats in the House of Representatives and Senate. Incumbent president Donald Trump won a non-consecutive second term; per the limits set by the 22nd Amendment, he is constitutionally barred from being elected president again.[1]

Background
See also: 2024 United States elections
The Republican Party returned to power in the United States with a government trifecta in January 2025 following the 2024 election. Trump, who was elected president in 2016 but lost a re-election bid in 2020 to Joe Biden, and JD Vance, a then-senator from Ohio defeated vice president Kamala Harris, who began her campaign following Biden's exit from the 2024 election, and Minnesota governor Tim Walz. Trump's victory was credited to a post-pandemic surge in inflation,[a] a migrant crisis at the U.S.–Mexico border,[b] and a global anti-incumbent backlash.[8][9][10] In addition, Republicans secured control of the Senate, flipping four seats and earning a three seat majority, while also retaining a House majority, though the party's majority narrowed to three seats after losing two seats.[11]

Electoral system
Main article: United States Electoral College
See also: United States presidential primary and Primary elections in the United States
The president and vice president of the United States are elected through the Electoral College, determined by the number of senators and representatives with an additional three representatives for Washington, D.C. A majority of 270 votes is needed to win the election. Forty-eight states use a winner-take-all system, in which states award all of their electors to the winner of the popular vote. In Maine and Nebraska, two votes are allocated to the winner of the popular vote, while each of the individual congressional districts have one vote. Electoral votes are certified by state electors in December and by Congress on January 6.[12] Presidential candidates are selected in a presidential primary, conducted through primary elections run by state governments or caucuses run by state parties which bind convention delegates to candidates.[13] A brokered convention occurs when a candidate does not receive a majority of votes on the first round of voting,[14] or when a candidate withdraws.[15]

Election Day in the United States has been held on the first Tuesday that falls after the first Monday in November.[16] Previously, states could determine their own Election Day prior to the first Wednesday in December. The 2028 presidential election will occur on November 7, 2028.[17]

Eligibility
The United States Constitution limits occupancy of the presidency to individuals who are at least thirty-five, who have been a resident in the United States for at least fourteen years, and who are a natural-born citizen.[18] Section three of the Fourteenth Amendment prevents current and former federal, state, and military officials from holding office—including the presidency—if they have "engaged in insurrection or rebellion" against the United States;[19] in March 2024, the Supreme Court unanimously ruled in Trump v. Anderson that former president Donald Trump could seek office after challenges to his ballot eligibility were raised by several state attorneys general.[20] A convicted felon may serve as president.[21] Elon Musk, who emerged as a political influencer in the 2024 presidential election, is ineligible to serve as president as he was born in South Africa and is a naturalized citizen.[22]

Trump is ineligible to be elected to a third term, as the Twenty-Second Amendment forbids any person from being elected president more than twice.[23] Nonetheless, he has repeatedly suggested running for a third term, an idea supported by several of his allies, including Steve Bannon.[24] In January 2025, Tennessee representative Andy Ogles proposed a resolution to amend the Twenty-Second Amendment, allowing for presidents who have served two non-consecutive terms to seek a third term. The verbiage of the amendment would prevent living presidents Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, and Barack Obama, all currently ineligible under the 22nd Amendment, from running for a third term.[25] At CPAC 2025, conservative groups, such as the Third Term Project, supported the Ogles resolution and promoted the idea of Trump running for an as-yet unconstitutional third term.[26][27] In response, New York Democratic representative Dan Goldman planned to introduce a resolution affirming the Twenty-Second Amendment.[28]

Raphael Gamaliel Warnock[1] (/ˈrɑːfiɛl ˈwɔːrnɒk/ RAH-fee-el WOR-nok; born July 23, 1969) is an American politician and Baptist pastor serving as the junior United States senator from Georgia, a seat he has held since 2021. A member of the Democratic Party, Warnock has been the senior pastor of Atlanta's Ebenezer Baptist Church since 2005.[2][3]

Warnock was the senior pastor of Douglas Memorial Community Church from 2001 to 2005.[4] He came to prominence in Georgia politics as a leading activist in the campaign to expand Medicaid in the state under the Affordable Care Act. He was the Democratic nominee in the 2020 United States Senate special election in Georgia, defeating incumbent Republican Kelly Loeffler in a runoff election.[5]

Warnock and Jon Ossoff are the first Democrats elected to the U.S. Senate from Georgia since Zell Miller in 2000.[6][7] Their elections were critical in securing a 50–50 Senate majority for Democrats, with Vice President Kamala Harris serving as the tie-breaking vote.[8] Warnock was a reliable supporter of Joe Biden's legislative efforts during his presidency.[9][10] He was reelected to a full term in 2022, defeating Republican nominee Herschel Walker.

Warnock is the first African American to represent Georgia in the Senate, the first Black Democrat elected to the Senate from a Southern state, and the second black U.S. Senator directly elected from a Southern state, after Tim Scott.[11][12][13]

Early life and education
Warnock was born in Savannah, Georgia, on July 23, 1969.[14] He grew up in public housing as the eleventh of twelve children born to Verlene and Jonathan Warnock, both Pentecostal pastors.[15][16] His father served in the U.S. Army during World War II, where he learned automobile mechanics and welding, and subsequently opened a small car restoration business where he restored junked cars for resale.[17] His mother picked cotton and tobacco in the summers in Waycross, Georgia, as a teenager and became a pastor.[18]

Warnock graduated from Sol C. Johnson High School in 1987,[19] and having wanted to follow in the footsteps of Martin Luther King Jr., attended Morehouse College, from which he graduated cum laude in 1991 with a Bachelor of Arts degree in psychology.[20][21] He credits his participation in the Upward Bound program for making him college-ready, as he was able to enroll in early college courses through Savannah State University.[19][21] He then earned Master of Divinity, Master of Philosophy, and Doctor of Philosophy degrees from Union Theological Seminary, a school affiliated with Columbia University.[22][23][17]

Religious work

Warnock with John Lewis at a "Souls to the Polls" event. Warnock later officiated Lewis's funeral at Ebenezer Baptist Church.[24]
Warnock began his ministry as an intern and licentiate at the Sixth Avenue Baptist church in Birmingham, Alabama,[25] under the civil rights movement leader John Thomas Porter.[25][26] In the 1990s, he served as youth pastor and then assistant pastor at Abyssinian Baptist Church in New York.[27][28] While Warnock was pastor at Abyssinian, the church declined to hire workfare recipients as part of organized opposition to then-mayor Rudy Giuliani's workfare program.[29] The church also hosted Fidel Castro on October 22, 1995, while Warnock was youth pastor. There is no evidence Warnock was involved in that decision. During the 2020–21 United States Senate special election in Georgia, his campaign refused to say whether Warnock attended the event.[30]

In January 2001, Warnock was elected senior pastor of Douglas Memorial Community Church in Baltimore, Maryland.[31][32] He and an assistant minister were arrested and charged with obstructing a 2002 police investigation into suspected child abuse at a summer camp run by the church. The police report called Warnock "extremely uncooperative and disruptive". Warnock had demanded that the counselors have lawyers present when being interviewed by police.[33] The charges were later dropped with the deputy state's attorney's acknowledgment that it had been a "miscommunication", adding that Warnock had aided the investigation and that prosecution would be a waste of resources.[34][35] Warnock said he was merely asserting that lawyers should be present during the interviews[36] and that he had intervened to ensure that an adult was present while a juvenile suspect was being questioned.[37] Warnock stepped down as the church's senior pastor in 2005.[4]

On Father's Day 2005, Warnock was named senior pastor of the Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta, Georgia, Martin Luther King Jr.'s former congregation;[38] he is the fifth and the youngest person to serve as Ebenezer's senior pastor since its founding.[19][39][40] He has continued in the post while serving in the Senate.[41][42]

As pastor, Warnock advocated for clemency for Troy Davis, who was executed in 2011.[43] In 2013, he delivered the benediction at the public prayer service at the second inauguration of Barack Obama.[44] After Fidel Castro died in 2016, Warnock told his church to pray for the Cuban people, calling Castro's legacy "complex, kind of like America's legacy is complex".[30] In March 2019, Warnock hosted an interfaith meeting on climate change at his church, featuring Al Gore and William Barber II.[45] He presided at Representative John Lewis's funeral at Ebenezer Church in July 2020.[46][24]

On Easter Sunday 2021, Warnock's Twitter account tweeted, "The meaning of Easter is more transcendent than the resurrection of Jesus Christ. Whether you are a Christian or not, through a commitment to helping others we are able to save ourselves." Some conservative Christians and political commentators criticized the tweet, including Benjamin Watson, Allie Beth Stuckey, and Jenna Ellis, who called it "heretical". The tweet was deleted that afternoon, with a spokesperson for Warnock saying, "the tweet was posted by staff and was not approved" but declining to say whether it reflected Warnock's beliefs.[47][48]

Lawes Divine, Morall and Martiall
SUMMARY
Lawes Divine, Morall and Martiall, the rules and regulations issued in Jamestown beginning in 1610 and 1611, are the earliest extant English-language body of laws in the western hemisphere. It was not a legal code in the modern sense. No legislation created it, and no court enforced it. The laws were orders that the governor, appointed by the Virginia Company of London that settled and managed the colony between 1607 and 1624, issued to regulate the conduct of its members, employees, and servants. The laws recognized none of the principles of the English common law and did not provide for jury trials, even though the royal charters of the company specified that residents of the colony were entitled to all the rights of Englishmen.

The three men who issued and first administered the laws were all career army officers, and because the largest part of the code was the law martial for the governing of the soldiers, the code has been misunderstood as imposing martial law on everyone in the colony. It has also been wrongly called Dale’s Laws, as if Deputy Governor Sir Thomas Dale, who administered the code for much of the time that it was in effect, was its sole or principal author.

The Virginia Company received a new charter in 1609 that authorized it to send a military governor to the struggling colony. Sir Thomas Gates sailed for Virginia in 1609, but his ship, the Sea Venture, was wrecked on Bermuda in a hurricane. When he arrived in Virginia in May 1610, he found the remnant of the garrison at Jamestown that had survived the deadly winter known as the Starving Time. On May 24, 1610, Gates issued the first of the orders that William Strachey compiled and published in England in 1612 in a book entitled For the Colony in Virginea Britannia. Lawes Divine, Morall and Martiall, &c.

Gates and the surviving colonists decided within weeks to pack up and sail for Newfoundland to catch a ride back to England aboard the fishing fleet. On the way down the James River, they met a relief expedition under the command of Thomas West, baron De La Warr, who had been appointed governor of the colony by the Virginia Company. The survivors returned to Jamestown. On June 12, 1610, De La Warr confirmed and began adding to the regulations that Gates had first announced. It is not possible from Strachey’s compilation to know in most instances who issued which orders or whether the governors issued them in the same sequence in which Strachey published them. Some orders, such as those mentioning a new well that was dug later, clearly postdate the first Gates and De La Warr orders. The whole body of laws that Strachey compiled before returning to England in 1612 fills eighteen pages in his book. In the title he called them “Divine” and “Morall” laws and in another part “Divine” and “Politique” laws.

In May 1611, Sir Thomas Dale arrived in Virginia with supplies, livestock, and many new settlers. He commanded a large and well-equipped military force and on June 22, 1611, issued a detailed law martial for the governing of the soldiers. It fills sixty-nine pages of Strachey’s book and was a fairly standard military code prescribing the duties and responsibilities of all the officers and men and imposing severe corporal punishments or death for infractions of discipline. Dale ordered that the guard publicly read a seven-page prayer twice each day. He administered the colony most of the time until the spring of 1616 during the long absences of Gates and De La Warr, but it is unlikely that he subjected the civilian residents of Virginia to the law martial. The orders imposed on civilians, to which Dale very likely added others, were strict enough to give the laws an evil reputation, and Dale’s administration of them was harsh enough to earn him much criticism then and thereafter.

The laws specified the responsibilities of ministers and required every person to attend church twice every Sunday. The laws established procedures for the disposal of the property of colonists who died, regulated trade with Indians, prohibited unnecessary killing of livestock, required houses and bedding to be kept clean, and forbade washing soiled clothing and cooking utensils or doing “the necessities of nature” within a quarter mile of the new well. The laws also regulated the collection of debts and trading with men aboard ships, and they required tradesmen, cooks, laundry women, and others to work at their tasks and the men to muster for defense when summoned.

The laws ordered severe corporal punishment for many offenses, such as having a bodkin driven through the tongue for cursing or speaking disrespectfully of the clergy or company officials. The code imposed whippings and other physical punishment for gambling, failing to attend church, fornication, adultery, unnecessarily killing livestock, or stealing agricultural implements or other people’s crops.

The list of crimes to be punished with death was long: blasphemy, uttering treasonous words or words critical of the company, murder, sodomy, robbery, swearing false oaths, bearing false witness, trading with Indians without permission, stealing from Indians, cheating the company or the cape merchant (who operated the company’s storehouse), trading with sailors without permission, and sending goods out of the colony without permission. It prescribed death for a third offence for several of the crimes to be punished in the first or second instance by whipping, standing in the stocks or at the pillory, or having the tongue bored through or cut out.

The laws required that every minister “read all these lawes and ordinances, publickly in the assembly of the congregation.”

It is very likely that Dale (as well as Gates and De La Warr during their occasional short residences in Virginia) issued more orders after Strachey left Virginia early in 1612, but those orders, or laws, have not survived. Strict enforcement of the code, for which Dale was noteworthy, helped the company restore order and discipline in Virginia. The company’s military governors administered the code until April 18, 1619, when Sir George Yeardley arrived in Jamestown and began governing under the new Great Charter of 1618. Resounding Echoes: Why Women's Voices Must Be Heard

​For centuries, history was largely recorded in a baritone. The narratives of nations, the laws of lands, and the philosophies of existence were predominantly written, spoken, and decided by men. 
While women have always been present—working, building, thinking, and revolutionizing—their voices were often relegated to the private sphere, whispered in domestic spaces rather than broadcast in public halls. 

Today, the call for women to have a voice is not merely a demand for fairness; it is a fundamental requirement for the intellectual, economic, and moral evolution of humanity.
​Beyond the Seat at the Table
​There is a distinct difference between being present and being heard. 

In recent decades, great strides have been made in representation. We see more women in boardrooms, in legislative bodies, and in scientific laboratories. However, presence often masquerades as power. A seat at the table is meaningless if the microphone is turned off.

​For women to truly have a voice, society must move beyond tokenism—where a woman is included solely to meet a quota—to active listening. This means valuing female perspectives not just on "women's issues" like childcare or reproductive health, but on the economy, defense, urban planning, and technology. When a woman speaks on these topics, she brings a lived experience that is often distinct from her male counterparts, revealing blind spots in policy and strategy that would otherwise go unnoticed.

​The Diversity of Thought
​The argument for amplification is rooted in the necessity of diversity. Homogeneity in decision-making leads to stagnation. When only one demographic controls the narrative, solutions tend to be one-dimensional.

​Research consistently shows that diverse teams—those that include women in meaningful roles—perform better. In business, companies with strong female leadership often see higher profitability and innovation. 

In conflict resolution, peace treaties are more likely to last when women are involved in the negotiation process. This is not because women are inherently magical, but because they often emphasize community, long-term stability, and social infrastructure differently than men have been socialized to do. By silencing half the population, we are effectively operating at half-capacity.

​Intersectionality and the Margins
​It is crucial to recognize that "women" is not a monolithic category. The struggle to be heard is compounded for women of color, women with disabilities, LGBTQ+ women, and women from lower socioeconomic backgrounds. Historically, even when the feminist movement gained traction, it often prioritized the voices of white, middle-class women.

​To truly honor the concept of women having a voice, we must pass the microphone to the margins. We must listen to the indigenous woman fighting for climate justice, the working-class mother navigating the labor market, and the refugee woman seeking safety. These voices carry the weight of complex, intersecting systems of power and offer the most urgent critiques of our current societal structures.

​The Art of Active Listening
​Granting women a voice requires a shift in the behavior of men and institutions. It requires a culture of "amplification." In the Obama White House, female staffers famously adopted a strategy where, when a woman made a key point in a meeting, another woman would repeat it and give credit to the author. This prevented the idea from being ignored or claimed by a male colleague.

​Society needs a similar strategy on a macro scale. We must stop interrupting. We must stop "mansplaining"—the act of explaining a concept to a woman who is already an expert in that field. We must credit ideas to their originators and dismantle the unconscious bias that views a man’s voice as authoritative and a woman’s voice as emotional or tentative.

​Conclusion
​A world where women are heard is not a world where men are silenced; it is a world where the conversation is complete. It is a chorus rather than a solo. When we unlock the voices of women, we unlock solutions to global crises, we unleash economic potential, and we create a culture of empathy and equity. The silence has been broken; now, it is time to listen to the song.

Interview with Pastor Mkwani.

1. How do you believe spirituality can be used to address social issues like povert and inequality in our community?  

Answer:
Spirituality rooted in Christ calls believers to love, justice, mercy, and humble service, shaping how we address poverty and inequality in our communities.

Biblical mandate to care for the poor  
God’s people are to care for the vulnerable, reflecting His heart for justice. “Learn to do right; seek justice. Defend the oppressed. Take up the cause of the fatherless; plead the case of the widow.” (Isaiah 1:17). In the New Covenant, Jesus proclaims good news to the poor and calls us to generosity that honors Him (Luke 4:18; 2 Corinthians 9:6-7).

Spiritual formation that overflows into action  
Spirituality is not merely inward piety but transformation that produces fruit in action. “If anyone has material possessions and sees a brother or sister in need but has no pity on them, how can the love of God be in them?” (1 John 3:17). Faith without works is dead (James 2:17, 26), so communities must translate belief into practical help, advocacy, and systemic change.

Jesus as model and aim  
Jesus identifies with the poor and marginalized, calling His followers to serve “the least of these.” “Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.” (Matthew 25:40). This frames social care as worship and obedience.

Practical avenues anchored in Scripture  
- Community generosity and equitable sharing: “There were not any who lacked, for from time to time those who owned land or houses sold them, brought the money... and laid it at the apostles’ feet.” (Acts 4:34-35, summarized)  
- Restorative justice and advocacy: seek righteous policy that protects the vulnerable (Micah 6:8).  
- Economic justice through fair labor, just wages, and opportunity (Ephesians 4:28).

Hopeful, gospel-centered approach  
Proclaim the kingdom and live out its implications: reconciliation, dignity, and provision through Christ’s gospel, not as social programs alone but as gospel-driven transformation (Galatians 5:22-23).

“For I know the plans I have for you,” declares the LORD, “plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future.” (Jeremiah 29:11).

2. What role do you think the church should play in promoting mental health awareness and support?

 Answer:
 The Church is called to embody Christ’s love, steward God’s grace, and shepherd souls. Biblical care for mental health begins with recognizing every person’s value as created in God’s image (Genesis 1:27) and honoring their suffering with compassion (Colossians 3:12-13). The church should promote mental health awareness by preaching hope in Christ, offering practical support, and connecting people to wise, professional care when needed.

Firstly, nurture and inclusion: “Be kind and compassionate to one another” (Ephesians 4:32) and “carry each other’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2). Create safe spaces for confession, prayer, and accountability, acknowledging vulnerability as a doorway to God’s grace. “Cast all your anxiety on him because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7).

Secondly, educate biblically and humbly: teach that mental distress can be affected by sin, brokenness, and spiritual warfare, yet healing comes through Jesus (Luke 4:18-19). Encourage seeking professional help when necessary (Proverbs 11:14; Proverbs 15:22).

Thirdly, advocate for justice and access: support affordable care, reduce stigma, and partner with health professionals to serve the community (James 2:14-17; Isaiah 1:17).

Prayerful leadership, pastoral training, and ongoing discipleship are essential to embody the church’s role in mental health.

“Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you” (John 14:27).

3.How do you approach interfaith dialougue and building relationships with people of other faiths or backgrounds? 

Answer:
 Interfaith dialogue and building relationships with people of other faiths should be approached with Christ-centered love, truth, and humility, seeking to reflect the gospel while respecting others as image-bearers.

Rooted in Christ’s example, engage with grace and patience. “Be wise in the way you act toward outsiders; make the most of every opportunity” (Colossians 4:5). “Let your conversation be always full of grace” (Colossians 4:6). Seek common ground in justice, mercy, and compassion, bearing witness to the transforming power of Jesus through humble living.

Speak truth with gentleness, recognizing the freedom of others while upholding the unique gospel message. “Sanctify Christ as Lord in your hearts. Always be prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks you to give the reason for the hope that you have. But do this with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15). “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6) should be held with reverent humility, inviting dialogue rather than coercion.

Practice hospitality and listening. “Love your neighbor as yourself” (Mark 12:31) and “Be devoted to one another in love” (Romans 12:10). Build relationships that reflect integrity, avoid syncretism, and point toward Christ’s lordship and salvation.

Pray for wisdom and discernment, trusting God to gentle hearts. “If any of you lacks wisdom, you should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to you” (James 1:5).

“Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you” (John 14:27).

4. What are some of the biggest challenges facing spiritual leaders in Africa today?

Answer: 
Spiritual leaders today face Christ-centered callings amid a world of distraction, division, and pressing moral questions. Biblical authority must be anchored in Christ and Scripture: leaders are shepherds called to feed God’s sheep, guard the flock, and model humility, repentance, and love (Ephesians 4:11-12; 1 Peter 5:2-3; John 13:34-35).

Cultural pressures and moral compromise challenge leaders to distinguish truth with grace. Scripture urges discernment and courage: “Be on your guard; stand firm in the faith” and “take up the shield of faith” (1 Corinthians 16:13; Ephesians 6:16).

Pastoral burnout and accountability threaten sustainable ministry; biblical leadership requires humility, transparency, and accountability within the body (1 Peter 5:2-3; James 5:16).

False teaching and unity demand vigilant teaching of sound doctrine and reconciliation within the body (Titus 1:9; Ephesians 4:3-15).

Prayer, worship, and reliance on God anchor endurance; Jesus teaches that apart from Him we can do nothing (John 15:5; Philippians 4:13).

In every challenge, leaders must cling to the gospel, shepherd like Jesus, and seek the Spirit’s wisdom (Colossians 1:28-29; James 1:5).

Verses: John 15:5; 1 Corinthians 16:13; Ephesians 6:16; 1 Peter 5:2-3

5. How do you balance spiritual growth with community service and social responsibility?

 Answer:
 Our growth in Christ always flows from our union with Him and outward in love to others. Scripture ties personal Spirit-led transformation to faithful obedience in the world God loves.

Biblical foundation  
Salvation by grace through faith unites us to Christ, who transforms us to good works. Ephesians 2:8-10 teaches that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared in advance for us to do, so growth and service are inseparable. Matthew 28:19-20 commands making disciples, which includes teaching, baptizing, and embodying Christ’s mercy. James 2:14-17 warns that faith without deeds is dead, showing service proves and strengthens genuine faith.

Balancing growth and service  
Seek intimate daily fellowship with the Spirit, applying Scripture to heart and hands. Pray for discernment to identify when study becomes action and when service deepens understanding. Philippians 2:3-4 calls us to value others above ourselves and look to their interests. Galatians 5:22-23 shows the fruit of the Spirit—love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control—that shape both personal growth and social action.

Practical rhythm  
Prioritize worship, Scripture, and prayer as the soil of growth, then commit to mercy-ministry that aligns with your gifts (teaching, hospitality, service, advocacy). Romans 12:4-8 uses the body metaphor to show varied gifts working together. 1 John 3:17-18 reminds us that love must be active toward those in need.

Biblical guardrails  
Guard against legalism or burnout by resting in Christ’s finished work. Hebrews 4:9-11 invites us into rest and ongoing discipleship. Always aim for gospel-centered service that honors God and blesses neighbors.

Verse references  
Ephesians 2:8-10, Matthew 28:19-20, James 2:14-17, Philippians 2:3-4, Galatians 5:22-23, Romans 12:4-8, 1 John 3:17-18, Hebrews 4:9-11

"Our team did really well and I would like to congratulate all the participants from various counties, as well as everyone involved in making the event a success," said County Executive Committee Member for Education and Social Welfare and Family Affairs Hon. Yaqub Mumin.

"We celebrate not just the winners but all those who contributed to the success of this wonderful event, along with the collective effort in promoting inclusivity and empowerment through sports and fashion," added Hon. Yaqub.

KILE CHEMA ALICHOKIANZISHA MUNGU NDANI YAKO ATAKITIMIZA TU 

TAREHE: JUMATANO 10 DESEMBA 2025 

ANDIKO: WAFILIPI 1:6 

[6] Nami niliaminilo ndilo hili, ya kwamba yeye aliyeanza kazi njema mioyoni mwenu ataimaliza hata siku ya Kristo Yesu; 

TAFAKARI 

Siku zote moja ya changamoto za imani ni kujiuliza: Je, nitaweza kuendelea? Je, Mungu bado yupo pamoja nami? Je, kazi yake kweli itakamilika maishani mwangu?. 

Mtume Paulo, akiwa gerezani, anawaandikia Wafilipi maneno haya yenye nguvu ya faraja. Anasema: “Niliaminilo…”— maana yake hana shaka hata kidogo kwamba Mungu hatamuacha mtu yeyote ambaye alianza naye safari ya wokovu au wema. 

Paulo anawaandikia Wafilipi kwa moyo wa shukrani na imani. Anawakumbusha jambo kuu: Mungu ndiye aliyeanzisha kazi njema ndani ya waamini, na haitabaki nusu—Yeye mwenye nguvu, mwaminifu na asiyeacha kazi, ataikamilisha.

Hii kazi njema inajumuisha:

》Wokovu uliotolewa kwa neema
》Ukuaji wa kiroho  unaoendelea kila siku
》Mabadiliko ya tabia na maisha yanayoonekana
》Matendo Mema
》 Kutimilika kwa kusudi la Mungu katika maisha ya muumini

Paulo anasema kuwa hakuna kinachoweza kumzuia Mungu kukamilisha alichoanza: si magumu, si udhaifu wetu, si mapito ya maisha.

Kumbuka kuwa, Mungu hakukuita ili kukuacha njiani. Ikiwa unaona udhaifu, mapito au kurudi nyuma, kumbuka: Aliyeanza kazi ndani yako bado yupo kazini, kwa upendo na kwa uaminifu. Muombe akutie nguvu, akakuinue, na akusogeze mbele katika njia ya nuru na ushindi.

1. CHANZO CHA KAZI NJEMA – “Yeye aliyeanza…”

Kazi njema haikuanza kwa nguvu zetu, mapenzi yetu, au ustadi wetu.Ilianza kwa Mungu mwenyewe.

* Ni Yeye aliyekuita wakati ulikuwa mbali.
* Ni Yeye aliyekugusa moyo ukaamini Injili.
* Ni Yeye aliyekuja kwa Roho Mtakatifu kuanzisha mabadiliko ya ndani.
*Ni Yeye alikuumba na moyo wa huruma na matendo Mema.

Hivyo Paulo anasema: “Yeye aliyeanza…”Hapa unamwona Mungu kama Msanifu, Mjenzi, na Mfundishaji wa maisha ya kiroho. Mungu haanzishi kitu kwa bahati tu; chochote anachoanzisha kinakusudiwa kiendelee na kukamilika.Kama mwanadamu unaweza kuchoka, kushuka nguvu, kuvunjika moyo—lakini Mungu ambaye alianza kazi ndani yako hapunguki nguvu, hapotezi ramani, hasahau alipoanzia.

2. HALI YA KAZI NJEMA – “kazi njema ndani yenu…”

Kazi ambayo Mungu anafanya na mtu si ya nje tu, bali ni ya ndani

A. Kazi ya mabadiliko ya tabia

Inabadilisha moyo wa mwili kuwa moyo wa roho. Tabia zinabadilika, maamuzi yanatakaswa, maisha yanabadilishwa.

B. Kazi ya kutakasa na kuimarisha imani

Ni safari ya kila siku. Wakati mwingine ina kasi, wakati mwingine inaonekana polepole.Lakini ndani ya yote, Mungu yupo akikuchonga kama dhahabu kwenye moto.

C. Kazi ya kukutia nguvu kupitia majaribu

Majaribu hayamaanishi Mungu amekusahau; mara nyingi yanaonyesha kuwa kazi yake inaendelea.Kama vile dhahabu inavyoongezewa moto ili ionekane mfano unaotakiwa, ndivyo Mungu anaendelea kufanya kazi ndani ya maisha yako.

Hivyo kazi njema ni zaidi ya kubadilisha tabia—ni kukuunda kwa mfano wa Yesu Kristo. 

3. UHAKIKA WA UKAMILISHO – “ataikamilisha mpaka siku ya Kristo Yesu”

Hii ndiyo nguzo ya ujumbe huu: "Mungu hatakuacha nusu."

A. Mungu si mjenzi wa miradi inayosimama katikati 

Mwanadamu anaweza kuanza kwa moto na kuishia baridi; anaweza kuanza mradi na kuacha; anaweza kuanza wito na kuishia njiani. Lakini Mungu hana tabia hiyo.Chochote Mungu anachoanza hukamilishwa.

B. Ukamilisho huu ni wa rohoni na hatimaye wa milele 

Kukamilishwa kwa kazi ya Mungu kunahusisha:

* Ufahamu wa kina wa Neno
* Ushindi juu ya dhambi zinazorudia
* Kukua katika upendo
* Kutimilika kwa wito wako
* Hatimaye kuonekana kwa utukufu siku ya Kristo

Kazi ya Mungu katika maisha yako ni safari inayoenda mbele, na kila hatua ya maisha—mizuri au mibaya—ni sehemu ya mpango wake wa kukamilisha alichoanza.

C. Hakuna nguvu ya giza itakayozuia kazi ya Mungu

Kuanguka kwa muda hakutangushi kazi ya Mungu. Kosa la jana halifuti kusudi lake. Udhaifu wako hautoshi kusimamisha ujenzi wa Mungu. Kama alivyomwambia Yeremia,
“Ninacholenga kukijenga, hakitavunjika.”

4. JINSI YA KUISHI KATIKA KAZI YA MUNGU

A. Weka imani yako kwa Mungu anayefanya kazi ndani yako

Hata kama huoni maendeleo, Mungu hajawahi kukoma kufanya kazi.Mambo ambayo hujayaona kwa macho, Mungu anayatengeneza katika siri.

B. Shirikiana na kazi ya Roho Mtakatifu

Toa miyo wako kwa Mungu. Sikiliza Neno. Omba.Hii si kazi ya kupambana peke yako—ni kushirikiana na Roho Mtakatifu.

C. Kuwa na subira na safari yako ya kiroho

Kazi hii si ya haraka.Wakati mwingine Mungu hubadilisha kitu ndani ya siku moja; mara nyingine hubadilisha ndani ya miaka.

Kama mfinyanzi, Mungu haendi kwa haraka bila sababu—mwisho wake ni umbo kamili.

D. Kumbuka kwamba kila jaribu lina kusudi

Majaribu ni zana za Mungu.Anafanya kufinyanga, kuosha, kusafisha, na kuimarisha tabia yako kupitia moto unaoruhusu.

HITIMISHO

Wafilipi 1:6 ni kifungu cha faraja kwa kila Mkristo anayehisi udhaifu, anayepambana na kuanguka, au anayehisi yuko mbali na mahali anapotakiwa kuwa.

》Mungu hakukuita kwa makosa.
》Hakukuokoa kwa ajali.
》Hakukupa mwito kwa bahati mbaya.

Kazi yake ndani yako ni ya thamani, ya kiwango cha juu, na imepangwa kukamilika.Usiigeuke kwa sababu ya changamoto. Angalia mkono wa Mungu unaochonga maisha yako taratibu lakini kwa uaminifu.Aliyeanza kazi njema ndani yako yuko kazini leo, kesho, na hadi siku ya Kristo—na atasimama mbele yako akisema, “Kazi imekamilika.”

SALA NDEFU – WAFILIPI 1:6

“Ewe Mungu uliyeanza kazi njema ndani yangu, ikamilishe…”

Ee Baba wa milele, Mwenyezi Mungu, Muumba wa mbingu na nchi,Mungu wa neema, rehema na huruma zisizokoma, ninakuja mbele zako kwa unyenyekevu, kwa moyo ulio wazi, nikiwa na kiu ya uwepo wako. Nakushukuru kwa neno lako takatifu ambalo limenikumbusha kwamba wewe ndiye uliyeanza kazi njema ndani yangu, na kwamba wewe ni Mungu mwaminifu wa kukamilisha kile ulichokianza.

Bwana, ninakuinua na kukutukuza kwa sababu wewe huandaa mwanzo wenye baraka, na pia huweka mwisho wenye ushindi.

Leo, Bwana, nasimama juu ya ahadi hii kutoka Wafilipi 1:6, na ninakuomba:

1. KAMILISHA KAZI YA WOKOVU NDANI YANGU

Ee Mungu, uliyenichagua katika Kristo kabla ya kuwekwa misingi ya dunia, nakushukuru kwa kuniokoa.Lakini nakiri kwamba bado nina mapungufu, dhambi zinazojitokeza, na vita vinavyoendelea ndani ya moyo wangu.
Bwana, kamilisha kazi ya wokovu ndani yangu— niepushe na majaribu, nibadilishe tabia, uniinue juu ya udhaifu, nifanye niwe mtu unayemtaka niwe.

*Nioshe kwa damu ya Mwanakondoo.
*Nijaze kwa Roho Mtakatifu.
*Nifanye nichukie dhambi na nipende haki.

2. KAMILISHA KAZI YA MATENDO MEMA NA TABIA TAKATIFU

Mungu wangu, kuna maeneo ndani yangu ambayo bado hayajakamilika: eneo la hasira, kiburi, udhaifu wa moyo, maamuzi magumu, na magonjwa ya tabia yaliyonyemelea kwa muda mrefu. Bwana, nakupa mapungufu yangu—tengeneza, safisha, finyanga, kaza, timiza.

》Usinichoke ninapoporomoka kitabia
》Usiniachie ninaposhindwa.
》Usinikatie tamaa ninapoteleza.
Badala yake,endelea kunichonga kama chombo chenye heshima** katika nyumba yako.

3. KAMILISHA KAZI YA WITO WANGU NA KUSUDI LA MAISHI YANGU

Bwana, wewe unajua kusudi uliloweka ndani yangu.Unajua nafasi yangu duniani, huduma yangu, kazi yangu, maono yangu, na safari yangu ya kiroho.Ninakuomba, Ee Mungu, usiruhusu hofu, vikwazo, au watu zizuie kile ulichokusudia nifanye.

》Fungua milango inayotoka kwako.
》Funga milango isiyo ya mapenzi yako.
》Nipe neema ya kusimama katika wito wangu bila kuogopa.

Na pale ambako nimechelewa, nikuombe Bwana—nipatie urejesho wa kasi na muda, ili nikamilishe kila agizo ulilonipa kabla ya siku yangu kufika.

4. KAMILISHA KAZI YA UPONYAJI, UREJESHO NA AMANI NDANI YANGU

Ee Bwana, kuna majeraha ya ndani, huzuni za zamani, maumivu ya moyo, na magumu niliyopitia ambayo yameacha makovu moyoni.Najua hujaanza kazi ya uponyaji ili uiache nusu—kwa hiyo, kamilisha uponyaji wangu.
Niondolee mawazo ya hofu.
Nivunje vifungo vya kukata tamaa.
Nilinde na roho ya nguvu, upendo na moyo wa kiasi.

Nipe amani inayopita akili, amani ambayo dunia haiwezi kutoa, na ambayo hali zangu haziwezi kuiondoa.

5. KAMILISHA KAZI YA UKUAJI WA IMANI

Mungu wangu, ninahitaji imani imara. Imani ambayo haitaangushwa na hali.Imani inayoendelea kukua.
Imani inayoamini hata wakati haiwezi kuona.

Panua upeo wa imani yangu.
Nipe ujasiri mpya.
Niongezee nguvu ya kusimama juu ya ahadi zako bila kuyumbishwa.
Nifundishe kusimama juu ya neno lako kama msingi wa maisha yangu yote.

6. KAMILISHA KAZI YA UTUKUFU ULIOANZA NDANI YANGU

Asante Baba, kwa maana siku ya Kristo inaweza kuwa mbali au karibu, lakini ahadi yako ni ya hakika:kazi uliyoinza ndani yangu leo itaendelea hadi nitakapokutana na Bwana uso kwa uso.

Ninakuomba, Ee Mungu, katika siku zangu zote zilizosalia:

* Nipatie moyo wa kumtumaini Yesu
* Nipe maisha ya ushuhuda wa wema wako
* Nipe mwisho wa utukufu
* Na nifikishe salama katika safari yangu ya imani

Bwana, ninainua mikono yangu na moyo wangu kwako.
Ninakushukuru kwa sababu sitembei peke yangu.
Hakuna nguvu itakayozuia kazi yako ndani yangu.
Hakuna giza litakalozima nuru yako.
Hakuna mapito yatakayonifanya ushindwe.

Kwa hiyo nasema kwa imani: Ee Mungu, uliyeanza kazi njema ndani yangu—ikamilishe.Kwa uwezo wa Yesu Kristo. Amin.

The Nobel Peace Prize: Holy Grail of the Globalist Priesthood — A Satanic-Wrapped Weapon of Empire
⸻

The Nobel Peace Prize stopped being an award decades ago. It is now an instrument of the globalist Western cartel — a polished, gold-plated stamp of approval used to anoint the obedient, sanitize regime-change agents, and wrap imperial projects in the language of “democracy,” “rights,” and “peace.”

This institution does not stand above geopolitics.

It functions as a ceremonial arm of the global order, laundering the reputations of people who serve Western strategic interests while demonizing those who refuse to bow. It is the Vatican of secular imperialism — complete with rituals, symbolism, and global media absolution — except its religion is regime change, its scripture is Western foreign policy, and its “saints” are whoever Washington, Brussels, and Oslo decide are useful at the moment.

For over a century, the Nobel Peace Prize has been handed out like a baptismal certificate for empire — blessing wars, coups, sanctions warfare, and destabilization efforts behind the disguise of humanitarian virtue. You don’t win for bringing peace; you win for playing your assigned role in the architecture of Western domination.

The prize has honored drone commanders, warmakers, privatized humanitarians, architects of foreign invasions, and political operatives whose careers revolve around destabilizing the Global South. It rewards obedience, not courage; alignment, not morality; Western-approved democracy, not genuine sovereignty.

And nothing reveals this corruption more clearly than the latest page in their theater.

⸻
The Venezuelan Selection: A Case Study in Manufactured “Peace”

Watch the moment Ana collected the Nobel Prize on behalf of her mother, María Corina Machado — not as a celebration of peace, but as a funeral service for the last shreds of Nobel credibility.

Machado, canonized by Western powers as the champion of “democracy,” has a portfolio that reads like a résumé for CIA recruitment:

• Two failed coup attempts
• Participation in violent riots aimed at toppling a sovereign government
• Public calls for US military intervention in Venezuela
• Advocacy for apartheid Israel and foreign armies to attack her own country
• Loyal alignment with Washington’s maximum-pressure strategy

This is not Gandhi.
This is not Mandela.
This is a regime-change darling, sponsored, groomed, and protected by the same Western institutions that have spent the last century installing leaders, toppling governments, and redesigning entire nations to fit the needs of global capital.

To award her the Nobel Peace Prize is not an act of recognition —
it is an instruction.
A signal.
A message to the world:

“This is who we want to rule Venezuela. This is our chosen vessel. This is the person who will carry out our geopolitical interests in the region.”

The medal isn’t an honor — it’s a leash.

⸻

Nobel as an Extension of Empire

This is how the globalist architecture works:

1. Western governments identify an asset
Someone willing to undermine their own country’s sovereignty for Western “partnership.”

2. Western institutions legitimize the asset
Think tanks, NGOs, media platforms, and “human rights” organizations elevate them.

3. The Nobel Peace Prize seals the arrangement
Now the individual is consecrated by the global order — shielded from criticism, protected from scrutiny, and armed with international legitimacy.

4. Any opposition to that individual becomes “anti-democratic”

The West no longer needs evidence.
The prize itself becomes the argument.

5. Regime change narratives grow around the award like vines
Sanctions, foreign intervention, destabilization — all suddenly justified.

This is not peacekeeping.
This is geopolitical engineering disguised as virtue.

⸻

The Nobel Peace Prize Has Become a Weapon

It rewards:
• Destroying governments not aligned with the West
• Advocating sanctions that starve populations
• Supporting foreign military intervention
• Advancing Western geopolitical interests

It punishes:
• Sovereignty
• Non-alignment
• Independent foreign policy
• Leaders who refuse to kneel

Every medal is a message.
Every speech is a coded order.
Every televised ceremony is a ritual of empire dressed in academic robes.

⸻

The Moment Machado Won, the Mask Fell Off Completely

When the Nobel Committee decided to coronate a woman whose political legacy includes riots, coup attempts, and open calls for foreign military violence, they exposed themselves fully:

The Peace Prize is no longer about peace.
It is about obedience.
It is about empire.
It is about manufacturing legitimacy for Western intervention.
It is part of a globalist mafia network that baptizes its chosen operatives in gold and applause.

They can polish it.
They can dress it up.
They can play the orchestra and wave the Norwegian flag.

But the world saw it for what it was:

A ceremonial rubber stamp for Western regime change.
A relic of imperial mythology.
A prize that now serves only the architects of global domination.

The nail was already in the coffin.
Machado’s award simply lowered the lid — and hammered it shut

Adrienne Rich understood that truth is rarely solitary. It does not move through speeches alone.
It moves through permission.
When a woman tells the truth, she disrupts the silence others have been trained to protect. She
names what many recognize but have been warned never to say aloud. In doing so, she
changes the atmosphere.
Truth is contagious.
So is courage.
One voice challenges the idea that silence keeps us safe. It reveals that quiet often only
protects the status quo. As honesty enters the room, fear loosens its grip. What once felt
unspeakable begins to feel possible.
This is why truth telling is resisted. It spreads. It makes isolation harder to maintain. It reminds
people they are not alone in their experience or their doubt.
A woman who speaks honestly does more than describe reality. She alters it. Her words
become an opening others can step through.
The first truth does not fix everything.
But it creates space.
And in that space, more voices gather. More stories rise. More clarity forms.
Change does not always begin with consensus.
Sometimes it begins with one woman deciding to be precise instead of quiet.

Christmas lights and Pakistan’s colours illuminate a message of love and harmony
  By Anwar Iqbal 

WASHINGTON — The hall at the Pakistan Embassy glowed in Christmas colours on Saturday evening. Red and gold decorations framed the space, while green — the unmistakable green of Pakistan — appeared everywhere: in flags, ribbons, and lapel pins. White lights shimmered softly, echoing both the season and the crescent-and-star that defines the country these guests continue to call their own.

The pre-Christmas gathering, hosted for Pakistani Christians and their neighbours, began and ended with a chant that left little doubt about that bond: “Pakistan Zindabad.”

It was not a slogan offered for form’s sake. It was spoken with warmth, conviction, and an insistence born of long experience.

For more than a decade, speakers noted, such gatherings have brought together Muslims, Christians, Hindus, Sikhs and Jews — a quiet tradition of interfaith fellowship that has survived politics, violence and neglect. A message from the Virginia governor praised the organisers’ work over the past twelve years and encouraged the embassy to continue supporting initiatives that unite people across faiths.

Dr Srilekha Palle, an advisor to the Virginia governor, spoke of India and Pakistan as neighbours “so much alike,” expressing a hope to visit Pakistan one day. Loving one’s country, she said, was inseparable from faith itself: to love your homeland is to reflect your love of God.

Several speakers returned to that theme — patriotism without exclusion, faith without hierarchy.

  Pakistan's Deputy Ambassador Batool Kazim described the dinner as a long-standing tradition meant not only to celebrate Christmas but to welcome Christian brothers and sisters and their neighbours into a shared Pakistani space. Visits to Pakistan by members of the Christian diaspora, she said, often become moments of rediscovery — encounters that help them understand the country beyond headlines and fear, and help others see their place within it.

This, she said, was a time for reflection: on what had gone wrong, and on how the coming year might be made better — for everyone.

  Speakers stressed that pluralism and interfaith harmony were not borrowed ideas but a vital part of Pakistan’s national fabric. The contributions of Christians to education, healthcare and defence were acknowledged repeatedly, described not as favours but as facts — a source of collective pride. When Pakistani Christians live abroad, one speaker noted, they often become an unrecognised bridge between Pakistan and the West, carrying stories of both pain and belonging.

There were also references to law and responsibility: protecting minority rights, proposed legislation on minority commissions, and the need for collective will to translate words into protection.

  Pastor John Nuzum of Church of the Holy Spirit  offered a simple prayer, blessing both Pakistan and the United States. The Jewish-Islamic Dialogue Society of Washington also sent a representative, stressing the importance of sustained conversation across faiths, especially in times when identity is weaponised.

Throughout the evening, the mood remained warm — deliberately so. The reds and golds of Christmas blended with Pakistan’s green and white, mirroring the message speakers returned to again and again: faiths may differ, but citizenship should not.

That message carried an added weight because it echoed words written more than a decade ago, in moments of far darker national grief.

This evening was not about charity, tolerance, or exception. It was about belonging.

When the final prayers were offered and the gathering drew to a close, the chant rose again — unprompted, confident, almost defiant:

“Pakistan Zindabad.”

It came from voices that have known grief, accusation, and silence. It came from people who, despite everything done to them — and sometimes in their name — continue to claim the country as theirs.

Under red Christmas lights and Pakistan’s green and white, that claim felt both ordinary and extraordinary at once.

“Please, feel our attachment to Pakistan,” said the event’s organiser, Ilyas Masih. “Despite subzero temperatures, every seat in this large hall is occupied, and people are standing along the sidelines.”

"The Catholic Church does not reject anything true and holy found in other religions," for in them "reflects a ray of truth that illuminates all men."

With these words, Pope Leo XIV recalled, on the night of Tuesday, October 28, in Room Paul VI, the sixty years since the declaration of Nostra Aetate, dedicated to the relations of the Church with non-Christian religions. The event, with the theme "Walking Together in Hope", gathered about two thousand people and eighty representatives of the world's major religious traditions.

The Pope said in his speech that “authentic dialogue does not begin in the middle-term, but in the deep conviction of faith itself, which moves us to approach others with love.”

Recalling that Our Aetate “planted a seed of hope for interfaith dialogue”, Leo XIV said it became “a majestic tree, offering fruits of friendship and peace”. According to him, "dialogue is not a tactic, but a way of life, a path of the heart that transforms who speaks and who listens".

The Pope warned that Our Aetate's message is "more urgent than ever", in the face of a world marked by wars, poverty and division:

“As religious leaders, guided by the wisdom of our respective traditions, we share a sacred responsibility: to help our people break free from the chains of prejudice, anger, and hatred; to help them rise above selfishness and self-reference; to help them overcome the greed that destroys both the human soul and the soul.” earth. ”

In reference to the Jubilee of Hope, he invited everyone to "walk together":

"When we do, hearts open, bridges are built, and new paths emerge where it seemed impossible. It is a sacred task of all humanity — to keep hope, dialogue and love alive in the heart of the world. ”

The meeting ended with a moment of silent prayer. "Prayer has the power to transform our hearts and the world," concluded Pope Leo XIV, recalling a famous quote from Saint John Paul II: "If the world must go on, you cannot do without prayer. Before leaving Room Paul VI, the Pontiff greeted the religious leaders.

Thank you to my community for believing in the power of peace.  

The journey continues — and it’s only just begun.

Giuseppe Pinelli, railway worker and anarchist, was the leader of the Ponte della Ghisolfa Anarchist Circle. He died in Milan on the night of December 15 to 16, 1969, "falling" out of the window of the Milan police headquarters, where he was illegally held in connection with the investigation of the massacre at Piazza Fontana. 

On December 12, 1969, at 16:37 in Milan, a bomb exploded at the headquarters of Banca Nazionale dell'Agricoltura in Piazza Fontana, killing 16 people and injuring 88. At the same time more bombs exploded in Rome. Eventually, a bag with a bomb was found at Banca Commerciale in Milan, which was quickly detonated, eliminating valuable evidence in the investigation.
Immediately, demonstrating a previously accepted plan, the investigation, despite the lack of evidence, turned to anarchist traps. Commissioner Luigi Calabresi, already at 19:30 (three hours after the massacre), arrested several anarchists in front of the club at Via Scaldasole.

On the night of December 12 to 13, 1969, about 84 people were illegally arrested, including Giuseppe. On the evening of the 15th, after three days of uninterrupted interrogations, Pinelli died after falling from the fourth floor of the police headquarters. The police immediately reported through the police commissioner Marcello Guida (in 1942. Benito Mussolini's right-hand director of the Ventotene political arrest) that Pinelli fell down the stairs because "his alibi fell apart." A few days later, it was discovered that the ambulance had been called two seconds before midnight (two minutes before Pinelli's collapse). Moreover, the interview room measuring 3.56 by 4.40 meters, housing several closets and a desk, as well as the presence of six people, prevented Pinelli from accessing the window. It was strange that the window was open considering it was December and night. Pinelli fell while slipping on a gutter. So he didn't put in any effort; he fell without screaming and without raising his hands to cover his head, as if he was already still.

Nobel Dario Fo's book "The Accidental Death of an Anarchist" was dedicated to this terrible event.

NCTC Debunks Claims of Arming Socio-Cultural Groups, Urges Media Restraint on Counter-Terrorism Operations

The National Counter Terrorism Centre (NCTC), under the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA), has called on the media to exercise greater responsibility in reporting security matters, warning that inaccurate and unverified reports could compromise ongoing counter-terrorism operations.

In a statement issued by the Head of Strategic Communications, Abu I. Michael, the NCTC said recent reports by some online platforms necessitated clarification on counter-terrorism activities currently being conducted in parts of the country, particularly in forested areas of Kwara State.

The Centre reaffirmed that, in line with the Terrorism Prevention and Prohibition Act, 2022, it continues to coordinate and support law enforcement, security and intelligence agencies in tackling all forms of terrorism nationwide. It explained that Nigeria’s counter-terrorism framework, guided by the National Counter Terrorism Strategy (NACTEST), includes the deployment of hybrid forces combining regular security personnel with trained auxiliary elements such as hunters and vigilantes, especially in difficult terrains.

According to the NCTC, this hybrid approach is not new, noting its previous application in the North East where trained civilian volunteers under the Civilian Joint Task Force (CJTF) supported military operations against Boko Haram. The same strategy, it added, is currently being employed in parts of the North West and North Central to degrade the capabilities of bandit, criminal and terrorist groups, with recorded operational successes.

Addressing the situation in Kwara State, the Centre described media reports on the operations as inaccurate and misleading. It explained that limited public information on the exercise was deliberate due to the sensitive nature of the operations, aimed at preventing operational compromise and ensuring the safety of both security personnel and auxiliary forces.

“For the avoidance of doubt, the Federal Government and its agencies are not conducting kinetic operations with any socio-cultural groups,” the statement said. It also dismissed claims that the Office of the National Security Adviser had provided arms to any socio-cultural organisation, describing such assertions as false and unfounded.

The NCTC clarified that all auxiliary personnel involved in hybrid operations are recruited directly by authorised security and intelligence agencies following due diligence, and that all operations are conducted in strict adherence to the law and established standard operating procedures.

The Centre urged the public to disregard unverified reports that misrepresent the conduct of counter-terrorism operations, while calling on media organisations to protect sensitive security information and seek clarification through designated official spokespersons.

It reiterated its commitment to an open-door policy aimed at deepening stakeholder understanding of Nigeria’s counter-terrorism efforts.

CONFIDENTIAL MEMORANDUM

SUBJECT: Rebuttal to Press Release by the Government of the United Republic of Tanzania Concerning Engagement with the UN Secretary-General Following 29 October 2025 Events

Prepared for: UN Officials, Special Rapporteurs, Permanent Missions, and International Partners
Date: December 2025
Classification: For internal briefing and reference

1. Purpose of the Memorandum

This memorandum provides a factual and legal clarification in response to the press release issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and East African Cooperation of the United Republic of Tanzania dated 14 December 2025, concerning the alleged assessment by the UN Secretary-General of Tanzania’s conduct surrounding the General Elections of 29 October 2025.

The memorandum seeks to correct misleading impressions created by the release and to restate applicable international standards.

2. On the Nature of the UN Secretary-General’s Engagement

The press release implies international validation of the Government’s handling of the post-election period. This interpretation is inaccurate.

The UN Secretary-General:
•Received a message conveyed by a Special Envoy.
•Did not conduct an investigation, verification mission, or fact-finding exercise.
•Did not issue a determination regarding responsibility for violence or legality of state conduct.

Receipt of correspondence by the Secretary-General does not constitute endorsement, certification, or approval of the actions described therein. Diplomatic protocol must not be conflated with substantive validation.

3. On Claims of “Peace, Social Cohesion, and Stability”

International standards define peace not as the absence of visible unrest, but as the presence of:
•accountability for unlawful use of force,
•protection of civilian life,
•and respect for constitutional and human rights guarantees.

Credible reports indicate that on and after 29 October 2025:
•civilians were killed and injured by state security forces,
•excessive force was deployed against unarmed demonstrators,
•military units were deployed in civilian settings without transparent legal justification.

Such conditions are incompatible with internationally accepted definitions of peace and social cohesion.

4. On the Use of “National Dialogue” as a Remedial Measure

While dialogue may play a role in long-term reconciliation, it cannot substitute for accountability in cases involving:
•loss of life,
•grave bodily harm,
•or alleged violations of international human rights law.

International norms require that allegations of unlawful killings be addressed through:
•prompt, independent, impartial, and transparent investigations,
•identification of individual and command responsibility,
•and access to effective remedies for victims.

Dialogue without accountability risks entrenching impunity.

5. On the Commission of Inquiry Referenced

The Commission of Inquiry referenced in the press release raises concerns regarding independence and effectiveness.

Under international best practice, an inquiry must demonstrate:
•institutional independence from the executive implicated in alleged violations,
•operational autonomy over evidence and witnesses,
•protection mechanisms for victims and whistleblowers,
•public disclosure of findings and recommendations.

Absent these guarantees, such a commission cannot meet the threshold of a credible accountability mechanism under international law.

6. On the Risk of Narrative Misrepresentation

The framing of the press release risks:
•misrepresenting diplomatic engagement as substantive endorsement,
•obscuring unresolved allegations of serious violations,
•and undermining the credibility of international accountability processes.

Such misrepresentation complicates future engagement and risks eroding trust between the Government, its citizens, and international partners.

7. Conclusion

The events of 29 October 2025 remain unresolved from a legal and accountability perspective.

International engagement with the United Republic of Tanzania:
•should not be interpreted as absolution,
•does not negate the obligation to investigate alleged violations,
•and does not preclude future international scrutiny.

Sustainable peace and stability require truth, accountability, and institutional restraint, not reputational management through diplomatic communications.

Closing Note

The United Nations’ role is not to legitimize state narratives, but to uphold international law, protect human rights, and ensure that justice is neither deferred nor denied.

Jean Perrot: Born on December 19, 1861 in Tula (Limousin Lower, Occitania), the anarchist Jean Perrot was the son of Léger Perrot, journalist, and Jeanne Mugnier. Professional shipperman, he was mobilized on November 18, 1882 and integrated with the 38th Line Regiment, but transferred to the reserve in 1886. From 1892, he lived at 168 Avenue de Clichy in Paris. On July 1, 1894, his home was unsuccessfully searched by the police and he was arrested during an important raid, along with 154 other anarchists. The next day, July 2, 1894, he was registered as an "anarchist" in the anthropometric register of the Parisian police laboratory of Alphonse Bertillon. He then lived for a while in Bois-Colombes ( isle-de-France). On August 5, 1905, he was demobilized due to "arthritis of the left knee". The date and place of his death are unknown.

Burkina Faso has become a ‘Church on the move,’ says Catholic priest

In an interview with Crux, Father Patrickmary Afamefuna Dike outlines the dire reality facing the Catholic Church in the Diocese of Dori, Burkina Faso, where extremist violence has forced the closure of parishes and the abandonment of historic buildings.
The situation is summarized by the following key themes:
1. A Crisis Beyond Religion
While extremist groups target visible symbols of the Church to dismantle social order, Father Dike emphasizes that this is not purely religious persecution. The violence stems from a collapse of state authority, extreme poverty, and environmental pressures. Both Muslims and Christians are suffering, and the Church views the crisis as a broader rejection of human dignity rather than a simple interfaith conflict.
2. From Buildings to "The Church on the Move"
With many rural areas now inaccessible or under militant control, the Church has shifted its strategy to remain resilient:
 * Relocation: Pastoral activities have moved to safer hubs like Dori.
 * Lay Leadership: Catechists and laypeople now lead prayer services and Sunday gatherings where priests cannot travel.
 * Technology: Radio broadcasts are used to reach the faithful in isolated or displaced communities.
 * Humanitarian Focus: Through Caritas, the Church prioritizes aid for the displaced, regardless of their faith.
3. Root Causes and Future Challenges
Father Dike identifies the "evolution of insecurity" from isolated incidents to permanent territorial instability. He warns that the next decade poses risks of generational trauma, permanent displacement, and radicalization fueled by despair.
4. A Message of Resilience
Despite the silence of the church bells in towns like Sebba and Gorgadji, the Church's mission has adapted. By focusing on interreligious dialogue and trauma healing, they aim to act as a bridge of peace. The ultimate goal remains a return to their homes, holding onto the hope that "the bells will ring again."

*We Leave Home to Build a Home” Turns Into a Painful Reality for Young Kenyan Woman;

We leave home to build a home” is a phrase often used by young people who travel far in search of better opportunities, hoping to uplift their families. For a young Kenyan woman identified as Trixie, this belief shaped one of the most painful chapters of her life.

After finishing high school and failing to secure a job in Kenya, Trixie decided to seek work abroad. With the help of a sponsor, she obtained a visa and travelled to Dubai, determined to change her family’s fortunes and make her mother proud.

In Dubai, Trixie worked for two years, faithfully sending money home to her mother. Her dream was to build her a modern house and move her out of the semi-permanent home she had known all her life. To achieve this, she sacrificed time with loved ones and saved every possible coin.

By the time her contract ended, the house had been completed, and Trixie returned to Kenya hopeful and proud. She was warmly welcomed at first, but the joy did not last long. Having sent most of her earnings home, the little money she returned with was soon exhausted.

That was when her life began to unravel.

Trixie said her mother’s attitude towards her changed drastically. She claimed her mother constantly criticised her, picked fights, and insulted her, leaving even neighbors confused by the sudden tension in the household.

“She changed so much. Every day she came home from work, there would be chaos,” Trixie recalled.

With no income and no support from friends, Trixie fell into deep depression. At one point, she said she went days without food and sought prayers from a man of God, only to be asked to pay tithe before receiving help.

Three months after her return, matters worsened when her mother told her to leave the house.

“She told me to leave and never come back. I was heartbroken after everything I had sacrificed for her,” Trixie said, noting that her mother still had money, worked regularly, and lived comfortably while she struggled emotionally and financially.

By the fourth month, Trixie was forced to pack her belongings and leave. She claimed her mother disowned her completely, denying she was her daughter.

Unknown to her mother, Trixie had already applied for a work visa. Days after being chased out, she received confirmation that her visa had been approved. She soon secured a job in Qatar, and hope finally returned.

On the day she left, she quietly packed her bags and departed without revealing her destination.

“I met her at the gate as I was leaving. When she asked where I was going, I said nothing and boarded a boda boda to the bus stage,” she said.

Now living and working in Qatar, Trixie revealed that her mother never tried to look for her. Six months later, she received a brief WhatsApp message with no apology—just casual conversation.

“I replied with a simple ‘hi.’ I now know my place in her life,” Trixie said.

Nearly two years on, the two have not spoken again.

“I consider myself homeless and an orphan until further notice,” she concluded.
