Sometimes all moms need is peace and quiet after a long day.

No phone calls.
No replying to messages.
No explaining.

Just silence that feels safe.
A room that finally slows down.
A moment to breathe without being needed.

It’s not ignoring people.
It’s recharging after pouring yourself into everyone else all day.

Calm isn’t selfish.
It’s survival.

And some nights
quiet is the kindest thing you can give yourself.

As a mom, I’ve learned that protecting my peace is not selfish.
It’s responsible.

My nervous system sets the tone of our home.
My calm becomes their calm.
My overwhelm spills into their little worlds whether I want it to or not.

So when something or someone brings constant chaos, drama, or heaviness into my life, I step back. Not out of anger. Not to punish. But out of love.

Because when my mind isn’t calm, my patience thins.
When my heart feels heavy, my presence suffers.
And my children deserve a version of me that is steady, safe, and available.

I don’t owe access to anyone who disrupts the peace I work hard to protect.
My kids don’t need to grow up watching their mom tolerate emotional noise for the sake of politeness.

They need a home that feels soft.
A mom who can breathe.
A space where calm is the baseline, not the reward after surviving chaos.

Protecting my peace is part of protecting them.
And I will always choose that.

🇺🇦Ukraine took second-to-last place in the Global Peace Index, with Russia in last place.

The Global Peace Index (GPI), developed by the Institute for Economics and Peace (IEP), ranks the world's leading measure of global peacefulness. It covers 99.7% of the world's population and calculates rankings based on 23 indicators across three domains: societal safety and security, ongoing domestic and international conflicts, and degree of militarization.

Ukraine ranked 162nd out of 163 countries, receiving the lowest scores in areas such as:

▪access to weapons
▪intensity of internal conflict
▪arms imports
▪deaths from internal conflicts
▪military expenditures
▪refugees and IDPs
▪relations with neighboring countries

Russia ranked last (163rd), with the lowest scores in parameters including nuclear and heavy weapons, relations with neighboring countries, and deaths from external conflict.
Other key findings from the index:
▪️The top 5 most peaceful countries are: Iceland, Ireland, New Zealand, Austria, and Switzerland.
▪️Global peace is at its lowest level since the index's creation (with deteriorations in recent years).
▪️Preconditions for armed conflicts are the worst since World War II.
▪️There are currently 59 active state-based conflicts — the highest number since the end of World War II.
Note: These rankings directly reflect the ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine, which has significantly impacted both countries' scores in conflict-related and militarization indicators. The 2025 GPI report highlights a continued global decline in peacefulness.

MANENO YA MZEE WARIOBA HAYANA UPONYAJI KWA TAIFA, VIPI KUHUSU HOTUBA ZA RAIS NA WAZIRI MKUU ZINAPONYA?

Na George Kabadi

Kumekuwa na shutuma toka kwa watetezi wa serikali dhidi ya waziri mkuu mstaafu Jaji Joseph Sinde Warioba kuhusu matamshi yake ya kukosoa mwenendo mbovu wa serikali kabla na baada ya uchaguzi mkuu wa 29 October 2025, madai ya mzee Warioba kwa lugha rahisi ni serikali ilishiriki kuchochea kinachoitwa vurugu za October 29, vyombo vya dola vilitumia nguvu kubwa kuwathibiti wananchi hali iliyopelekea watu wengi kupoteza maisha, idadi ya kutisha kuzidi watu waliyopoteza maisha katika vita ya Kagera ya 1978-1979, pia akidai Bunge la 12 ndiyo Bunge la hovyo kuliko mabunge yote tangu tupate Uhuru. 

Mzee Warioba amesema kilicho mioyoni mwa wengi, kumshutumu ni kutokukubaliana na ukweli wa njia sahihi ya kumrudia Mwenyezi Mungu ni kutubu kwa kusema ukweli, hatuwezi kuliponya taifa, tukiwa tumeweka pamba masikioni, hatuwezi kuliponya taifa ikiwa viongozi hawataki kujitafakari na hatuwezi kuridhiana maridhiano ya kisiasa bila kuwashirikisha wananchi ambao ndiyo wahanga.

Tuweke mizania sawa, tutafakari ili kupata uzito wa madhara ya kauli za Rais Samia, Waziri Mkuu Mwigulu na Mzee Warioba kabla na baada ya October 29.
1. Rais Samia akiwa katika kampeni za uchaguzi, alilitaka Jeshi likae tayari wakati tukielekea katika uchaguzi, kauli iliyotafsiriwa kama kulihusisha Jeshi na siasa, kauli  iliyopingwa vikali na wananchi, wanasiasa, wadau wa maendeleo na viongozi wastaafu akiwemo mzee Warioba. Utata wa kauli ya Rais, ulitoa ishara ya uwepo wa utawala wa kijeshi katika vazi la ki raia, kwani wagombea wa upinzani waliondolewa katika kinyang'anyiro cha uchaguzi na serikali kupitia mwanasheria mkuu wa serikali ikimuwekea pingamizi Luhaga Mpina aliyekuwa akiomba ridhaa ya Urais kwa tiketi ya chama cha Act-Wazalendo, huku Jeshi la Police lilijihusisha na kuwashughulikia wapinzani wa Rais Samia katika mchakato wa uchaguzi vijana wengi wa upinzani walikamatwa na kuwekwa mahabusu muda mrefu bila kufikishwa mahakamani.

Baada ya uchaguzi mkuu wa October 29, kugubikwa na maandamano yaliyogeuka kuwa makabiliano ya vyombo vya dola na raia, wengi walipoteza maisha na wengi zaidi wakiathirika, hata hivyo Rais Samia wakati akipokea cheti cha ushindi kutoka kwa tume ya uchaguzi, alivikingia kifua vyombo vya Ulinzi na Usalama.
1. Rais Samia alisema waandamanaji walitoka nje ya nchi, wamelipwa hata hivyo misiba na vilio vibaki nchi kwake kwa kuwapoteza watu mashuhuri kama Shekhe Sharifu Majini na Master Tindwa.

2. Katika siku ya kuapishwa kwake, Rais Samia aliyatuhumu mataifa ya magharibi na wanaharakati kwa kuchochea vurugu, alidai vijana walilipwa ili kuingia barabarani, huku akitambua wazi rundo la changamoto zinazowakabili vijana wa taifa analoliongoza.

3. Kwa mtazamo wangu rais tangu aapishwe hadi sasa naweza kusema; Rais hajatoa hotuba hata moja ya kuliponya taifa, isipokuwa hotuba zake nyingi hujaa mihemko ya kisiasa, vijembe na kashfa dhidi ya wapinzani wake, licha ya kuunda tume ya kuchunguza yaliyotokea kabla na baada ya uchaguzi, cha kusikitisha hotuba yake siku  akiongea na wazee wa Dar es salaam aliongea kana kwamba tume ilishatoa ripoti ya uchunguzi.

Kwa muono wangu, mtu wa kwanza anayepaswa kutoa mwelekeo wa taifa na kauli za kuponya mioyo ya watu ni Rais, kutokukiri mapungufu ya serikali yake ni ishara ya yeye Rais kukwepa uwajibikaji, jambo ambalo wengi wanaona rais hayupo tayari kuona taifa likipata suluhu.

Waziri Mkuu Mwigulu Nchemba pia amekuwa na mwendelezo ule ule wa kutokukubali makosa ya serikali, badala yake amekuwa akivishutumu baadhi ya vyama haswa Chadema kwa kusababisha yaliyotokea,  hotuba zake nyingi hujaa propaganda, bila kuonyesha daraja la kulivusha taifa.

Ushauri wangu ni serikali iachane na propaganda za kufikri matatizo yetu yanatokana na vita ya uchumi, Tanzania tuna madini ya Tanzanite hayapo sehemu yoyote duniani isipokuwa kwetu tumechimba miaka nenda rudi kwanini hatukuwahi kuuana, tunauamana kwa sababu kuna wanaofikri uongozi wa taifa hili ni haki yao.

Kwa mantiki hiyo nakubaliana kwa kutokukumbaliana na matamshi ya mzee Warioba kwa sababu viongozi wa serikali hawaonyeshi kujutia, kujisahihisha wala kuonyesha juhudi za kulirejesha taifa katika umoja, ni dhahiri Udini umetamaraki nchini wala haulaniwi huku wapambe wa serikali wakifikri Rais Samia anakosolewa kwa sababu ya Jinsia au dini yake jambo ambalo si kweli, bali anakosolewa kama kiongozi wa taifa la kidemokrasia.

Kosa inaloendelea kulifanya serikali ni kuruhusu isemewe na watu wasiyo na akili, hali inayoendelea kuchochea chuki za wananchi dhidi ya serikali, badala ya kuzima, tunawasha kwani si kweli kwamba tunapaswa kuwa na taifa linalochukia ukweli, amani isitumike kama kivuli cha kufunika haki, nitanukuu; "Naomba kuthubutu kusema kwamba Watanzania wengi hawashabikii haki siyo wadau wa haki, Watanzania wengi kwa ujinga au kutokujua wanajidai wadau wa amani," amesema Askofu Rwa'ichi wa Jimbo kuu katoliki la Dar es salaam.

Mapambano ya watetezi wa serekali aliyokuwa wakilishambulia Kanisa Katoliki, yamehamia kwa Mzee Warioba, hata hivyo haiondoi ukweli kwamba Rais na Waziri Mkuu bado hawajaamua nchi itokeje ilipo, hatuwezi kutoka tulipo ikiwa chawa wameachiwa kuisemea serikali, Polisi wameachiwa wakamate watu kwa sababu ya Itikadi za ki siasa. To my busy mom who’s wondering if she’s even cut out for this…Let me gently remind you of something important…no one else can mother your children the way you can. Not one person in the world has your voice, your instincts, your love, or your unique way of showing up. You were chosen for this family, these kids, and this season for a reason. It’s okay to feel tired. It’s okay to feel overwhelmed. Being busy doesn’t mean you give up…it means you’re carrying a lot. And questioning yourself doesn’t make you a bad mom…it means you care deeply about doing this well. So when the noise in your mind gets loud and the mental blocks start stacking up, that’s often your cue to pause…not quit. Inner peace isn’t about having a perfect life or perfectly behaved kids. It’s about learning how to calm your nervous system, breathe through the stress, and meet challenges with a little more clarity and compassion…for yourself. Even small moments of grounding, quiet reflection, or intentional breathing can help you reset. When your mind feels steadier, those challenges that once felt impossible become more manageable. And you begin to trust yourself again.

Girl, your kids don’t need a flawless mom. They need their mom…present, loving, learning, and growing right alongside them. And that mom…She’s already doing better than she thinks. Give yourself some credit! Okay! 🫶🏻 you! Bye!

Mirwaiz Office Fires Back: 'Opportunists' Twist X Bio tweak into betrayal of Kashmir's soul

Rejects 'Abandonment' narrative; Stresses accountability before Allah and J&K

Srinagar, December 26: In a pointed rebuke to what it terms a "vicious stretch of imagination," the Office of the Mirwaiz has issued a stern statement condemning attempts by a "coterie of opportunists" to portray the removal of the Hurriyat Conference chairperson designation from Mirwaiz Umar Farooq's X handle as a betrayal of his lifelong principles. 

The clarification comes amid a flurry of social media commentary that has sought to equate the administrative tweak with an abandonment of the separatist alliance's core ideals of dialogue and resolution for the Kashmir conflict.

The statement, attributed to Mirwaiz Manzil – the historic seat of Kashmir's chief cleric and a symbol of moral authority in the Valley – underscores that the change was a procedural matter, fully explained in prior communications from Mirwaiz Umar Farooq himself. 

"The attempt to twist this into abandonment of principle is both misleading and mala fide," it asserts, calling out the "moralising" narrative as a deliberate distortion designed to sow discord.

At the heart of the defense is an invocation of legacy and accountability. Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, a towering figure in Kashmiri resistance and interfaith dialogue, is portrayed not as beholden to fleeting critics, but to the "people of J&K and to Allah – who will judge him for his conduct and intentions." 

This spiritual and communal framing elevates the response beyond petty politicking, reminding detractors of the profound trust placed in the Mirwaiz institution by generations enduring "one crisis after another for decades."

The statement's tone turns poignant when addressing the human cost of such campaigns. It laments the "pain, confusion and dismay" inflicted on a populace already "in the grind" – families shattered by conflict, youth stifled by uncertainty, and communities scarred by decades of unrest. 

"It is regrettable that in their desperation to target the Mirwaiz personally, these individuals show little concern for" this collective anguish, the Office notes, framing the attacks as not just personal but profoundly irresponsible.

In a gesture blending admonition with grace, the Mirwaiz Office urges restraint: "Refrain from further vitiating the public atmosphere by creating doubts and misgivings where none exist." Yet, even in rebuke, there is an olive branch – a prayer that these critics, in pursuing "political ambitions to come to power," might channel their energies toward "genuinely serving the people of Jammu and Kashmir," rather than personal gain.

This episode unfolds against a backdrop of evolving dynamics in Kashmir's fractured political landscape, where symbols like social media bios carry outsized weight in the absence of broader platforms for discourse. The Hurriyat Conference, once a unified front for azadi, has splintered amid arrests, exiles, and shifting allegiances post-Article 370's abrogation in 2019. Mirwaiz Umar Farooq's house arrest during much of that period only amplified his symbolic resonance as a voice for peaceful resolution.

As winter blankets the Valley in silence, this clarion call from Mirwaiz Manzil serves as both shield and salve – defending a leader's integrity while pleading for a politics that heals, not harms. In a land where words are weapons and whispers can ignite storms, the message resonates: True service to Kashmir demands truth, not torsion.

Voices of Peace in a Land of Many Beliefs, FGA Cristmas Celebration

By Dr.  Farhat Abbas Shah 
Pakistan is a pluralistic society where people of different religions, cultures, and traditions have lived together for centuries. The spirit of interfaith harmony and brotherhood is deeply rooted in the social fabric of the country and is essential for peace, stability, and national cohesion. In a time when societies across the world are facing polarization, intolerance, and religious misunderstandings, Pakistan’s need for dialogue, mutual respect, and coexistence among faith communities has become even more critical. Interfaith initiatives help dispel misconceptions, reduce social divides, and strengthen the collective identity of the nation. Literary, cultural, and musical gatherings play a particularly important role in this process, as they provide a peaceful space where ideas, emotions, and shared human values transcend religious boundaries. Such events remind society that compassion, love, and service to humanity are common teachings across all faiths.

In this spirit, on the blessed occasion of Christmas, a Christmas Mushaira and Musical Evening was organized under the auspices of the esteemed Christian institution Full Gospel Assembly. The annual event was hosted and supervised by Chairman Full Gospel Assembly, Reverend Liaqat Qaiser, along with his dedicated and well-organized team. The gathering brought together representatives from Muslim, Hindu, Sikh, and Christian communities, as well as prominent religious scholars, poets, artists, intellectuals, social workers, and members of civil society. Their collective presence and active participation presented a powerful and living example of interfaith harmony, mutual respect, tolerance, and national unity in Pakistan.

The event was marked not only by its literary and musical richness but also by its inclusive atmosphere. People belonging to different faiths sat side by side, listening attentively to poetry and music, engaging in conversation, and sharing the joy of celebration. This atmosphere reflected the broader message of the evening: that diversity is not a weakness but a strength, and that peaceful coexistence is possible when respect and understanding guide social interaction.

While welcoming the guests, Reverend Liaqat Qaiser expressed heartfelt gratitude to all participants and attendees for making the event meaningful and successful. In his address, he emphasized that Christmas is not only a religious festival for Christians but also a universal message of peace, love, and hope for all humanity. Quoting verses from the Bible, he shed light on the teachings of Jesus Christ (Peace Be Upon Him), highlighting that the core message of Jesus is based on love for humanity, compassion for the weak, forgiveness, humility, and service to mankind. He noted that these values are not confined to any single religion but resonate deeply with the ethical teachings of Islam and other faiths as well.

Reverend Liaqat Qaiser further stated that in today’s troubled world, where violence, hatred, and intolerance often dominate public discourse, the teachings of Jesus Christ offer a moral compass for humanity. He stressed that religious leaders and institutions have a collective responsibility to promote peace, discourage extremism, and encourage dialogue among communities. He also reaffirmed Full Gospel Assembly’s commitment to working for interfaith harmony, social welfare, and national unity, emphasizing that Pakistan belongs equally to all its citizens, regardless of faith.

The Mushaira segment of the evening was presided over by renowned Christian poet Nazir Qaiser, whose literary stature and thoughtful presence added intellectual depth to the gathering. The Mushaira featured a wide range of poets from different religious and cultural backgrounds, each contributing their creative expressions to the collective narrative of peace and human connection. Poet Farhat Abbas Shah, singer Adeel Barki, and classical music legend Perviaz Paris attended as special guests, further enhancing the prestige of the event.

A large number of poets presented their poetic tributes, including Adeel Barki, Perviaz Paris, Toqeer Ahmad Sharifee, Rabia Rehman, Dr. Ponam Noreen Gondal, Aftab Javeed, Dawood, Nasir Masih, Waris Hundavi, Stella Zafar, Arslan Christy, Ezaz Haroon, Irfan Nishat Chudhary, Javeed Daniel, Munir Bhatti, Tariq Javeed Tariq, David Parsi, Naveed Anjum, Ali Sadaf, Farhan Lala, Dr. Adil Amin, Zahid Jarpalvi, Ahtsham Ahsan, Khalid Emmanuel, Naseer Ahmad, and Abbas Mirza. Each poet brought a unique voice, style, and perspective, yet their themes converged around shared human emotions and values.

The poetry presented during the Mushaira reflected hope, peace, tolerance, love, spiritual reflection, and the sanctity of human relationships. Some poems explored the pain caused by hatred and division, while others celebrated unity, empathy, and the beauty of coexistence. Several poets emphasized the idea that humanity itself is a shared religion, and that love for mankind should be the ultimate guiding principle. The attentive audience responded with warmth and appreciation, creating a vibrant and emotionally resonant literary environment.

Following the Mushaira, the Musical Evening added another layer of spiritual and cultural depth to the celebration. The musical session was presided over by maestro Perviaz Paris, whose lifelong contributions to classical and spiritual music were widely acknowledged and admired by the audience. Javed Gabriel attended as the chief guest and expressed appreciation for the efforts of Full Gospel Assembly in organizing such a meaningful and inclusive event.

Vocal performances were delivered by Nazia Younas, Jainte Youhana, Abia, Nobel Shahzad, Malvin Mall, and Javed Gabriel. Their soulful renditions, blending spiritual devotion with artistic expression, captivated the audience and created an atmosphere of serenity and joy. The songs carried messages of love, peace, faith, and hope, resonating deeply with listeners from all religious backgrounds.

Instrumental accompaniment was skillfully provided by Solo on Tabla, Waqas on Tabla, and Ufaaz Naseem on Swarmandal. Their refined and sensitive musical support enhanced the overall impact of the performances, adding rhythm, depth, and emotional texture to the evening. The harmonious blend of vocals and instruments elevated the musical session into a spiritually uplifting experience.

Throughout the event, it became evident that the Christmas Mushaira and Musical Evening was not merely a cultural or artistic gathering, but a purposeful and symbolic initiative. It served as a platform to promote interfaith harmony, mutual love, respect, unity, and peaceful coexistence. The event highlighted the collective ability of people from diverse faiths, languages, and cultural backgrounds to come together for a shared cause: the betterment of society and the promotion of peace.

Participants and attendees repeatedly emphasized that such gatherings are essential in countering narratives of division and intolerance. By celebrating each other’s festivals, listening to one another’s creative expressions, and engaging in respectful dialogue, communities can build trust and understanding. The event also sent a strong message that Pakistan’s cultural and spiritual heritage is enriched by its diversity, and that interfaith harmony is both a moral responsibility and a national strength.

The ceremony concluded with the cutting of a Christmas cake, symbolizing shared joy and unity, followed by a special prayer for the country, global peace, and the welfare of humanity. Religious leaders and participants prayed collectively for harmony, stability, and prosperity, reinforcing the idea that despite differences in belief, the aspirations of peace and well-being are universal.

In essence, the Christmas Mushaira and Musical Evening organized by Full Gospel Assembly stood out as a memorable and meaningful celebration. It reflected the true spirit of Christmas, rooted in love, compassion, and service to humanity, while also embodying Pakistan’s ideals of brotherhood and coexistence. The event left a lasting impression on all who attended, reaffirming faith in the power of culture, literature, and music to bridge divides and bring hearts closer together.

Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, a towering figure in Kashmiri resistance and interfaith dialogue, is portrayed not as beholden to fleeting critics, but to the "people of J&K and to Allah – who will judge him for his conduct and intentions." 

This spiritual and communal framing elevates the response beyond petty politicking, reminding detractors of the profound trust placed in the Mirwaiz institution by generations enduring "one crisis after another for decades."

In a gesture blending admonition with grace, the Mirwaiz Office urges restraint: "Refrain from further vitiating the public atmosphere by creating doubts and misgivings where none exist." Yet, even in rebuke, there is an olive branch – a prayer that these critics, in pursuing "political ambitions to come to power," might channel their energies toward "genuinely serving the people of Jammu and Kashmir," rather than personal gain.

This episode unfolds against a backdrop of evolving dynamics in Kashmir's fractured political landscape, where symbols like social media bios carry outsized weight in the absence of broader platforms for discourse. The Hurriyat Conference, once a unified front for azadi, has splintered amid arrests, exiles, and shifting allegiances post-Article 370's abrogation in 2019. Mirwaiz Umar Farooq's house arrest during much of that period only amplified his symbolic resonance as a voice for peaceful resolution.

As winter blankets the Valley in silence, this clarion call from Mirwaiz Manzil serves as both shield and salve – defending a leader's integrity while pleading for a politics that heals, not harms. In a land where words are weapons and whispers can ignite storms, the message resonates: True service to Kashmir demands truth, not torsion.

ထို့နောက် သိက္ခာတော်ရ ဆရာဒေါက်တာအေးမင်းမှ ခရစ္စမတ် သတင်းစကားပြောကြားခဲ့ပြီး ဗဟို နာယက ဒေါက်တာ ညွန့်လှ(ခရစ်ယာန်ဘာသာ)မှ ခရစ္စမတ် ဓမ္မသီချင်း သီဆို၍ အထူးဆုတောင်းစကားပြောကြားခဲ့သည်။
ဆက်လက်၍ ဗဟို အလုပ်အမှုဆောင် ဒေါက်တာ သိန်းသန်းထွန်းမှ ခရစ္စမတ် အထူးဆုတောင်းခဲ့ပြီး

ဆက်လက်ပြီး သိက္ခာတော်ရ ဆရာစပ်ဖမှ ကောင်းချီးဆုတောင်းပေးခဲ့ပြီး ကရင်နှစ်ခြင်းအသင်း တော် ဥက္ကဋ္ဌ ဆရာဦးလှအောင်မှ အစားအသောက်အတွက် ကျေးဇူးတော် ချီးမွမ်းဆုတောင်းပေးခဲ့၍ ဗဟိုဒုတိယဥက္ကဋ္ဌ ဦးအောင်ဇော်ဝင်းမှ သင်္ဃန်းကျွန်းခရိုင် ဘာသာပေါင်းစုံချစ်ကြည်ညီညွတ်ရေးအဖွဲ့သို့ ရန်ပုံငွေကျပ်သိန်း(၅၀) ပေးအပ် လှူဒါန်းခဲ့ပြီးအခမ်းအနားသို့ တက်ရောက်လာသော ဧည့်သည်တော်များအား ခရစ္စမတ် ဂုဏ်ပြုညစာဖြင့် တည်ခင်း ဧည့်ခံခဲ့ကြောင်း သိရသည်။

Third Christmas Festival Held by Thingangyun District Myanmar Interfaith Dialogue Organization

December 27, 2025

The Third Christmas Festival Ceremony, organized by the Myanmar Interfaith Dialogue Organization (Thingangyun District), was held in a lively and festive atmosphere on the evening of December 27, 2025, at the compound of the Evangelical Theological College, located on Weizayanta Inner Road, Section (Z) South Ward, Thingangyun Township, Yangon.

The ceremony was attended by Dr. Nyunt Hla (Christian Affairs), Central Patron of the Myanmar Interfaith Dialogue Organization; Dr. Tu Tu (Christian Affairs), Central Vice Chairperson; U Aung Zaw Win (Islamic Affairs), Central Vice Chairperson; Dr. Aye Min, Honorary Patron of the Yangon Region Myanmar Interfaith Dialogue Organization; U Win Myint, Chairperson of the Yangon Region Organization; executive committee members; chairpersons and members from Thingangyun District and townships; specially invited guests; and Christian clergy, families, and fellowship members.

The program commenced with the singing of Christmas hymns by the Peace Church Choir, followed by an opening prayer offered by Reverend U Taik Chhun Sein.

Subsequently, Christmas greetings were delivered by Dr. Tu Tu, Central Vice Chairperson (Christian Affairs); U Aung Zaw Win, Central Vice Chairperson (Islamic Affairs); and U Win Myint, Chairperson of the Yangon Region Organization. Christmas hymns were then presented by Grace Evangelical Church, Shalom Church, Naw April Htun, and Daw Linda Grace.

Following this, a Christmas message was delivered by Reverend Dr. Aye Min, after which Dr. Nyunt Hla, Central Patron (Christian Affairs), sang a Christmas hymn and offered a special prayer. A further special Christmas prayer was led by Dr. Thein Than Tun, Central Executive Member.

The Chairperson and executive members of the Thingangyun District Myanmar Interfaith Dialogue Organization then presented commemorative Christmas gifts to distinguished guests in attendance.

Afterward, the Emmanuel Church of Thingangyun Township performed Christmas hymns, and U Kyaw Syi Thu, Chairperson of the Thingangyun District Organization, delivered a vote of thanks. This was followed by a blessing prayer offered by Reverend Sapha, and a thanksgiving prayer for the meal by Reverend U Hla Aung, Chairperson of the Karen Baptist Church.

During the event, U Aung Zaw Win, Central Vice Chairperson, donated MMK 5 million to the Thingangyun District Myanmar Interfaith Dialogue Organization as a fundraising contribution. The ceremony concluded successfully with a Christmas honorary dinner hosted for all attending guests.

"On December 30, 2025, King Charles III became the first British monarch to participate in formal prayer alongside a reigning Pope within the sacred walls of the Sistine Chapel, kneeling beneath Michelangelo's 'The Last Judgment' fresco as Pope Leo XIV led Midday Prayer in a ceremony that symbolically healed wounds dating back to 1570 when Pope Pius V excommunicated Queen Elizabeth I and declared her subjects released from allegiance to the Crown. The historic Vatican state visit, only the second full state visit by a British monarch to the Holy See following Queen Elizabeth II's groundbreaking 2014 visit to Pope Francis, showcased Charles's lifelong commitment to ecumenical dialogue and his revolutionary vision of the monarchy as a unifying force across all faith traditions rather than solely defending Anglican Christianity. Charles, who has studied Islamic architecture, visited Orthodox monasteries, attended Jewish synagogue services, and hosted Hindu and Sikh leaders at Buckingham Palace throughout his decades as Prince of Wales, brought this same interfaith sensitivity to his meeting with Pope Leo XIV, with palace officials revealing the two leaders had been corresponding privately for months on shared concerns about environmental degradation, forced migration, and the persecution of Christians in the Middle East and Africa. My husband had a habit of ending every serious argument the same way.
He wouldn’t shout.
He wouldn’t threaten.
He would simply adjust his shirt, pick up his phone, and say:

“Don’t be here when I come back.”

The words were simple.
But they ruled me.

Not because I lacked strength.
Because I carried a fear that had followed me since girlhood.

I grew up in a house built on my mother’s silence and survival.
She walked away from a violent man and raised us alone.
People did not applaud her courage.
They called her names.
They reduced her to gossip.
They measured her life and found it wanting.

I watched her break and rebuild herself every day.
I also watched the world refuse to forgive her for choosing life.

So I made a promise that hardened inside me:
I would never be the woman who returned home with her marriage in pieces.

Years later, I repeated that promise to the man who became my husband.
I told him on a quiet evening when love still lived between us.
I trusted him with my scars.
I didn’t know I was sharpening his weapons.

Marriage did not collapse all at once.
It thinned out slowly.

He stopped carrying responsibility.
Bills became my burden.
Meals came from my earnings.

I learned how to manage money, patience, and hope.

Sometimes his relatives stayed for days.
They treated my kitchen like a hotel and my heart like it didn’t matter.
I smiled.
I cooked.
I kept the peace.

When I finally spoke — careful, respectful, exhausted — he laughed.
“You make problems out of nothing,” he said.
“If it’s too much, you’re free to leave.”

There it was again.

I became quieter.
Smaller.
Better at hiding bruises that weren’t always on my skin.

One evening, he reached for the money I had saved for rent.
I told him no.
The room changed.
His voice rose.
Then his hand.

My children’s cries filled the house before my own pain did.

As he walked out, he tossed the words over his shoulder:
“Be gone before I return.”

I sank to the floor and pulled my children close.
My face throbbed.
My body shook.
But something in me was still.

I did not weep.
I did not plead with heaven.
I did not ask what I had done wrong.

For the first time, I said to myself:

This ends here.

Yet fear stood at the doorway — the old fear, the familiar one.
The fear of becoming the woman I had sworn I would never be.

The question waited with me in the silence:

Would I finally choose my life… or continue surviving inside it?

By the time the police called her, the rain had already washed most of the blood away.
Nkiru stood in her kitchen, holding a cup of tea she hadn’t touched, listening to the officer explain that her younger sister, Amara, had been found dead in an abandoned building on the edge of town.
Stab wounds.
No ID.
No witnesses.
But her name was on the sister’s lips when she died.
“We just need you to come in and identify the body,” the officer said gently.
Nkiru agreed. Her voice didn’t shake. That surprised her.
She dressed slowly, carefully. Black trousers. A grey sweater. The kind of outfit people wore when they wanted to look like grief hadn’t completely undone them.
As she locked her door, her phone buzzed.
Unknown number:
You promised you wouldn’t leave me there.
Her fingers went numb.
She deleted the message without replying.
At the morgue, the air smelled of bleach and something older. The attendant pulled back the sheet.
Amara’s face was swollen, lips slightly parted, eyes closed like she was finally resting. There was a thin line across her throat where the knife had kissed before sinking deeper.
Nkiru stared.
No tears came.
“She was found with this,” the officer said, placing a small, muddy phone in an evidence bag. “It was smashed, but we recovered one message draft.”
He hesitated before reading it aloud.

“She was found with this,” the officer said, placing a small, muddy phone in an evidence bag. “It was smashed, but we recovered one message draft.”
He hesitated before reading it aloud.
If anything happens to me, it was my sister. She.... 
He stopped.
Nkiru’s breath caught, sharp and painful. “That’s… that’s not possible.”
The officer studied her. “You were the last person she called.”
Nkiru nodded slowly. “She was… unstable. Always accusing people. She’d been hiding from someone.”
“From you?”
The word hung in the air.
“No,” Nkiru said quickly. “From her boyfriend. He was violent.”
But as she spoke, memory slipped through the cracks.
Amara crying on the phone.
Amara saying, Please, just come get me. I made a mistake.
Amara texting an address Nkiru knew too well.
The abandoned building used to be theirs.
Where they’d grown up.
Where their father taught them silence.
Where secrets were buried.
That night, after leaving the station, Nkiru drove there.
The building crouched in darkness, broken windows like empty eyes. Police tape fluttered in the wind.
She slipped under it.
Inside, the air smelled like rust and rot. Her footsteps echoed too loudly. She reached the spot where Amara had died.....dark stains still visible on the floor.
Her phone vibrated.

Unknown number: You came back. Just like I knew you would.
Her chest tightened. “This isn’t real,” she whispered.
The screen lit again.
You told me to wait. You said you’d come back with help.

Her hands began to shake.
Another message appeared.
But you didn’t. You locked the door instead.
The memory hit her full force.
Amara hiding behind her.
Their father drunk, raging.
The door handle slick with blood.
Nkiru choosing silence over courage.
Choosing herself.
A sound came from behind her.
Footsteps.
She turned, heart slamming only to find no one there.
Then her phone buzzed one last time.
"I survived long enough to tell them it was you."

Her breath broke. “No… you died. I saw...”
That’s when she noticed the red light blinking on the far wall.
A camera.
Still recording.
The door behind her slammed shut.
And outside, sirens wailed close now, inevitable.
Nkiru sank to her knees, realization tearing through her.
Amara hadn’t come back for revenge.
She had stayed alive just long enough to make sure the truth did.

The struggle for multiparty democracy in Kenya during the late 1980s and early 1990s was not fought by politicians alone. Religious leaders—especially from Christian churches—played a courageous and central role. At a time when criticism of the government attracted detention, exile, or death, clerics used the pulpit to demand justice, constitutional reform, and respect for human rights. Their moral authority gave strength to the Second Liberation movement.
1. Bishop Alexander Kipsang Muge (Anglican Church of Kenya)
Bishop Muge was one of the boldest clerics in Kenya’s democratic struggle. As the Anglican Bishop of Eldoret, he openly criticised the KANU government under President Daniel arap Moi.
He condemned:
  -Detention without trial
  -Torture of political dissidents
   -Corruption and abuse of power
Despite threats from senior government officials, Muge continued to preach reform. He famously ignored a public warning not to visit Busia. Shortly after that visit, he died in a suspicious road accident in 1990, widely believed to be politically motivated. His death intensified public pressure for political pluralism.
2. Reverend Timothy Njoya (Presbyterian Church of East Africa – PCEA)
Rev. Timothy Njoya became the most visible clerical activist for democracy. He consistently called for:
-Repeal of Section 2A of the Constitution
-Legalisation of multiparty politics
-Free and fair elections
Njoya was beaten by police, arrested several times, and threatened with death. In 1997, he was brutally assaulted during protests at Nairobi’s All Saints Cathedral. His courage made him a symbol of resistance against authoritarianism.
3. Bishop Henry Okullu (Anglican Church of Kenya)
Bishop Okullu was a leading intellectual and theologian in the fight for democracy. As the Bishop of Maseno South, he advocated for:
-Constitutional reform
-Political accountability
-Democratic governance
He authored books and articles criticising dictatorship and promoting people-centred leadership. His writings helped shape public debate and inspired reform-minded politicians and civil society.
4. Archbishop Manasses Kuria (Anglican Church of Kenya)
As the Archbishop of the Anglican Church of Kenya (1990–1997), Manasses Kuria used his position to pressure the government for reforms. He supported opposition voices and allowed churches to become safe spaces for political discussion.
Under his leadership, the Anglican Church played a key role in pushing for the return of multiparty democracy.
5. Archbishop Ndingi Mwana’a Nzeki (Catholic Church)
The Catholic Archbishop of Nairobi was an outspoken critic of corruption, ethnic politics, and authoritarian rule. He openly criticised President Moi’s government and defended political prisoners.
Archbishop Ndingi supported multiparty democracy and condemned election rigging and misuse of state power.
6. Sheikh Abdullahi Nassir (Supreme Council of Kenya Muslims – SUPKEM)
Though less highlighted, Muslim clerics also contributed. Sheikh Abdullahi Nassir advocated for political inclusion, constitutional reform, and equal rights. He emphasised justice and accountability as Islamic values, aligning Muslim leadership with the democratic struggle.
7. Cardinal Maurice Otunga (Catholic Church)
Though more cautious, Cardinal Otunga played a behind-the-scenes role in advocating peace, dialogue, and political openness. His influence helped protect outspoken clergy and allowed churches to act as mediators during tense political periods.
    Clerics contributed by:
-Using sermons to educate citizens on their rights
-Offering churches as meeting venues for activists
-Speaking for detainees and political prisoners
-Challenging fear and silence under one-party rule
Their involvement gave the struggle a moral foundation that the government could not easily silence.

     The return of multiparty democracy in Kenya in 1991 was partly achieved because courageous clerics refused to separate faith from justice. Leaders like Alexander Muge, Timothy Njoya, Henry Okullu, and Ndingi Nzeki proved that religious leadership can be a powerful force for political freedom.

UMOJA NA MSHIKAMANO WA KITAIFA NI MWAMBA IMARA NA NGUZO YA MATUMAINI KUELEKEA SAFARI YA MARIDHIANO 

BY LUGETE MUSSA LUGETE.

Tanzania ni moja ya mataifa machache barani Afrika na duniani yaliyofanikiwa kudumisha amani, umoja na mshikamano wa kitaifa kwa miongo zaidi ya sita licha ya kuwa na watu wenye asili, imani, mitazamo na hali za kiuchumi tofauti. Uhalisia huu si wa bahati mbaya, bali ni matokeo ya maamuzi ya busara ya kizazi cha waanzilishi wa taifa letu na juhudi endelevu za Watanzania wenyewe waliotambua kuwa tofauti zetu zinaweza kuwa nguvu ya pamoja badala ya chanzo cha migawanyiko, mifarakano,husda na inda. Leo, katika dunia inayokabiliwa na migawanyiko ya kisiasa, migongano ya kiitikadi, misuguano ya kidini na mashindano ya kiuchumi, ni wajibu wetu kama Watanzania kujitafakari upya,kujitathmini , kujivunia utaifa wetu na kulinda kwa vitendo misingi ya uzalendo, umoja, upendo, mshikamano na utangamano wa kitaifa.

Tanzania ni taifa lililojengwa juu ya misingi ya utofauti mkubwa wa kisiasa, kiuchumi, kijamii, kiitikadi na kiimani. Tofauti hizi ni sehemu ya uhalisia wa jamii yoyote iliyo hai na inayokua. Hakuna taifa lenye watu wanaofanana kwa kila jambo, na wala hilo halipaswi kuwa lengo. Kilicho muhimu si kufanana, bali ni namna tunavyoishi pamoja licha ya kutofautiana. Tofauti zetu hazipaswi kamwe kutugawa au kutufanya tuone kana kwamba sisi ni maadui ndani ya taifa moja. Badala yake, zinapaswa kutumika kama nyenzo ya kutujenga, kutukamilisha na kuimarisha mshikamano wetu wa kitaifa.Katika nyanja ya kisiasa, Tanzania ni taifa linalotambua uhuru wa mawazo na haki ya watu kuwa na mitazamo tofauti kuhusu uendeshaji wa nchi. Tofauti za kisiasa ni ishara ya uhai wa demokrasia, na si dalili ya uadui. 

Ni kupitia mjadala wa hoja, heshima ya maoni tofauti na kufuata misingi ya kikatiba ndipo taifa linaweza kupata maamuzi bora. Tatizo halipo kwenye kuwa na mtazamo tofauti, bali kugeuza tofauti hizo kuwa chuki, matusi, au sababu ya kuvuruga amani. Watanzania tunapaswa kukumbuka kuwa vyama, itikadi na mitazamo ni vyombo tu; taifa ndilo lengo kuu. Maslahi mapana ya Tanzania lazima yawe juu ya maslahi ya kisiasa ya muda mfupi.

Kiuchumi, tofauti zetu za uwezo, vipato, taaluma na shughuli za uzalishaji ni fursa kubwa kwa maendeleo ya pamoja. Mkulima, mfanyabiashara, mfanyakazi, mjasiriamali, msomi na fundi wote wanachangia kwa namna yao ujenzi wa uchumi wa taifa. Badala ya kuoneana wivu au kudharauliana, tunapaswa kujifunza kushirikiana na kuthaminiana. Taifa haliwezi kusonga mbele kama makundi ya kijamii yanajitenga au yanajiona bora kuliko mengine. Uchumi imara hujengwa na mshikamano wa kijamii, ushirikiano na imani ya pamoja kuwa maendeleo ya mmoja ni faida ya wote.

Kijamii na kiutamaduni, Tanzania imebarikiwa kuwa na makabila zaidi ya 120, lugha, mila na desturi mbalimbali. Utofauti huu ni hazina adhimu ya taifa letu. Tamaduni zetu zinapaswa kutufundisha kuvumiliana, kuheshimiana na kuthamini utu wa kila Mtanzania. Pale tunapodharau au kubeza tamaduni za wenzetu, tunadhoofisha msingi wa umoja wa kitaifa. Badala yake, tunapaswa kujivunia utajiri huu wa kijamii kama alama ya upekee wa Tanzania katika dunia ya leo.Lugha ya Kiswahili imetusaidia kama taifa kuondoa sumu ya ukabila, ukanda na udini. Lugha ya kiswahili imetuunganisha ukiachilia mbali lahaja na lafudhi tofauti tofauti ambazo zinatumika kukuza utani na masharikiano mathalani kutoka Mahuta Mtwara kuna kiswahili cha Kimakonde mpaka Mwamgongo Kigoma, kutoka Kijenge Arusha mpaka Misenyi Kagera hakika najivunia kuwa Mtanzania kwa sababu hakuna taifa lingine la kukimbilia zaidi ya Tanzania na hatuna taifa lingine la kulipigania zaidi ya Tanzania hivyo tofauti zetu zinaweza kutumika kuwa nguzo imara na mwamba wa matumaini kwa mustakabali wa taifa letu pendwa Tanzania.

Katika masuala ya kiitikadi na kiimani, Tanzania ni taifa la waumini wa dini mbalimbali pamoja na watu wenye mitazamo tofauti ya kimaisha. Katiba na misingi ya taifa letu inatambua uhuru wa kuabudu na kuamini au kutoamini. Uwepo wa tofauti za kiimani haupaswi kuwa sababu ya migongano, bali chanzo cha maadili mema kama upendo, haki, amani na huruma.

Dini na itikadi zinapaswa kumjenga mwanadamu awe raia mwema, mzalendo na mlinzi wa amani, si chombo cha kuchochea chuki, mgawanyiko au uasi dhidi ya taifa.

Uzalendo wa kweli haupimwi kwa kauli kali wala kwa kudai ukamilifu wa mawazo, bali kwa vitendo vinavyolinda maslahi ya taifa. Mzalendo wa kweli ni yule anayeheshimu sheria, anayetanguliza amani, anayejali ustawi wa wenzake na anayekataa kutumiwa kuharibu umoja wa nchi yake. Watanzania tunapaswa kujivunia kuwa Watanzania.

Utambulisho wetu wa kitaifa ni ngao yetu kuu dhidi ya migawanyiko ya kikundi, dini, kabila au itikadi.

Three days before she died, Roza Shanina wrote something that would haunt Soviet officials for decades: "I'm not afraid to die. I'm afraid of dying for nothing."
The Soviet government loved Roza Shanina while she was useful—a photogenic young sniper with an impressive kill count, perfect for propaganda. But the moment she died and officials actually read her diary, they classified it immediately.
For twenty years, her words were buried in Soviet archives. The truth about what she thought, what she felt, what she witnessed—all censored. Because Roza hadn't written propaganda. She'd written the truth about war.
But before the censorship, before the 59 kills, before she became a symbol—there was just a brilliant girl from nowhere who refused to accept her brother's death as meaningless.
Roza was born in 1924 in Edma, a village so remote in northern Russia that maps barely acknowledged its existence. Six children in a wooden house with no electricity. Poverty that made survival itself an achievement.
But Roza was different. She learned to read before formal schooling. She devoured every book she could find in a village that had almost none. She was hungry—not just for food, but for knowledge, for something beyond the limitations of her birthplace.
At 14, she did something almost unthinkable for a peasant girl: she walked 200 kilometers to Arkhangelsk, found the nearest college preparatory school, and demanded admission.
They could have turned her away. Poor village girl with no connections, no money, no reason to believe she belonged.
But they gave her an entrance exam. And they couldn't deny what the results showed: brilliance.
Roza was accepted. She worked multiple jobs to survive—cleaning, serving, whatever paid. She was training to become a teacher, preparing to return to rural villages and educate the next generation of forgotten children.
Then June 1941 happened. Germany invaded the Soviet Union with 3 million soldiers. Operation Barbarossa—the largest military invasion in human history.
Roza's brother Mikhail was immediately drafted. He was 19 years old.
October 1941: the letter arrived. Mikhail had been killed in action near Leningrad.
Roza was 17. And she walked to the recruitment office.
"I want to enlist."
They laughed at her. A teenage girl wanting to fight in the most brutal war in human history? Go home. Work in a factory. Support the war effort from safety. Women didn't belong in combat.
Roza went home. Not to accept their answer, but to prepare a better argument.
She joined a civilian marksmanship program. Practiced obsessively. Within months, she was outperforming every man in the program—shooting with precision that turned heads, demonstrating natural talent that couldn't be dismissed.
In 1943, at age 19, she tried again. This time with marksmanship scores that proved she belonged.
By then, the Soviet Union's losses were so catastrophic they'd begun recruiting women for combat roles—not from progressive ideals, but desperate necessity. They'd established sniper schools specifically for women.
Roza was accepted into the Central Women's Sniper Training School in May 1943.
Sniper training wasn't romantic. It meant learning to lie motionless in mud for hours. Calculating wind speed, distance, bullet drop. Controlling your heartbeat, your breathing, your fear. Learning to see a human being through a scope and pull the trigger without hesitation.
Learning to kill and then learning to live with it.
Roza excelled at all of it.
April 1944: she graduated. Assigned to the 184th Rifle Division, operating on the Eastern Front where millions had already died.
She was 19 years old. She'd never been in combat. She was about to enter hell.
Her first confirmed kill: June 22, 1944.
That night, she wrote in her diary—not with pride or satisfaction, but with clinical precision: "Fired at 09:30. Officer. Distance approximately 300 meters. Confirmed kill."
Then, in the next entry, the clinical mask cracked: "I keep seeing his face through the scope. He looked young. He might have had a family waiting for him. But he was here to kill us, to destroy our country. I can't let myself think about it too much or I won't be able to do this again tomorrow."
This is what Soviet officials didn't want published—proof that their propaganda heroes were human beings struggling with the psychological horror of what they were being asked to do.
Over six months, Roza became one of the Eastern Front's most effective snipers. Her confirmed kills climbed: 12... 22... 37... 54... 59.
But she didn't operate like most snipers.
Standard doctrine: stay hidden, maintain distance, never expose yourself unnecessarily, retreat after a kill. Snipers were valuable assets—you didn't risk them foolishly.
Roza broke these rules constantly.
She moved forward to get better angles, exposing herself to enemy fire. She provided covering fire during infantry assaults, revealing her position to protect advancing soldiers. She volunteered for the most dangerous missions others refused.
Her superiors reprimanded her. Fellow soldiers begged her to be more careful. She ignored them all.
Because Roza wasn't trying to survive the war. She was trying to make her brother's death mean something. She was fighting with the recklessness of someone who'd already lost everything that mattered.
In her diary: "I don't think about tomorrow anymore. There might not be a tomorrow. There's only today, and today I can still fight."
By January 1945, Germany was collapsing. The Red Army pushed into East Prussia. Victory was weeks away.
Roza had 59 confirmed kills. She'd received the Order of Glory—one of the Soviet Union's highest military honors. Her photograph appeared in newspapers. She was famous.
She should have been pulled from the front lines, kept safe as a propaganda symbol.
She requested to stay in combat.
January 27, 1945. East Prussia, near Richau. The 184th Rifle Division engaged entrenched German forces. The Wehrmacht, cornered and desperate, fought with ferocious intensity.
Roza's unit advanced through a destroyed village when German artillery opened fire. Explosions tore through buildings. Shrapnel filled the air. Soldiers dove for cover.
Roza saw a Soviet artillery officer—Lieutenant Leonid Yakovlev—wounded and exposed in the open, unable to move, with another barrage incoming.
Every instinct, every bit of training screamed: take cover. You're a sniper. You don't engage in rescue operations. You're too valuable.
Roza ran into the open.
She reached Yakovlev and threw herself over him as the next barrage hit. Shrapnel tore through her body—abdomen, chest, multiple organs damaged.
Other soldiers reached them and pulled both to a field hospital.
Yakovlev survived. Roza lived for 24 more hours.
She remained conscious most of that time. Soldiers who were there reported she never complained about her pain. She asked repeatedly if Yakovlev had survived. When told he would live, she seemed at peace.
She died January 28, 1945, at 9:00 PM. She was 20 years old.
The war ended four months later.
Then something remarkable—and disturbing—happened:
The Soviet government initially celebrated Roza's death as heroic. They prepared to publish excerpts from her diary as propaganda—proof of Soviet courage and dedication.
Then someone actually read the full diary.
Roza hadn't just written about duty and patriotism. She'd written about fear, doubt, the psychological horror of killing. She'd written about watching friends die, questioning whether the suffering was worth it. She'd written about Soviet military incompetence, officers who sent soldiers to die in pointless assaults, chaos that cost thousands of lives.
She'd written the truth about war—messy, complicated, human truth that didn't fit propaganda narratives.
The diary was immediately classified. Buried in Soviet military archives for twenty years. When finally published in the 1960s, it was heavily edited—criticisms removed, doubts minimized, human struggle sanitized.
The full, uncensored diary wasn't published until the 1990s, after the Soviet Union collapsed.
And it revealed something the Soviet government had feared: Roza Shanina wasn't a fearless hero who loved war. She was a terrified young woman who hated every moment of combat but kept fighting anyway because she believed she had to.
That's not less heroic. That's infinitely more heroic.
Fighting without fear is easy. Killing without feeling is simple. Dying when you're certain of your purpose is straightforward.
Roza was afraid. She felt every kill. She questioned her purpose constantly. And she fought anyway.
But the Soviet government couldn't celebrate that version of heroism. It was too human, too honest, too dangerous.
Yet they couldn't suppress everything:
Lieutenant Leonid Yakovlev survived the war. He spent the rest of his life telling anyone who would listen about the 20-year-old sniper who saved him. He named his daughter Roza. He visited her grave every year until his death in 1992.
The soldiers who served with her never forgot. They told their children and grandchildren about the girl who volunteered for impossible missions, who broke every rule to protect her comrades, who died exactly as she'd lived—putting others first.
And the diary survived. Despite classification, despite censorship, despite decades of suppression, the truth survived. Because Roza wrote it down.
She wrote: "I'm afraid of being forgotten."
She was forgotten—officially—for twenty years. But the people who mattered remembered.
Roza Shanina matters not because she had 59 confirmed kills or received military honors or appeared in propaganda. She matters because she was 19 and volunteered for hell because her brother was dead and she couldn't accept doing nothing.
She matters because she kept a diary that told the truth about war—the fear, the doubt, the cost—even when truth wasn't heroic.
She matters because when she saw a wounded soldier in the open, she ran toward artillery fire, knowing exactly what would happen, because one person's life mattered more than her own survival.
She spent her last 24 hours dying and never asked "why me?" She asked "did he survive?"
That's not propaganda. That's heroism in its purest form.
Roza Shanina died January 28, 1945. She was 20 years old. She was weeks from seeing the war end.
And she ran into artillery fire to save one stranger.
Because that's what mattered to her. Not the kill count. Not the medals. Not her own survival. Just that one person might live.
The Soviet Union tried to bury her story for twenty years. But Lieutenant Yakovlev lived to tell it. His daughter carries her name. The truth survived.
Sometimes courage isn't about fearlessness. Sometimes it's about being absolutely terrified and acting anyway.
Sometimes heroism isn't about how many enemies you kill. Sometimes it's about how many friends you save.
Roza Shanina saved one person with her final act. And he spent the rest of his life making sure she wasn't forgotten.
That's enough. That's more than enough.

On January 1, 1933 an anarchist insurgence broke out, the second of the insurrections carried out by the National Labor Confederation (CNT) in Spain during the Second Republic. During the same time, the events of Old Houses took place that shocked contemporary Spanish public opinion, in the context of the end of the first biennium of the Second Spanish Republic.

The anarchist tactic of the CNT and the FAI, corresponding to carrying out social agitations that denounce the poor living conditions of the Spanish working class, situations that would produce the so-called "revolutionary contagion" in which the libertarian revolution would start in Spain.

The uprising started on January 1, when from seven in the afternoon to nine in the evening, they explode in La Felguera, (headquarter of the CNT in Asturias), several high-power bombs. Simultaneously, in Seville, street riots occur and shops and bars are raided. In the village of Real de la Jara, agitators set fire to the local church. There are also looting in Lérida, and confrontations in Pedro Muñoz (Ciudad Real), where unionists take over the City Hall, proclaiming libertarian communism. On January 2, Barcelona's Civil Guard discovers a bomb depot attributed to the same union. On the 3rd day another arsenal of explosives is discovered in Barcelona; on the 5th more artifacts explode in La Felguera, and in Gijón, and the strikes of typographers in Valencia, metalworkers and employees of the Electra company intensify.

On the 8th, members of the anarchosyndicalist movement of Madrid try to take the barracks of Carabanchel, de la Montaña and Maria Cristina, an exchange of shots with the Civil Guard. In Barcelona acts of violence take place in the vicinity of the Arc del Teatro, where the headquarters of the syndicate is installed. There are also shootings in front of the Atarazanas barracks, where an assault guard falls dead, and a corporal is injured. Three bombs explode at the Madrid police headquarters.

In Valencia, anarchosyndicalist organizations join the agitation in much of the region. There are disorders in Valencia and numerous villages in the province, such as Ribarroja del Turia, Bétera, Benaguacil and Utiel. Several bombs explode in Gestalgar. In Bugarra, anarchists after an intense fight with law enforcement take over the town, with a total of more than five dead and several wounded, and proclaim libertarian communism. In Castellón de la Plana the agitation begins on the 10th. In Bugarra, a civil guard and an assault guard died during the uprising; when the Civil Guard restored the order it caused the death of ten countrymen and detained 250.

The agitation is spreading to Zaragoza, Murcia, Oviedo and other provinces, reaching its greatest resonance in Andalucia, where numerous strikes are being initiated. Cars and trams are on fire in Seville, where the public force faces off in several shootings. In La Rinconada, libertarian communism is proclaimed.

In Casas Viejas (Cadiz), the farmworkers anarchosyndicalists rise proclaiming libertarian communism. Law enforcement forces under the command of Captain Rojas provoke a killing of local neighbors, which becomes a major political scandal.

An Open Letter to Vernacular Radio Stations: A Call to Turn a Listener's Pain into Purpose

To the station managers, program controllers, and owners of Kenya's vibrant vernacular radio airwaves,

A story has gripped the nation, not one of politics or scandal, but of profound human vulnerability. Wanjohi wa Kigogo-ini, a name familiar to your call-in segments, a voice that once contributed to the daily chorus of public opinion, is now at the centre of a national conversation about mental health and community care. His raw, on-air confession of personal devastation following his wife's departure was a moment of unfiltered humanity that transcended the radio signal.

We now understand he is receiving crucial psychosocial support. As a society, we must protect that space for his healing. But once that essential process reaches its conclusion, we—and especially you, the custodians of the medium he loves—must be ready with the next chapter.

Therefore, this is not merely a suggestion but a public challenge: Your station has a unique opportunity and a moral responsibility to offer Wanjohi wa Kigogo-ini a formal role on your team.

The rationale is clear and compelling:

1. He Has Already Auditioned, Live on Air.
Wanjohi is not an unknown quantity. For years, he has been a "fan" in the truest sense—an engaged, passionate, and regular contributor. He understands the rhythm of your programming, the pulse of your audience, and the power of the vernacular to express complex emotions. You have heard his authenticity, his relatability, and his innate radio sense. This is a diamond you have already mined; it only requires polishing.

2. It Would Be the Ultimate "Give Back to the Community."
Vernacular stations rightly pride themselves on being the heartbeat of their communities. Community is not just about reporting news; it is about mutual uplift. What greater act of community restoration could there be than lifting one of your own most recognizable voices from a period of darkness into a position of dignity and purpose? This would move beyond charity into empowerment, showing every listener that their voice matters and that their struggles are seen.

3. It Makes Sound Editorial and Business Sense.
This is not just philanthropy; it is smart broadcasting. Wanjohi's story has shown he connects with people on a deep, empathetic level. Imagine a weekly segment—"Mukorwo wa Wanjohi" (Wanjohi's Perspective) or a dedicated listener-advice slot. He could host a program focusing on personal resilience, community issues, or mental wellness advocacy. His lived experience, processed through professional support, would bring an unparalleled credibility and depth to your content, attracting and retaining listeners.

The Proposal:

We call on any leading Gikuyu-language station—be it Inooro FM, Kameme FM, or Coro FM—to publicly extend a commitment. Draft a letter not of sympathy, but of opportunity. Offer him a role as a Program Researcher, a Segment Producer, or an On-Air Contributor with a defined developmental path. Provide the training, the mentorship, and the studio resources to help him transition from a caller to a colleague.

Do not wait for him to apply. Proactively create the position and offer it to him, with the clear understanding that it commences upon the full and satisfactory conclusion of his rehabilitation. Partner with the wellness professionals at ARS Hospital to ensure a supported transition.

In doing so, you will do more than fill a job vacancy. You will validate the humanity of your entire audience. You will turn a moment of collective pain into a lasting narrative of hope and second chances. You will prove that the community you speak to every day is, in fact, a family.

The nation is listening. It is time to make the call.

Editorial Board Of Directors.

Kwanza, niungane na Watanzania wenzangu wote kumshukuru Mwenyezi Mungu [S.W] kwa kutufikisha hatua hii ya kuuhitimisha mwaka wa 2025 na kuukaribisha mwaka mpya wa 2026. Pamoja na majaribu, mitihani na maafa makubwa yaliyotokea, lakini kama Taifa, tumeweza kusimama, jambo linalotupa fursa adhimu ya kuungana pamoja kutafakari na kuamua mustakbali wa Taifa letu.

Pili, kwa dhati kabisa nachukua fursa hii kuwapongeza Watanzania wenzetu mbali mbali, kila mmoja kwa nafasi yake, ambao wamechukua hatua mbali mbali zilizoirejesha nchi yetu katika utulivu. Pamoja na kwamba sote tunafahamu kuwa utulivu uliopo si kielelezo cha furaha wala amani endelevu katika nchi, lakini si sawa na vurugu na inatupa fursa nyengine ya kujenga mustakbali mwema wa Taifa endapo kila mmoja wetu kwa nafasi yake atakuwa na dhamira ya dhati na kutimiza wajibu wake kwa ukweli na nia safi kwa maslahi ya Taifa.

Aidha, nachukua fursa hii kuwapongeza kwa dhati wale wote ambao wamepaza sauti zao kueleza ukweli wa matukio mbali mbali ya ufisadi, ukiukwaji wa Katiba, Sheria, Maadili na taratibu ambayo yameleta maafa makubwa dhidi ya misingi ya Taifa na usalama wa watu wake, maafa dhidi ya uhai wa watu na maafa dhidi ya mali za raia.  Kibaya pia ni kwa Taifa letu kuingia doa kubwa sana katika wajihi wake kimataifa hata katika mataifa ambayo yamekuwa marafiki wa jadi wa Jamhuri ya Muungano wa Tanzania.

Kwa Watanzania Wenzangu, yaliyotokea katika Taifa letu katika mwaka 2025 na matukio kadhaa hata kabla ya 2025 tumeyanukuu na kuyakariri vya kutosha, sio tu idadi yake bali pia athari yake.  Niwasihi, kwa kupitia salamu hizi, tuutumie mwaka mpya wa 2026 kuchukua hatua za kuliponya Taifa na kulirejesha kwenye mstari sahihi.  Ni wakati kwa wenye Mamlaka kutanabahi kuwa yaliyotokea yametufunza jambo moja MUHIMU sana, nalo ni kuwa tunahitaji kuchukua hatua za kujenga misingi ya Taifa kwa nia njema na kwa dhamira ya dhati.

Hatuhitaji maafa ya ziada.  Tunahitaji kuchukua hatua za kuliunganisha Taifa lote.  Tuachane na dhana ya kuwa Taifa hili, wenye haki na hadhi ya kuliongoza ni kikundi, jumuiya ama chama fulani pekee.  Tukubali kuwa wenye haki ya Kikatiba, wenye Mamlaka ya kuamua nani waendeshe Nchi na Mamlaka zake mbali mbali ni Wananchi wa Tanzania kama ilivyoelezwa waziwazi katika Ibara ya 8 ya Katiba ya Jamhuri ya Muungano wa Tanzaniana Ibara ya 9 ya Katiba ya Zanzibar.  

Wajibu wa Kikatiba na hata wa kimaadili wa Viongozi ni kuhakikisha Wananchi wanapewa fursa ya kutimiza haki yao hiyo.  Sheria yoyote, amri yoyote na hatua yoyote ya kiutawala inayoweka kikwazo katika hilo, ndio chanzo cha kuchafua amani katika Taifa.  Adui yetu namba moja ni yeyote anayetumia nafasi au wadhifa wake kukwaza haki hiyo ya msingi ya raia. 

Hakuna maendeleo yoyote tunayoweza kujinasibu nayo katika mazingira ambayo Wananchi wa Taifa hili hawana haki ya kuamua nani awaongoze, hawana haki ya kuchagua wala kuchaguliwa na hawana haki ya kuwawajibisha Viongozi wenye kushikilia Ofisi za Umma.  Wananchi kuwa katika hali hiyo ni sawa na kuwa katika utumwa na hakuna maendeleo ya Taifa la Watumwa.

Mageuzi ya mapambio, mageuzi ya funika kombe, mageuzi yanayolenga kufaidisha ama kulinda maslahi ya Chama fulani ama kikundi mahsusi ni sawa na kufuja fursa hii adimu ya kuliponya na kulijenga upya Taifa letu. Hivyo, tuungane kama raia wa Taifa hili, kuhakikisha tunajenga mfumo wa kikatiba, wa kisheria, wa kimaadili na kiuendeshaji ulio madhubuti na ambao hautalirejesha Taifa letu katika Utawala wa Utashi wa mtu mmoja au kikundi kilichojitwalia mamlaka ya nchi kwa mgongo wa Katiba au Sheria ambayo kwa ukweli haikufuatwa wala kuzingatiwa.  

Kwa Wazanzibari wenzangu, nyote ni mashahidi, kwamba sababu kubwa ya Zanzibar kutotokea maafa ya kuuliwa mtu ni uamuzi wa busara muliouchukua Wananchi wa Zanzibar kuwaachia waliopanga vitendo vya wizi, udanganyifu na uvunjifu wa sheria uliojaa kiburi na kutojali wafanye walivyotaka katika Uchaguzi.  Laiti Wazanzibari wangeamua kuchukua hatua hata ndogo za kupambana na uhalifu uliotokea katika siku mbili za Uchaguzi, tarehe 28 na 29 Oktoba, ni dhahiri kuwa maafa makubwa sana ya vifo na watu kujeruhiwa yangetokea kwa sababu waliojipa mamlaka walishaamua kujipa mamlaka tena kwa gharama yoyote ile.

Hatua kadhaa ambazo Chama cha ACT Wazalendo tumeamua kuzichukua baada ya Uchaguzi zikiwemo za kisheria ni uamuzi ambao tumeufanya ili kuipa Zanzibar na wananchi wake fursa nyengine ya kutafuta kujenga mustakbali mwema kwa njia ya amani hata kama ni kwa gharama ya subira kubwa na ngumu sana.  Tunaamini kuwa si kila siku amani lazima ipatikane baada ya vurugu na maafa.  Tunawashkuru sana wanachi wenzetu wa Zanzibar bila kujali itikadi zao kwa kutuunga mkono katika hatua hizo.  Tumefarajika sana na salamu na ujumbe wa kutuunga mkono ambao tumekuwa tukiupokea kutoka kwa watu wengi wa itikadi na nafasi mbali mbali.

Hatua tunazochukua sasa za kutafuta suluhisho la kadhia ya Uchaguzi wa Zanzibar, zinakusudia kutibu mzizi wa fitna, mzizi wa tatizo.  Serikali ya Umoja wa Kitaifa ililetwa ili kutoa fursa, kutoa jukwaa rasmi kwa Wazanzibari kujenga amani ya kweli, umoja, mshikamano na maridhiano ya kitaifa. Serikali ya Umoja wa Kitaifa haikuanzishwa kwa madhumuni ya kutumiwa kuiba Uchaguzi ili baadaye aliyeiba uchaguzi amkaribishe mshindi halali aliyeporwa ushindi wake katika Serikali ambayo haikutokana na ridhaa ya umma ili kujipa uhalali.

Tunachotafuta sio ushindi wa Chama chetu, bali ushindi wa Zanzibar, ushindi wa Wazanzibari wote. Tunaamini tutapata muafaka katika hili chini ya usimamizi wa viongozi na wazee wetu wenye busara. Taarifa kamili tutaitoa kwa umma pale hatua hizi zote zitakapokamilika. Ninalowaomba Wazanzibari ni kuvuta subira na kuendelea kumuomba Mwenyezi Mungu ailinde nchi yetu.
 
Kwa Viongozi na wanachama wa ACT Wazalendo, nawashukuru mno kwa kazi kubwa mliyoifanya katika mwaka 2025 ya kukijenga Chama katika mazingira magumu na kukiwezesha kuungwa mkono na wapiga kura kwa kiwango ambacho hakijawahi kutokea kabla.  Pamoja na yaliyotokea katika chaguzi za Serikali za Mitaa, Uchaguzi Mkuu wa Zanzibar na Tanzania kwa jumla, tumejenga mshikamano na kubaki na Chama kikiwa imara.  Dhamira yetu ni kuendelea kushiriki katika harakati za mageuzi ya kuliponya Taifa na kulirudisha kwenye mstari, ikiwemo kuhakikisha uwajibikaji kwa yaliyotokea, kwa kushirikiana na wadau wote makini.  Aidha, kuchukua hatua za kuimarisha Chama kwa kufanya mapitio ya Kanuni na taratibu zinazokiongoza, kuimarisha uongozi katika ngazi mbali mbali, utendaji na miundombinu.  Aidha, kuimarisha Uchumi wa Chama ili kitekeleze majukumu yake kwa ufanisi.

Petro: Shambulizi la Marekani Venezuela lililenga kiwanda cha ELN cha kusindika kokeini

Rais wa Colombia, Gustavo Petro, amesema kuwa shambulizi lililofanywa na Marekani nchini Venezuela lililenga kiwanda cha Jeshi la Ukombozi wa Taifa (ELN) ambacho kilikuwa kinatumika kuchanganya unga wa coca na kuutengeneza kuwa dawa ya kulevya ya kokeini.

Petro alieleza kuwa boti nyingi zilizoshambuliwa kwa makombora katika oparesheni ya kijeshi ya utawala wa Rais wa Marekani Donald Trump katika eneo la Caribbean, hazikubeba kokeini bali bangi (cannabis).

“Tatizo ni la kushangaza: nchini Marekani, katika maeneo mengi bangi ni halali kisheria. Bunge la Colombia halikupaswa kuruhusu bangi kubaki haramu; muswada huo ulipotea kwa kura moja tu. Kura hiyo moja imegharimu maisha ya wavua samaki maskini wengi, lakini haijamdhuru hata mtumiaji mmoja wa bangi nchini Marekani wala duniani,” alisema Petro.

Aliongeza kuwa Trump yuko katika makosa makubwa, akieleza kuwa kokeini inayokwenda Ulaya husafirishwa kwa kutumia manowari na makontena, huku akisisitiza kuwa bangi ndiyo inayoshambuliwa bila uhalali.

Kwa mujibu wa Petro, ni takribani asilimia 5 tu ya kokeini inayozalishwa Colombia hupitia eneo hilo.

“Tuna uhakika kuwa Trump alilipua kiwanda kilichopo Maracaibo. Tuna hofu kwamba hapo ndipo wanachanganya unga wa coca kuwa kokeini, wakitumia fursa ya eneo la Bahari ya Maracaibo. Hiyo ni shughuli ya ELN. Kupitia biashara haramu na misimamo yao ya kizamani, ELN inaruhusu uvamizi wa Venezuela,” alisema Petro kupitia ukurasa wake wa X (zamani Twitter).

Ndugu zangu Watanzania! 
Mvua ya Haki na Amani toka kwa Mungu wa Mbinguni iwe nanyi!

Ashukuriwe Mungu kwa kutuwezesha kuuona mwaka mpya. Kwani siyo jambo rahisi kwetu sisi Watanzania tuliobaki. Maana tumeshuhudia  maelfu ya wenzetu wakiuawa, kutekwa na hawajulikani walipo huko wengine wako magerezani. Sio kwamba sisi tuliouona mwaka mpya kuwa tumejilinda wenyewe, wala kwamba ni wema sana kuliko wengine, la hasha! Ni ni neema zake Mwenyezi Mungu tu!

Ndugu zangu Watanzania! Mimi Askofu Mwanamapinduzi nikiwa huku nchi ya ugenini kama mkimbizi ninatoa salamu hizi nikiwa nimejawa na simanzi nzito sana. Simanzi juu ya taifa letu la Tanzania ambalo kwa nyakati hizi limepoteza haki, Amani na utulivu kwa watu wa tabaka la chini yaani wananchi wa kawaida. Na hii ni kutokana na kushamiri kwa matukio mabaya yanayoharibu taswira ya taifa letu, ikiwa ni pamoja na uvunjwaji wa haki za binadamu kama vile utekaji na mauaji ya raia wasio na hatia.

Ndugu zangu Watanzania hususani Watanganyika! Taifa letu limekuwa taifa lenye usalama mdogo kwa raia wake. Hii inatokana na kushamiri kwa  matukio mengi ya utekaji na mauaji kwa wakosoaji wa serikali. Lakini pia nchi yetu imepoteza kabisa sifa ya kuitwa nchi ya kidemokrasia; inayofuata mfumo wa vyama vingi kama ulivyoasisiwa mwaka 1992. Kwa kweli siasa za nchi yetu kwa sasa zinazomilikiwa na chama kimoja hasa CCM mtandao. Hali iko hivyo huku vyama vingine hususani chama kikuu cha upinzani (CHADEMA) vikizuiliwa kufanya siasa kwa namna yoyote ile. Hali hiyo imepelekea viongozi wengi wa upinzani kuwindwa na kupewa kesi za uongo kama magaidi na wahaini. 

Ndugu Watanzania! Mtakumbuka ya kwamba mwaka 2025 kanisa letu la Ufufuo na Uzima ambalo mimi ni naibu katibu mkuu wake tulifutiwa usajili kihuni na kwa uonevu mkubwa pasipo kuambiwa sababu za msingi. Hii ni kutokana na msimamo wa Askofu wetu mkuu Dr.Josephat Gwajima kukemea matukio ya utekaji hadharani ambayo yanafanywa na watu wenye jina la "Wasiojulikana". Hawa wasiojulikana, wanachukuliwa kama ni kundi la wahalifu wenye nguvu kuliko vyombo vya ulinzi na usalama. Kutokana na hatua ya Askofu wetu Mkuu kukemea utekaji na Kisha kanisa kufungwa, mamilioni ya waumini wetu walikosa haki yao ya msingi ya uhuru wa kuabudu. Katika kipindi hiki ambacho Tanzania inaelekea katika mzunguko mwingine wa kisiasa, maridhiano si chaguo bali ni hitaji la lazima ili kuhakikisha taifa linabaki kuwa kitu kimoja. Maana ya hatua hii kwa mwaka 2026 ni kuweka msingi wa kuaminiana kati ya serikali, vyama vya siasa, na wananchi, ili tofauti za kiitikadi zisiwe chanzo cha mpasuko bali ziwe chachu ya ujenzi wa demokrasia iliyokomaa.

Pamoja na kauli hiyo ya upole bado kuna baadhi ya watu katika mitandao waliendelea kutoa maoni ya dhihaka, matusi ya nguoni, na lugha za kashfa ikiwa ni kielelezo cha mmomonyoko wa maadili na ukosefu wa staha ambao unahatarisha jitihada hizi za kuwa na taifa lenye utulivu na amani.

Ni jambo la kusikitisha kuona kuwa badala ya kujadili muundo na majukumu ya tume hiyo kwa hoja, baadhi ya watu wanatumia uhuru wa maoni kupandikiza mbegu za chuki na utengano. Hali hii inathibitisha kuwa ukombozi wa fikra unahitajika kwa haraka ili jamii itambue kuwa matusi si suluhu ya changamoto za kisiasa.

Kwa upande mwingine, sauti za busara zinazowahimiza vijana kulinda amani na kutumia mazungumzo badala ya vurugu ndizo zinazopaswa kupewa kipaumbele.

Tukio la tarehe 29 Oktoba linapaswa kubaki kama funzo la kudumu kuwa amani ikishapotea, gharama ya kuirejesha ni kubwa mno. Maridhiano ya kweli hayawezi kufikiwa ikiwa upande mmoja unatoa mkono wa heri huku upande mwingine ukiwa umejaza matusi na kashfa viganjani. Ni lazima vijana watambue kuwa wao ndio walinzi wa urithi wa Tanzania, na kutumiwa kama vyombo vya kuchochea taharuki ni kujihujumu wenyewe na vizazi vijavyo.

Jukumu la viongozi wa dini na taasisi za kijamii katika kipindi hiki ni kuwa daraja la kweli la upatanisho. Tunahitaji sauti zinazounganisha raia na viongozi wao, si kuta zinazowatenganisha.

Mwaka 2026 unapaswa kuwa mwaka wa ukomavu, ambapo maridhiano yanatazamwa kama fursa ya kurekebisha makosa ya nyuma na kuimarisha mshikamano.

Tanzania ni nyumba yetu sote, na ujenzi wa nyumba hii unategemea utulivu, heshima kwa mamlaka, na uwezo wetu wa kukaa meza moja na kukubaliana kutokubaliana bila kutukanana. Huu ndio wakati wa kuweka nchi kwanza na kuacha siasa za chuki ambazo hazina tija kwa maendeleo ya taifa letu.
