UMOJA WA CHAMA: NGUZO YA MAPAMBANO YA KITAIFA

Watanzania wenzangu,

Umoja wetu ndani ya Chadema si kauli—ni pumzi ya uhai wa harakati zetu. Ni katika mshikamano ndipo chama kinaishi, kinapona na kinashinda. Tofauti za mawazo ndani ya chama cha kidemokrasia si ufa; ni misingi ya kujenga hoja bora na uamuzi thabiti. Tunapokubaliana kutofautiana kwa heshima, na kusimama pamoja mara maamuzi ya chama yanapofikiwa, tunaifanya Chadema iwe na nguvu ya kimaadili na kisiasa isiyoyumbishwa. Kama alivyosema Aristotle, “Umoja wa wengi ni nguvu kuliko nguvu ya mmoja.”

Chadema itaendelea kuishi mioyoni mwa wanachama na wananchi wote kwa sababu si nembo wala majengo—ni dhamira ya pamoja ya kupigania haki. Ni taasisi ya kitaifa, si mali ya mtu, familia au kundi; ni chombo cha wananchi cha kudai mabadiliko ya kweli. Chama kinapitia misimu, lakini roho ya umoja haifi; hujizalisha upya kila inapojaribiwa. Hapo ndipo harakati zinapokuwa kubwa kuliko hofu, na matumaini kuwa makubwa kuliko vikwazo.

Tukumbuke: umoja na mshikamano wa chama ndio nguzo ya mapambano ya kitaifa. Tunapolinda umoja, tunalinda mustakabali wa demokrasia. Na kama alivyoonya Martin Luther King Jr., “Nguvu ya kweli hupatikana pale watu wanapoungana kwa haki.” Umoja wetu ni ahadi—kwa wanachama, kwa wananchi, na kwa Tanzania tunayoitaka.

UCHAGUZI ULIONAJISIKA WA 29 OKTOBA 2025: UVUNJWAJI WA MAMLAKA YA WANANCHI

Watanzania wenzangu,

Kile kinachoitwa uchaguzi wa tarehe 29 Oktoba 2025 uliiacha Tanzania ikiwa na jeraha la kisiasa ambalo litachukua muda mrefu sana kupona. Tulishuhudia matumizi mabaya ya vyombo vya dola, ofisi ya Msajili wa Vyama vya Siasa na mahakama dhidi ya wakosoaji wa serikali, wanaharati na wapinzani wa kisiasa, hususan Chadema.

Chama chetu kilifungiwa kufanya shughuli zake za kisiasa kwa visingizio vya kesi za uongo. Mwenyekiti wetu, Ndg.Tundu Antipas Lissu, alibambikiziwa kesi nzito za kisiasa kwa lengo la kutisha na kuzima sauti ya mabadiliko. Wimbi la utekaji, utesaji na upotezwaji wa raia wasio na hatia lilienea nchini. Takribani Watanzania 200 walitekwa au kupotezwa katika mwaka huu pekee.

Kinachoitwa uchaguzi wa Oktoba 29 haukuwa uchaguzi; ulikuwa ubatilishaji wa haki ya wananchi kuchagua na kuchaguliwa. Matokeo yaliyotangazwa hayakuwa na uhalali wa kikatiba, kisheria wala kimaadili. Mkwamo wa kisiasa tulionao leo ni zao la mifumo dhaifu ya uchaguzi iliyoshindwa kulinda Ibara ya 8 ya Katiba yetu — inayotamka wazi kwamba mamlaka yote hutoka kwa wananchi.

“NO REFORMS, NO ELECTION”: SAUTI YA WANANCHI NA MSINGI WA MAGEUZI YA KIMFUMO

Watanzania wenzangu,

Katika kipindi ambacho taasisi za umma zimepoteza uhalali wa kimaadili na kikatiba, Chadema ilisimama si kama chama cha siasa pekee, bali kama dhamiri hai ya wananchi waliokata tamaa na mfumo wa uchaguzi uliotekwa na nguvu za dola. Kauli ya “No Reforms, No Election” haikuwa tishio wala ukaidi; ilikuwa ni hoja ya kifizikia ya haki—kwamba uchaguzi bila mageuzi ya kimfumo na kitaasisi si zoezi la kidemokrasia bali ni ibada ya kuhalalisha dhuluma. Kama linavyosisitiza Tamko la Kimataifa la Haki za Binadamu (Kifungu cha 21), “Mapenzi ya watu ndiyo msingi wa mamlaka ya serikali; mapenzi hayo yaonyeshwe kupitia chaguzi huru na za haki.” Bila misingi hiyo, sanduku la kura hubaki kuwa tupu bila maana.

Madai ya wananchi yalikuwa ya msingi na yasiyopingika: Tume Huru yenye mamlaka kamili ya kikatiba; marekebisho ya sheria kandamizi zinazonyima raia sauti; na ulinzi halisi wa haki za kisiasa na kiraia. Msimamo huu haukulenga kuvuruga amani bali kuilinda, kwa sababu amani isiyo na haki ni ukimya wa makaburini. Kama alivyoonya John Rawls, “Sheria isiyo ya haki si sheria bali ni vurugu iliyorasimishwa.” Hivyo, mageuzi hayakuwa hiari ya kisiasa, bali ni sharti la uhalali wa dola.

Ni jambo la kusikitisha kwamba badala ya majadiliano ya kitaifa, mamlaka zilichagua mabavu, vitisho na nguvu kupita kiasi. Lakini historia ina tabia ya kuwakumbuka waliokataa kupiga magoti mbele ya udhalimu. Vuguvugu la “No Reforms, No Election” linaibaki kuwa alama ya mwamko wa kihistoria—ushahidi kwamba wananchi waligundua ukweli wa kimsingi: bila mageuzi ya kimfumo, uchaguzi si suluhisho bali ni tatizo linaloendelezwa. Hapo ndipo sauti ya wananchi ilipogeuka kuwa falsafa ya ukombozi wa kisiasa.

MAUAJI YA HALAIKI NA JERAHA LA TAIFA

Watanzania wenzangu,

Kutekwa kwa watu zaidi ya 200 na mauaji ya Watanzania zaidi ya 2000 si takwimu za kawaida; kwa mizani ya kimataifa, hizi ni namba zinazolingana na nchi zilizoko kwenye migogoro ya silaha au vita vya wenyewe kwa wenyewe. Katika mataifa yanayojitambulisha kama ya amani na utulivu wa kisiasa, hata vifo kumi vya kisiasa huibua uchunguzi wa kimataifa na misukumo ya uwajibikaji. Hivyo basi, kilichotokea Tanzania kinakiuka hadhi yake kama nchi yenye amani, na kinaiweka katika ramani ya dunia kama taifa linaloshindwa kulinda uhai wa raia wake.

Haya si matukio ya kawaida ya kisiasa; ni makosa makubwa dhidi ya ubinadamu yanayopingana na misingi ya haki za binadamu inayotambuliwa kimataifa. Ndiyo maana Chadema inasisitiza uchunguzi huru, unaoaminika, na wenye uwakilishi wa kimataifa, kwa sababu kiwango cha madhara kimevuka uwezo wa taasisi za ndani pekee kujihakiki. Taifa lolote linalojali heshima yake duniani haliwezi kunyamazia damu ya raia wake ikimwagika bila ukweli na uwajibikaji.

Na hapa kuna ukweli mchungu kwa watawala: “Damu ya raia inapomwagika bila majibu, majonzi ya familia yanapogeuzwa takwimu za kutisha, na kilio cha wahanga kinaponyamazishwa na dola, serikali hupoteza si tu uhalali wa kutawala, bali pia utu wa kimaadili wa kuongoza binadamu wenzao".

“Tunadai haki kwa wahanga, kwa waliopoteza viungo vyao, na kwa familia zilizobaki na majonzi yasiyo na majibu. Taifa haliwezi kujengwa juu ya damu ya raia wake, na haki ikicheleweshwa, kwa vigezo vya kitaifa na kimataifa, ni haki iliyonyimwa”.

MAUMIVU YA MWANANCHI: DEMOKRASIA NA MAISHA YA KILA SIKU

Watanzania wenzangu,

Uchaguzi batili hauishii kwenye siasa pekee—huingia moja kwa moja kwenye tumbo la mwananchi na heshima ya maisha yake ya kila siku. Ndiyo chanzo cha mkulima kukosa soko la mazao yake licha ya jasho lake, kijana kukosa ajira hata akiwa na elimu, mama kushindwa kulipa ada ya mtoto, na mfanyabiashara mdogo kunyimwa mtaji kwa mifumo isiyo ya haki. Takwimu huonesha mwelekeo huu kwa ukali: pale uwazi na uwajibikaji vinapodhoofika, uwekezaji hushuka, mapato ya kaya hupungua, na gharama za maisha hupanda, mzigo unaobebwa na mwananchi wa kawaida, si watawala.

Demokrasia ikifa, uchumi hufa; haki ikikandamizwa, matumaini yanakufa; na hofu ikitawala, maendeleo husimama. Hizi si kauli za hisia pekee bali ni ukweli unaothibitishwa na uzoefu wa mataifa mengi: nchi zenye chaguzi huru na taasisi imara huongeza ajira, hupunguza umaskini, na kuboresha huduma za jamii. Kinyume chake, pale sauti ya wananchi inaponyamazishwa, takwimu hubadilika kuwa maumivuna gharama hulipwa na wananchi, kila siku.

MUELEKEO WA TANZANIA TUNAYOITAKA

Watanzania wenzangu,

Tunaitaka Tanzania inayosimama juu ya Katiba iliyo hai, si maandishi matupu bali mkataba wa haki kati ya wananchi na dola. Tanzania inayotawaliwa na sheria, si matakwa ya wachache; inayolinda haki za binadamu kama msingi wa utu, si hisani ya watawala. Tunakataa dhana potofu kwamba mamlaka huzaliwa kwenye hofu—mamlaka ya kweli hutoka kwa wananchi, si kutoka kwenye mtutu wa bunduki, wala mihuri ya taasisi zilizotekwa na kupotoshwa.

Tunadai Katiba Mpya ya wananchi—Katiba itakayorudisha heshima ya kura, kusimika uwajibikaji, na kufungua njia ya haki kwa wote. Tunadai Tume Huru ya Uchaguzi—ili sauti ya mwananchi isizimwe, ili uamuzi wa wengi usipinduliwe na wachache. Haya si matamanio ya kisiasa; ni haki za msingi zinazostahili kutekelezwa sasa, bila kuchelewa.
Na tunadai uchumi unaomjali mwananchi wa kawaida—uchumi unaopima mafanikio kwa chakula mezani, ajira zenye staha, na huduma bora, si kwa takwimu zisizoishi maisha ya watu. Kama alivyosema Jean-Jacques Rousseau, “Mtu huzaliwa huru, lakini kila mahali yuko katika minyororo.” Minyororo hii ikivunjwa, Tanzania mpya itawezekana—Tanzania ya utu, haki na ujasiri wa mabadiliko.aa

HIKI KINACHOITWA MARIDHIANO YA KITAIFA: UKWELI, HAKI NA UWAJIBIKAJI
Watanzania wenzangu,

Ni ubatili na dharau kubwa kwa Watanzania kuyaita maridhiano sasa katika mazingira ambapo serikali iliamua kwa makusudi kuwapuuza wananchi, vyama vya siasa na wadau wa demokrasia juu ya hitaji la nchi kuhusu mabadiliko (reforms) ya mifumo ya uchaguzi nchini.

Hiki kinachoitwa maridhiano, kinatamkwa tamkwa katika mazingira ambayo serikali batili inaendelea na uchunguzi chini ya tume iliyokataliwa na wananchi kufanya uchunguzi wa matukio ya tarehe 29 Oktoba 2025. Watanzania sio wajinga, wanaona hiki ni kiini macho, hakuna kitu hapo. 

Ni wazi kabisa, hakuna maridhiano bila haki, na hakuna haki bila uwajibikaji. Maridhiano yanapogeuzwa kuwa wito wa “kusonga mbele” baada ya kuamua kwa makusudi kuwaapuza wananchi juu ya madai ya msingi waliyoyatoa na tahadhari walizozitoa awali na matokeo yake serikali na vyombo vya dola vikaunajisi uchaguzi na kujitangazia matokeo batili na kwa makusudi kufanya uhalifu wa kisiasa uliopelekea mauaji ya raia na uharibifu wa mali, wito huo wa maridhiano ni wa kupumbaza na hauna ukweli nyuma yake. Bila ukiri wa makosa na kuwawajibisha waliotenda makosa, hapo maridhiano hugeuka kuwa aina ya ukandamizaji wa kumbukumbu wa mambo yaliyotokea. Watu wameuwawa kwa maelfu, watu wamekuwa vilema, wamesingiziwa kesi za uongo za uhaini, Taifa linaomboleza kwa machozi ambayo mpaka leo hayajakoma, kama chama tulishauri kuwa ni vema familia za wote waliouwawa na kupata vilema zipewe fidia kama sehemu kuonyesha kujali utu wa mtu lakini watawala dhalimu wamepuuzia, halafu leo unaita maridhiano? Tunafahamu, haki si kulipiza kisasi; haki ni kurejesha utu wa waathirika na imani ya wananchi katika taasisi za dola. Bila uwajibikaji wa waliohusika, iwe ni kupitia vyombo vya haki, tume huru za ukweli, au marekebisho ya taasisi, maridhiano hubaki kuwa kauli ya kisiasa, si mkataba wa kijamii. Chadema, tumeendelea kuomboleza nanyi Watanzania katika huzuni tuliyopitia wote na tunaendelea kuwapa faraja na tumaini kuwa iko siku, siku itafika hakika kila uovu, ukatili na hila itawajibishwa kwa haki na Taifa litafikia kilele cha furaha na maendeleo ambayo tumesubiri kwa muda mrefu sana.

Chadema, chama chenu hakitakuwa tayari kwa maridhiano yenye kupambaza, kuhadaa, yenye ulaghai na yenye kuliondoa Taifa kwenye ukweli, haki na kile ambacho Taifa inataka, kamwe hatuwasaliti Watanzania.

MUELEKEO WA HARAKATI ZA CHADEMA

Watanzania Wenzangu, 

Chadema itaendelea kuwa sauti huru, imara na ya kuaminika ya wananchi, si kwa maneno bali kwa vitendo vinavyogusa maisha halisi ya Watanzania. Katika zama hizi za siasa mpya—zinazotawaliwa na teknolojia, taarifa, na mabadiliko ya kasi ya kijamii—chadema inajitambulisha kama harakati ya kisasa (modern political movement) inayosikiliza wananchi, inajifunza kutoka kwao, na inayowapa jukwaa la kushiriki kikamilifu katika maamuzi yanayowahusu. Siasa za kizazi kipya haziridhishwi tena na kauli za jumla au ahadi zisizo na mifumo ya utekelezaji; zinahitaji uwazi, uwajibikaji, na uongozi unaoonekana, unaogusika, na unaojibu changamoto za sasa kama ajira, gharama ya maisha, haki za kidijitali, na usawa wa kijamii.

Katika mwelekeo huo, Chadema itaendelea kujenga na kuimarisha ushirikiano mpana wa kimkakati na vyama vya siasa vinavyoamini demokrasia ya kweli, asasi za kiraia, taasisi za kidini, wanazuoni, wanahabari, na jumuiya ya kimataifa. Ushirikiano huu si wa kimaslahi ya muda mfupi, bali ni sehemu ya falsafa ya siasa shirikishi (inclusive politics) inayotambua kuwa mapambano ya haki, demokrasia, na maendeleo hayawezi kushindwa na chama kimoja peke yake. Katika dunia ya leo, ambapo demokrasia inakabiliwa na changamoto mpya kama udhibiti wa taarifa, siasa za hofu, na kudhoofishwa kwa taasisi, Chadema itaendelea kusimama kama nguzo ya kulinda maadili ya utawala wa sheria na haki za binadamu.

Tunaitaka ofisi ya msajili wa vyama vya siasa nchini kuacha kutumika kama chombo ya kuumiza na kugandamiza demokrasia na vyama vya siasa vya upinzani na hasa Chadema kwa lengo la kukilinda chama cha mapinduzi. Kesi tuliyo nayo mahakamani ya madai ya mgawanyo wa mali namba 8323 ya mwaka 2025 ya Ndg. Saidi Issa na wenzake ambayo imepelekea kutolewa amri ya kinachoitwa kusitisha shughuli za kisiasa na matumizi ya mali za chama, ni batili na ipo kwa lengo la kunyamazisha sauti ya haki na demokrasia nchini. Yanayoitwa madai ya wanachama hawa watatu hayawezi na sio haki madai yao yasimamishe shughuli za kisiasa  ambazo ni haki kwa mamilioni ya wanachama wengine nchi nzima. Hii ni kesi ya kihuni ambayo inaiingiza mahakama kuwa sehemu ya kuendekeza mambo ya kuhuni kwa faida ya watawala dhalimu. Kwa wote waliohusika na wenye mkono kwenye kesi hii, tunawataka waondoe kesi hii mahakamani mara moja. Kesi hii ni ushahidi wa kuwa tuna Taifa lenye mifumo ya kidekteta, mifumo yenye hila na kuwa chama cha mapinduzi kinaiogppa Chadema kwa sababu ni dhahiri sasa kuwa sisi Chadema ndio tumaini la Watanzania.

Zaidi ya yote, Chadema inatambua kuwa mustakabali wa mabadiliko ya kweli upo mikononi mwa kizazi kipya. Hivyo, tutawekeza kwa makusudi katika kuandaa, kulea, na kuwawezesha vijana—hasa kizazi cha Gen Z—ili wawe si watazamaji wa siasa, bali wawe wabunifu, wapangaji, na waendeshaji wa ajenda ya mabadiliko. Hiki ni kizazi kilichokulia katika dunia ya kidijitali, chenye ufahamu mpana wa haki, chenye ujasiri wa kuuliza maswali magumu, na kisichokubali tena siasa za mazoea. Chadema itaendelea kuwajengea vijana hawa misingi ya uongozi unaochanganya maadili, maarifa, na ubunifu, ili wabebe bendera ya mabadiliko kwa ujasiri, maarifa, na maadili, si kwa jazba tupu bali kwa dira, nidhamu, na uelewa wa kina wa changamoto za taifa.

Kwa kufanya hivyo, Chadema inajipambanua si tu kama chama cha upinzani, bali kama harakati ya kizazi na fikra, inayounganisha ndoto za vijana na matumaini ya taifa zima—harakati inayotazama mbele, inayokumbatia siasa za kisasa, na inayojitayarisha kuongoza Tanzania ya kesho kwa haki, uhuru, na maendeleo jumuishi, na katika hili tunajisikia fahari kuitwa Wanaharakati ambao mapenzi yetu katika haki na utawala wa sheria na uzalendo wetu utabaki kuwa alama njema mbele ya Watanzania wote.

WITO KWA KITAIFA

Watanzania wenzangu, 

Tunawaalika Watanzania wote, bila kujali itikadi, vyama au misimamo ya kisiasa—kusimama pamoja katika mapambano ya kizazi chetu: kudai haki isiyo na upendeleo, uhuru usio na hofu, na Katiba inayotokana na ridhaa ya wananchi, si matakwa ya wachache. Huu si wito wa chama, bali ni wito wa Taifa; si sauti ya hasira, bali ya dhamira; si mwamko wa muda, bali ahadi ya mustakabali. Taifa linapokosa haki, hata amani hubaki kivuli; na Katiba inapokosa uhalali wa wananchi, dola hubaki na nguvu bila uhalisia wa ridhaa.

Historia itatuuliza, na itafanya hivyo bila huruma—tulisimama upande gani wakati misingi ya Taifa ilipokuwa ikitetereka. Kama alivyoonya Edmund Burke, “The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing.” Ukimya wetu leo unaweza kuwa hatia ya kesho; kutochukua hatua ni uamuzi wenye athari zake. Huu ni wakati wa kuchagua ujasiri badala ya hofu, ukweli badala ya urahisi, na mshikamano badala ya mgawanyiko.

Tuchukue wajibu wa kizazi: tusimame kwa pamoja, tuseme kwa sauti moja, na tutende kwa hatua za kisheria na za amani—kwa sababu haki hujengwa na watu wanaokataa kunyamaza. Kama alivyosema Hannah Arendt, “The most radical revolutionary will become a conservative the day after the revolution.” Hivyo, mapambano yetu yasijengwe juu ya mihemko ya muda, bali juu ya misingi thabiti ya haki, uwajibikaji na heshima ya utu wa Mtanzania. Leo tunaitwa; kesho tutaulizwa. Sasa ndiyo wakati.

Kwa umuhimu, tunawaomba wanachama na Watanzania wote kuendelea kutuunga mkono na kuendelea kujiunga na Chadema kupitia mfumo wa Chadema Digital. Ni wakati sahihi sasa Watanzania tusimame na tuhesabiwe, hivyo hesabu yetu na isomeke kwa kujiunga kwa wingi kama wanachama wa chama hiki mnachokiamini.

Aidha, tunawaalika wananchi wote kushiriki na kuungana nasi katika wiki la maadhimisho kwa chama chetu ambayo yatahitimishwa kwenye kilele tarehe 21 Januari 2026, siku ambayo Chadema ilipata rasmi usajili wa kudumu kama chama cha siasa.

HITIMISHO

Watanzania wenzangu,

Mwaka 2026 usiwe mwaka wa ahadi tupu, bali uwe mwanzo wa awamu mpya ya mapambano ya kikatiba, kidemokrasia na kimaadili—mapambano yanayomrejeshea mwananchi heshima yake, sauti yake na mustakabali wake. Historia imetufundisha jambo moja lisilopingika: hakuna dola iliyo kubwa kuliko haki, na hakuna nguvu iliyo imara kuliko umoja wa wananchi walioamua kusimama upande wa kweli.

Tukiwa wamoja, tukijawa na ujasiri wa kusema kweli, na tukiwa na imani isiyotikisika katika haki, tutavunja ukimya wa hofu na minyororo ya udhalimu. Kama alivyosema Martin Luther King Jr.: “The arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice.” Huu ni wakati wetu wa kuupinda huo mkunjo wa historia kwa mikono yetu wenyewe.
 
Kwa umoja wetu, kwa ujasiri wetu, na kwa imani yetu katika haki—tutashinda. Sio kwa sababu ni rahisi, bali kwa sababu ni sahihi.

Mungu Ibariki Tanzania, Mungu Ibariki Afrika.

Asanteni kwa kunisikiliza.

Imetolewa leo Jumamosi, tarehe 03 Januari, 2026 na;

JOHN WEGESA HECHE

Pakistan and Bangladesh are reportedly exploring the possible sale of JF‑17 Thunder fighter aircraft as part of a broader push to expand bilateral defence cooperation, a development being closely watched in New Delhi amid signs of strain in India–Bangladesh relations.

High-level talks took place in Islamabad on Tuesday between PAF Chief Air Marshal Zaheer Ahmed Baber Sidhu and Bangladesh Air Force Chief Air Marshal Hasan Mahmood Khan. Discussions focused on operational cooperation, training exchanges, and the potential procurement of the JF‑17, Pakistan’s multi-role fighter jointly developed with China. While discussions are still at a preliminary stage, Pakistan’s willingness to supply the JF‑17, provide pilot training, and offer a full maintenance and ISR cooperation package signals a long-term strategy to strengthen operational ties with the Bangladesh Air Force. AFIC Responds to Royal Commission Announcement: Community Must Be Part of the Conversation

The Australian Federation of Islamic Councils (AFIC) notes the formal establishment of a Royal Commission into the Bondi attack and the broader issues of antisemitism and social cohesion.

While AFIC supports efforts to examine and understand the factors that led to this tragedy, we are deeply concerned that no consultation was undertaken with Muslim communities prior to the drafting of the Terms of Reference, despite the Commission’s clear intent to examine broader questions of racism, hate, and national cohesion.

“If the Commission is going to examine issues like antisemitism, racism, and social cohesion, then it is essential that the voices and experiences of all affected communities, including Australian Muslims, are part of the process,” said Dr Rateb Jneid, President of AFIC. “It is disappointing that the government did not engage with us from the outset.”

We recognise the pain caused by the Bondi tragedy and the importance of national efforts to ensure it is never repeated. But a meaningful exploration of racism and hate cannot be selective. Social cohesion cannot be built on exclusion.

AFIC remains committed to working constructively with the Royal Commission and will engage fully to ensure that:
• Matters impacting the Australian Muslim community are properly addressed
• Islamophobia and other forms of racism are not sidelined or minimised
• The Commission’s findings and recommendations reflect the full breadth of the Australian experience

We call on the Royal Commission to approach its work with integrity, balance, and transparency and to recognise that the goal of social cohesion cannot be achieved without inclusive dialogue and genuine community partnership.

She died at 41, never married, no children—and the world called her a tragic failure. Then they opened her journals.
Emily Dickinson spent most of her adult life in her family's home in Amherst, Massachusetts. She rarely left. She wore white. She never married. She had no children. And when she died in 1886, her neighbors whispered what they'd always suspected: what a waste. What a lonely, strange, tragic life.
They had no idea what she'd been doing in that room.
After Emily's death, her sister Lavinia discovered something extraordinary: nearly 1,800 poems, hand-sewn into small booklets, hidden in a locked chest. Poems that would eventually revolutionize American literature. Poems that scholars still study, that students memorize, that capture truths about existence most people spend lifetimes trying to articulate.
Emily Dickinson wasn't wasting her life in isolation. She was building a cathedral of language that would outlive everyone who pitied her.
But during her lifetime? She was the old maid. The spinster. The peculiar woman who chose solitude over society. The cautionary tale mothers whispered to daughters: Don't end up like Emily.
This wasn't unique to Emily. It was the story culture told about every woman who remained unmarried.
For centuries, the "old maid" wasn't just a descriptor—it was a weapon. A warning system designed to keep women compliant through fear. The message was simple: step outside the prescribed path of marriage and motherhood, and you'll die alone, bitter, and forgotten.
It didn't matter if you were brilliant, creative, fulfilled, or surrounded by love. If you weren't married with children, you were failing at womanhood itself.
This narrative served a specific function. Women who remained outside marriage retained something dangerous: autonomy. Control over their time, their bodies, their money, their choices. In systems built on channeling women's labor and reproduction into male-governed institutions, that autonomy was destabilizing.
So culture created a counter-story: You'll regret it. You'll be lonely. Your life will be meaningless. You'll wish you'd chosen differently.
Fear replaced legal coercion as the enforcement mechanism.
But here's what the myth erased: the actual lives of unmarried women.
Women like Florence Nightingale, who declined multiple marriage proposals to revolutionize nursing and save thousands of lives. Women like Jane Addams, who founded Hull House and won the Nobel Peace Prize. Women like Louisa May Alcott, who supported her entire family through her writing while never marrying.
Women like the millions of widows who declined to remarry. Women excluded from marriage by law or circumstance. Women who poured love and energy into communities, professions, friendships, and movements. Women whose capacity to nurture and contribute had nothing to do with whether they bore children.
The cruelty of the "old maid" myth lies in its erasure. It reduces a woman's entire existence to one question: Did your body fulfill its reproductive function on society's timeline?
Everything else—your work, your relationships, your mind, your heart, your contributions—becomes irrelevant.
But the myth persists not because it's true. It persists because it's repeated.
It shows up in "jokes" about cat ladies. In concerned questions about when you'll "settle down." In predictions that you'll "change your mind." In the assumption that childless women are somehow less nurturing, less fulfilled, less complete.
Yet research tells a different story. Studies consistently show that many unmarried and childfree women report high life satisfaction, strong social connections, and deep contentment. Their fulfillment isn't predicated on self-denial or biological legacy. They've simply built lives on different foundations.
The "old maid" was never a reflection of reality. She was a reflection of cultural anxiety—specifically, anxiety about women who prioritize their own sovereignty over social expectations.
Strip away the stigma, and what remains isn't tragedy. It's just a woman living on her own terms.
And that, apparently, has always been the real transgression.
Emily Dickinson died in 1886. The world pitied her as a lonely spinster who wasted her potential.
Today, she's one of the most celebrated poets in American history. Her poems are taught in every school. Her home is a museum. Literary scholars still debate the nuances of her dashes and slant rhymes.
And the people who pitied her? History forgot their names entirely.
Maybe Emily wasn't the tragedy. Maybe the tragedy was a culture so rigid it couldn't recognize fulfillment when it wore an unexpected face.
The "old maid" doesn't need saving. She never did. She just needed the world to stop insisting she was broken simply because she refused to break herself into an acceptable shape.
Emily Dickinson wrote: "The Soul selects her own Society—Then shuts the Door."
She knew exactly what she was doing. And history proved her right.

For 42 years, one little boy’s name all but vanished from the public record. 

This week, it came back.

Edward Noah Harwell was just five years old when he disappeared in March of 1983 near the Little Tallapoosa River in Carrollton, Georgia. 

He had been playing outside when a witness reported seeing him fall into the river. 

A major snowstorm had hit the area the day before, and melting snow and heavy rain left the water moving fast and dangerously high. 

Search crews looked for days, but Edward was never found.

As years passed, records went missing, answers never came, and the people who once spoke for Edward are no longer here.

Now, his brother Jason is determined to change that.

After reaching out to authorities in Carrollton, a detective began piecing together what little information existed, searching across departments and decades-old records. 

That effort led to the discovery of an incident report preserved on microfilm, and with it, the official reopening of Edward’s cold case.

Edward has now been entered into national missing children databases, including NCIC, bringing renewed attention to a disappearance that was nearly lost to time.

Jason is asking anyone who lived in the West Georgia Mobile Home Park in 1983 (now Lawrence Mobile Home Park), or anyone who remembers the search or that stretch of river, to come forward.

Edward was five years old. He was a twin. He mattered.

Sharing his story could help finally bring answers to a family that has waited more than four decades.

Garissa Farmers Field Day: Boosting Agriculture and Livestock in Arid Lands.

The County Government of Garissa, in partnership with the Kuza Jamii Project, is set to host a Farmers Field Day in Garissa Township on January 17, 2026. This event aims to bring together approximately 3,000 farmers from six sub-counties: Dadaab, Balambala, Lagdera, Fafi, Garissa Township, and Ijara.

The event, themed "Farm to Market: Creating Stronger Agricultural Supply Chains," will feature local cooperatives showcasing their products and success stories. Some of the participating cooperatives include Dadaab Safi Women Milk Cooperative Society, Dadaab Mercy Cooperative Society, and Garissa Camel Milk SACCO, among others.

Governor Nathif Jama is expected to officiate the event, which aims to exchange knowledge, showcase innovations, and strengthen the agricultural value chain.

Anthony Albanese has in a fiery exchange defended excluding intelligence chiefs from National Security Committee meetings during his government’s first term.

The heads of Australia’s domestic and foreign intelligence agencies were made non-permanent members of the NSC in 2023 and only attended meetings on a case-by-case basis.

They were reinstated as permanent members in 2024 after their exclusion sparked widespread criticism.

With intelligence and policing services facing heavy scrutiny in the wake of the deadly December 14 Bondi terror attack, the Prime Minister was on Friday asked if he had made a mistake by excluding the spy chiefs.

“The premise of the question is wrong,” Mr Albanese told the ABC.

“We have completely engaged with all of the national security (agencies).”

He was pressed further, with it put to him that ASIO Director-General Mike Burgess did not sit in national security committee meetings for two years.

Mr Albanese did not deny that but pointed out the journalist peppering him was not at the meetings and that he was.

“What Mike Burgess didn’t do was sit through all of the meetings when we were doing the AUKUS arrangements,” he said.

“But any time that there was anything to do with intelligence or anything else, Mike Burgess is always in the room – every single occasion.”

Mr Albanese last month announced a departmental probe into the country’s intelligence agencies and police forces to ensure information was flowing as needed.

Many have questioned how the Bondi suspects, Sajid Akram and his son Naveed, stayed under the radar of counter-terrorism watchers.

Sajid Akram, who was killed in the police response, had amassed six firearms since acquiring his gun licence in 2013.

Six years later, intelligence officers looked into Naveed for consorting with members of an Islamic State cell in Sydney.

He fell off their radar despite frequenting an Islamic centre in Sydney’s west infamous for extremist preachings.

That centre was shut down late last year after the local council found it did not hold necessary permits.

Mr Albanese picked respected former public servant Dennis Richardson to lead the review.

Separately, NSW Premier Chris Minns said his government was reserving the right to appoint an “independent person” to potentially probe security arrangements, particularly advice from the Jewish security service CSG to NSW Police and the potential arming of CSG employees.

“I don’t want that to read that we’ve got any concerns about our Commonwealth royal commission,” he said.

“It’s just that there are certain issues that are particular to NSW, particularly in relation to police activity on the day, the number of police, ongoing security for the Jewish community, that might require a quicker determination, and I reserve the right to do that.”

Probe must examine schools, arts sector: Lesser

Berowra MP and Jewish Australian Julian Leeser urged the royal commission to probe alleged anti-Semitism on university campuses, in the arts sector, and in the Australian Human Rights Commission if it “wanted to be taken seriously”.

The Coalition this week proposed wide-reaching terms for its proposed royal commission, which would seek to examine not only security arrangements, but the university, arts, and cultural sectors, as well as the media.

Mr Leeser released a statement on Friday in which he he said he had called for a judicial inquiry into anti-Semitism on university campuses in November 2023 and that, since his appointment as shadow spokesperson for education, it had become “clear” universities had not grappled with anti-Semitism.

He went on to claim Jewish creatives had also faced doxxing, de-platforming, and disrespect.

“A Royal Commission which does not examine anti-Semitism in the arts and cultural sector cannot be taken seriously,” he said.

“These matters are within the scope of the terms of reference. The royal commission not only has the power to examine these matters it also has the duty to do so.

“These matters must be given the time, depth and dignity that they deserve.

“A royal commission that does not properly examine the university, arts and human rights sector will fail in its charter.”

‘I have listened’

Mr Albanese was grilled on his backflip as he undertook his morning show blitz on Friday.

He stuck closely to his message that the decision was the product of careful consideration and that the overwhelming demands for a royal commission had not forced his hand.

“I have listened to people, we have considered everyone’s position,” Mr Albanese told the ABC, adding that he was “very pleased that it’s been welcomed across the political spectrum”.

“At no stage have I engaged in political rhetoric during this period.

“What I have done is engage and sit down with families.

“I’ve listened to them, I’ve sat down in people’s homes, I’ve had people to Kirribilli House, we’ve had people to Admiralty House.

“Even on New Year’s Eve, we sat down and discussed with families, with rabbis.”

He said he had also “engaged with others as well about social cohesion and how we build it going forward”.

“And I’ve determined that this is the right way forward,” he said.

Other senior government ministers fronting media on Thursday morning echoed Mr Albanese, with Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles saying that “in speaking with the community, in speaking with the families of victims, it is clear that a Royal Commission has a very significant role to play in bringing the country together and ensuring that the community is heard”.

Attorney-General Michelle Rowland – who is at the centre of complex snap laws being drafted in response to the Bondi attack – said the government had “taken time to get this right” and “listened to people” rather than play politics.

Both were asked if Mr Albanese had got it wrong in delaying calling a royal commission, but it was levelled at Mr Marles that he himself had been “dishonest” in previously saying it was not needed.

Mr Marles in December dismissed a royal commission as taking too long.

Talking to 2GB, he refused to admit he was wrong when asked point blank.

“Our concern was around time, and royal commissions do generally take years, but this will be a fast royal commission, and we’ve wanted to get it right,” Mr Marles said.

“I’d be the first to say we have listened, and … listening to people is what has seen the change in the position that we have put it put forward.”

Iqbal Akhtar:
Welcome again to our interfaith podcast for our FIU online course. My name is Professor Ikwalakar, in the Department of Religious Studies and Politics and International Relations. We’re very honored today to have Professor Juan Cole from the University of Michigan with us. He is one of the leading scholars of the Islamic world and the Middle East. He’s here for a conference, and we were very lucky to grab him for a few minutes.

To get started, could you talk a little bit about your background—where you grew up and what took you on this intellectual path? I know you eventually went on a Fulbright to India, but I’m curious about your early experiences that might have shaped this journey.

Juan Cole:
Sure. My father was in the U.S. military, and I grew up traveling. I went to twelve schools in twelve years. We had two long tours in Europe, in France. When I was a teenager, we had a posting of about a year and a half in Eritrea, which was then part of Ethiopia.

Eritrea is a multicultural place. It’s about one-third Muslim and two-thirds Christian. There were mosques, you heard the call to prayer, and we had Eritrean Muslim friends. That was my first serious contact with the Muslim world, there in the Horn of Africa.

When I got back to the United States, it was the late 1960s—still very much the 1960s. My generation was interested in spirituality and alternative states of consciousness. I read a lot about Sufism, for instance. When I went to college at Northwestern, I majored in the history of religions. I was interested in all the world religions, but especially in Asian ones—Islam, Hinduism, and Buddhism were particular interests of mine.

I began taking Arabic as an undergraduate. I was only nineteen when I started, which is early for most Americans. Often people don’t get to Arabic until graduate school. I think that early exposure helped me.

Northwestern had a wonderful program called the Traveling Scholars, endowed by an alumnus. It was competitive: you designed a research project. I put together a project on Christian–Muslim dialogue in Lebanon after the Second Vatican Council. The Catholic Church had encouraged dialogue with other religions, and the council’s documents on Islam were actually quite positive from a Catholic point of view. They spoke about the light of Christ being present in Islam and praised Muslims for honoring Jesus and Mary—something unimaginable a century earlier.

Lebanon was a perfect place for this dialogue. There were meetings and publications, and some prominent Lebanese intellectuals were involved. I went to interview the principals and participants. I had started Modern Standard Arabic, but only as a book language. While in Beirut, I took a class in colloquial Lebanese Arabic and learned to speak the language. When I first arrived, I would say things in Modern Standard Arabic and people would laugh—it was like speaking Shakespearean English to someone.

I didn’t realize it at the time, but I was already set on a path. Scholarship often runs along language lines. If you study Buddhism, you learn Sanskrit, Chinese, Japanese, and so on. Since I had decided to learn Arabic, that became what I had going for me.

Iqbal Akhtar :
That’s fascinating. A bit of a tangent, but in the 1960s people were experimenting with different forms of spirituality. Sufism seemed viable at one point as an alternative path. Buddhism, Hinduism, and Sufism were all competing, but Buddhism seems to have become the most prominent. Do you think Sufism didn’t resonate with Americans because of its inherent qualities, or because of geopolitics—like Iran and related issues?

Juan Cole:
It’s true there’s more awareness of and interest in Buddhism among Americans interested in Eastern religions. I don’t think Sufism ever really went away, though. There’s a small minority of people interested in it even today. There are directories of Sufi organizations in major cities. But it’s relatively small compared to Buddhism.

I couldn’t tell you exactly why. One of the problems in the history of religions is that we know things change, but people don’t usually write in their diaries why they made those changes. Answering why something didn’t happen is especially difficult. It would take a large research project with interviews.

Professor Iqbal Akhtar :
You spent time in Lebanon studying Christian–Muslim relations. What were some takeaways from that experience? What challenges did Vatican II present for relations between Christians and Muslims in Lebanon?

Juan Cole:
In Lebanon, religion was very siloed. I was amazed to find that I knew more about Islam than many Christian Lebanese did. They didn’t talk to their Muslim neighbors about religion, and Lebanese Muslims often didn’t know much about Christianity. That’s why the dialogue movement was useful.

One takeaway was how siloed people can be, and how ignorant they can be of realities living just across the hall from them. I’ve found this generally in my research in Africa and elsewhere: you have multi-ethnic, multi-religious societies, but people don’t really engage theologically. That’s a modern phenomenon, and the interfaith movement helped change it—talking about religion without proselytizing, simply to understand and reduce prejudice.

Another takeaway was that I was hobbled by not knowing enough history. I needed to know more about the history of the Maronite Church and of Islam. I spent a lot of time reading history. I was a religion major focused on theology, but I found I liked reading history. That was one transition toward becoming a historian.

Iqbal Akhtar:
Can you talk about that transition?

Juan Cole:
The nail in the coffin was the Lebanese Civil War. After graduating from Northwestern in 1975, I went back to Lebanon to try to do an MA in religion at the American University of Beirut. It was the only institution in the Middle East offering a non-seminary religion degree—the history of religions as an academic discipline. It wasn’t really allowed in Egypt at the time.

But when I arrived, the war had broken out. There was fighting for control of tall buildings downtown—hotels, which gradually looked like Swiss cheese. From the campus, you could see rocket trails. We were called together and told the university wouldn’t open that year.

I went to Jordan for a while, then applied to the American University in Cairo. Beirut wasn’t going to settle down. I did my MA in Cairo, determined to become near-native fluent in Arabic, which you can’t easily do in the United States. I also reacted against the American academic tradition of brief fieldwork followed by lifelong expertise. I wanted depth.

Cairo didn’t have a religion program, but it did have history, so I moved into history. I worked on nineteenth-century Muslim reformers from a historical rather than theological perspective. When I later went to UCLA, I already had historical training and began to think of history as my discipline.

I also reacted against some of the disciplinary assumptions of the history of religions as I had learned it. We were under the shadow of the University of Chicago, where phenomenology of religion was ascendant, and that approach was somewhat ahistorical. You know, it was all about myth cycles and things like that. First of all, it wasn’t very relevant to Islamic studies. It developed mostly out of Hinduism, Christianity, and Buddhism. I don’t know what “myth cycles” there are in Islam. That’s a bit silly.

Phenomenology also seemed detached from concrete reality. I became interested in how history is researched—the use of archives, personal papers, and getting deep into the details of a person’s mind and thought at a level that phenomenology doesn’t really allow. Personally and philosophically, I was drawn to being a historian.

Iqbal Akhtar:
That’s very interesting. Then you went on to a Fulbright?

Juan Cole:
When I went to UCLA for my PhD work, I had actually gone back to Lebanon in the meantime and worked for a newspaper there. We thought the Lebanese civil war might be over in 1978, but it wasn’t. I was working for this newspaper, and sometimes we couldn’t put the paper to bed because Syrian artillery had knocked out the electricity or similar things happened. I could see there wasn’t a future for me as a newspaper man in Beirut, so I went to UCLA to do a PhD.

While I was in Beirut, it was during the Iranian Revolution. That revolution was a local story in Beirut because it has a large Shiʿi population, and the Shiʿa mobilized. Our newspaper covered these events, and I worked mainly as a translator, taking Arabic wire services and putting them into English. I followed the Iranian Revolution very closely and its local reverberations in Lebanon.

I initially went to UCLA because it had the best Iranian studies program in the country. I planned to do my dissertation on Iran, which was plausible even after the revolution in the summer of 1979. Many American academics went to Iran for research then. But the hostage crisis happened, guerrilla groups took American diplomats hostage, and there was no embassy, no visas, no diplomatic relations. I couldn’t do research in Iran.

I had already done a lot of background research toward a dissertation topic I was interested in: the rise of the Shiʿi clergy as a ruling class. Where did that come from? There isn’t another modern country where clerics seized power as a group in the same way the military does. That seemed strange, and I wondered whether there was something about Shiʿi traditions that helped explain how it could happen. I was reluctant to let go of the subject, so I thought I might do it as a manuscript library project.

I went to manuscript library catalogues, and when I got into the India catalogues, I discovered something I hadn’t known, that there had been Shiʿi-ruled kingdoms in India between the fall of the Mughals and the rise of the British. The catalogues showed that these Shiʿi kingdoms had generated a great deal of writing and patronized clerics to produce texts. The manuscripts were sitting there. When I looked at the secondary literature, I found nothing about it. It was an unknown subject, which is exactly what you want as a PhD student.

So I applied for a Fulbright and Social Science Research Council grants. They accepted my application and sent me to South Asia. It was unexpected but also very appealing. As a teenager in the late 1960s, I had been interested in India and Gandhi. There was a mystique of India for me. I hadn’t imagined combining my interest in the Middle East and Islam with India, but this was the perfect opportunity.

I went to Lucknow in Uttar Pradesh and made contact with the local Shiʿa. Some were university professors who understood what I was doing. They opened their hearts to me, and more importantly, their libraries, including manuscripts. I came from a generation of scholars of Islam and the Middle East who were impatient with relying mainly on French and British archives to study the modern period. It wasn’t widely known in the 1960s how rich the surviving manuscript tradition was. Only a small portion had ever been printed. You could find handwritten books from 1750, 1790, 1830, often unique copies that required going to where they were held.

I wasn’t alone in this; scholars like Peter Gran were beginning to use these materials and publicize their existence. I wrote my dissertation primarily from these primary sources written by Indians, often in Arabic and Persian. Most Indians don’t read Arabic anymore. They can recite the Qur’an but wouldn’t read a book in Arabic. So I was doing work even local scholars might not have done. I wrote a history of Shiʿi religion and religious practices in North India in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

Historians had treated this period largely as a chess piece in the British conquest of India, focusing on diplomacy and economics. But an inner cultural history of Shiʿi practices, including their dialogue with Hindu practices, hadn’t been done. That became my dissertation and my first book. It got me the job at Michigan and laid the foundation for my career.

Iqbal Akhtar:
Your work is really groundbreaking, at least in English, in showing that these Shiʿi kingdoms were not only important but central to the creation of high Muslim culture in South Asia. That’s fascinating.

I’m interested in how you moved from teaching and historical work to more public-facing scholarship. What took you in that direction?

Juan Cole:
Because I had done my MA in Cairo and lived there in the 1970s, and then did PhD work in India and Pakistan, I had lived on the terrain where components of al-Qaeda later emerged. In Egypt, you read the newspapers and saw that members of Islamic Jihad had been arrested. It was impossible not to be aware of it. Being specialized in Islamic movements, I followed these developments.

When I was in Peshawar in 1982, Afghan refugees had arrived. I didn’t know it then, but I was in the same city as Bin Laden, Zawahiri, and later leaders of al-Qaeda, who were running what was called the Office of Services for the Afghan mujahidin fighting the Soviet invasion.

I came back to the United States and got the job at Michigan. I taught courses on the modern Middle East, South Asia, and the Mughal Empire. When 9/11 happened, America was seized with curiosity, fear, and anxiety about who these people were and why they had done what they did. I knew exactly who they were. I didn’t have to look it up. I had lived with it.

At that time, intellectual exchange of a specialized sort often happened through email round-robins. You had a CC list of people interested in a topic, and discussions unfolded rapidly. I was on a list called Gulf 2000, founded by Gary Sick, formerly of the National Security Council. Academics and policymakers asked questions there, and I could answer them quickly. The internet was useful because it was fast; if you waited a week, the question would be forgotten.

My answers about al-Qaeda were well regarded by colleagues. Although the list was supposed to be internal, people forwarded messages, and I began receiving emails from abroad. People asked for back issues. At the time, email programs didn’t have good search functions, so retrieving old messages was a hassle.

In the winter of 2001, blogging began to become well known. Andrew Sullivan was an early prominent blogger, and there wasn’t much serious content yet, mostly cats. I thought I would start a blog to archive my email messages, since I considered them public. Then I could just give people a URL. That was in the spring of 2002, when I began putting material on a weblog.

In the early days of the World Wide Web, pages were like index cards. You couldn’t scroll; the only movement was via hyperlinks. Each page had to be manually uploaded using file transfer protocol. You could go sideways through links, but not up and down. In 1999, young software engineers invented Blogger.com. It had a window where you could put text in, press “publish,” and it would FTP [file transfer protocol] it for you. You didn’t have to do it manually. It would push down whatever text was there before and put the new text on top. That became much more convenient, and that was the software most bloggers used initially to put up their web pages.

After a while, especially in the summer, when professors don’t teach, I would have time to do research and I would be tooling around the web. I knew Arabic, so I could find out things other people couldn’t. If I found an interesting article about al-Qaeda and its history, I would translate it and put it on the website. So I started making original entries. At first the website might get fifty people a day, or seventy-five. It was a small thing.

Then Bush decided to invade Iraq. The Shiʿa I had studied in India went on pilgrimage to Iraq, and there had been a lot of back-and-forth between Iran, Iraq, and North India because the Indian Shiʿi kingdom of Awadh that I studied was rich. There was patronage and pilgrimage and so forth. Two chapters of my dissertation were set in Iraq. I knew who the Iraqi Shiʿa were. I knew who their grandparents were.

When Bush decided to go to Iraq, I was able to talk knowledgeably about Iraqi history and society. Once Saddam fell, Iraqis put up hundreds of websites. Some were city-oriented, so you could read local news about what was happening in a particular neighborhood. There was no censorship. I could find out almost anything. A high-ranking U.S. general once wrote me in that period and said, “How do you know these things?” Apparently I was doing a better job than his intelligence people.

I blogged Iraq. Once Bush decided to go to war there and send U.S. troops, he sent a hundred thousand, a hundred and twenty thousand troops. Each of those troops had family and friends. That’s a big constituency of people who really wanted to know what was going on, because they cared about the fate of their loved ones. In addition, it was a national project. Bush promised Americans he was going to turn Iraq into a beacon on the hill, and people became emotionally invested in Iraq. It’s funny now. There were elections in Iraq last October and I don’t think the American public even knew it happened. But in the early 2000s, people were focused on Iraq like a laser.

Blog technology at the time had a side panel called a blogroll, where you recommended other sites to your readers. People with weblogs related to foreign affairs would put my weblog in their blogroll as a hyperlink. When readers finished something on that site, they would click and come to me.

Then some mega-bloggers with large followings linked to me. I woke up one morning and had sixty thousand hits. In April 2004, at the height of the struggles between the Marines and the Mahdi Army, I had a million hits that month. I’d never had a million of anything.

Then public television called, The [PBS] NewsHour, and cable news, CNN, and once Fox. I testified before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, then headed by Joe Biden and Dick Lugar, because they couldn’t get the Bush administration to tell them what in the world was going on in Iraq. I gained a certain odd sort of celebrity. I was recognized in restaurants in D.C. I remember being in Minnesota giving a talk, paying a taxi by credit card, and the driver looked at it and said, “Oh, are you the Juan Cole?”

It wasn’t a frivolous Hollywood kind of celebrity. I didn’t have the pink limousine. But I was well known. C. P. Snow said that a celebrity is someone who’s very well known for being very well known. In a minor way — I don’t want to make too much of it — I entered those ranks. It was because the country wanted the knowledge I had. They wanted the analysis I had, and I consulted with the government.

I had been against the Vietnam War and marched against it. But with al-Qaeda and Iraq, I thought the Iraq war was a bad idea, but I also wanted a soft landing for everybody. I really wanted to do whatever I could to help destroy al-Qaeda. So the government called me to consult. I went and told them what I knew. I thought, I’m a public intellectual. The people of Michigan, for whatever reason, pay me to tell the public these things. The government is part of that public. So I was willing to talk to other experts in D.C. and share that knowledge.

I kept expecting this to be a one-year adventure and to be over, but it lasted as long as people were interested in Iraq. Then ISIL arose, and there was that. There were twenty years when a big chunk of my career was telling people about Islam and the Middle East.

Then I found there was so much Islamophobia in my comments. As hard as I tried to inform people, I couldn’t always get through. It occurred to me that trying to explain radical groups like al-Qaeda and ISIL to people is not the best way to inform them about Islam more generally, because Americans didn’t realize it, but those are tiny little sects. Almost nobody pays attention to them in their home countries except to the extent that they’re violent.

I had been trained at the American University in Cairo and UCLA in early Islamic studies, so I decided to write a book about the idea of peace in the Qur’an. As far as I could tell, there had not been such a book. I found concepts of reconciliation, peace, moderation, and dialogue throughout the Qur’an. Muslims know this, but the Western public, including the Western academic public, mostly didn’t.

That became my project from the middle of the last decade. I wrote a book about Muhammad and peace. I edited a book about peace movements in Islam, looking at a range of them. There are many peace movements in Muslim societies, but people don’t think about them that way. They didn’t know about them. After the genocide in Bosnia and the Dayton Accords, Muslim women formed organizations to work for reconciliation with their Serbian neighbors. There is a literature on this, but it’s not in people’s consciousness.

Iqbal Akhtar:
We’re nearing our time to end, but I’m interested—given your varied career and the work you’ve done—what are the main takeaways you would want students to have, especially those interested in interfaith dialogue or the Middle East more generally? What are the key learnings people should know about the world, especially as we see things unfolding today?

Juan Cole:
With regard to the first part of your question — studying Islam, its history, its thought -— the Victorians in the nineteenth century developed a notion they called the enlargement of the self. It was common for people to go on vacation to Italy, for instance. We now do this routinely, but in the mid-nineteenth century it was a big deal, mostly for rich people. They were often hardline Protestants going into a Catholic environment. The churches were gaudy from their point of view. But they would be exposed to wonderful Renaissance art.

George Eliot, the novelist, who was a woman but wrote under a man’s name, talked about her trip to Italy and the way it was an enlargement of herself, of ordinary life, she called it. This was a whole concept at the time. It was also a time when the Victorian world was sticking its fingers all over the world, but intellectuals and cultural figures found beauty in other cultures in a way that administrators sometimes did not.

So that enlargement of the self, the ways in which you can widen your horizons and deepen your understanding, that’s worth gold. Learning another language, another way of expressing yourself, understanding concepts: the world looks different when you know another language.

There’s an Arabic proverb: kullu lisān insān, every language is a person. When you learn a new language, it’s like you have a new personality incorporated into yourself.

Although there may be more public interest in the history of Zen Buddhism, those Sufis in Islam are really interesting people. They have fascinating stories to tell, not only sermons and homilies, but tales, folk tales with spiritual import. They have large books full of these stories. They’re more spiritual kinds of stories, not like the Thousand and One Nights, which are also interesting. The study of that literature is rewarding in its own right, and it gives you spiritual insights useful in facing life.

With regard to geopolitics, I don’t think I have to make a strong pitch. We don’t understand the Middle East, but we rampage around it like an elephant in a china shop. I have been both pleasantly surprised and deeply disappointed by my interactions with officials in Washington. Some were on the ball. A very large number were completely ignorant of the places they were trying to run. That’s inadvisable.

If the U.S. public is going to keep having things to do with the Middle East, the public needs to get up to speed, do the reading, and investigate.

Iqbal Akhtar:
Thank you so much, Professor Cole. It’s an honor and a pleasure.

Juan Cole:
Thank you.” …

The 13th Pakistan–United States bilateral joint exercise, *Inspired Gambit–2026*, commenced on 09 January 2026 at the National Counter Terrorism Centre (NCTC), Pabbi. The two-week-long exercise is being conducted in the Counter Terrorism (CT) domain, involving professional contingents from the Armies of Pakistan and the United States.

Officials from both sides attended the opening ceremony.

The exercise is aimed at enhancing mutual understanding and interoperability through the sharing of counter-terrorism experiences, while further refining tactics, techniques, and procedures essential for effective CT operations. Emphasis is being laid on marksmanship skills during urban warfare, as well as on understanding each other’s operational doctrines and best practices.

Such joint training exercises are of vital importance in addressing evolving security challenges, improving professional military standards, and strengthening the capacity of both forces to operate in complex counter-terrorism environments. Inspired Gambit–2026 reflects the continued commitment of Pakistan and the United States towards collaborative efforts for peace and stability.

Wajir Elders Rubbish Gachagua’s Remarks on Somali Community, Demand NCC Probe

- Compiled Ahmed Salat AARAN TV KE News Desk 

Elders from Wajir County have rubbished remarks attributed to Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua on the Somali community, saying he should stop sidelining them, insisting they are Kenyans with equal rights like all other citizens.

The elders revisited several instances in which Gachagua has allegedly slammed the community, citing remarks on the recruitment of Somali professionals into government, the questioning of the credentials and abilities of the Hajj leadership, which they say created outrage across Northern Kenya and comments made following the removal of vetting for national identity cards.

They noted that Gachagua later claimed the move would lead to the issuance of identity cards to insurgents, a statement they say unfairly targeted the community.

They further pointed to his most recent remarks touching on BBS Mall and continued criticism of leaders from Northern Kenya, saying the pattern reflects sustained hostility and discrimination.

The elders called on Gachagua to call off what they described as negative and hateful remarks, stressing that the Somali community is made up of hardworking businessmen and businesswomen who pay taxes like other Kenyans and contribute significantly to the national economy.

They said they fully support President William Ruto and his leadership, adding that no one can intimidate their freedom of association or their right to own property.

 “We are Kenyans, and our rights are guaranteed by the Constitution,” the elders said.

In a strong statement, the elders also called on the National Cohesion and Integration Commission (NCIC) to conduct a probe into Gachagua’s remarks, investigate their impact on national unity, and take appropriate action in line with the law.

They termed his conduct as a case of “madman syndrome” and urged him to stop what they described as political shenanigans that threaten cohesion and peaceful coexistence in the country.

The Fading Bell
In the north-eastern counties of Kenya, the school bell once rang with pride. Its sound carried across dusty plains, calling children from manyattas and small towns to classrooms built with hope. Parents believed education was the one road that could lead their children beyond drought, conflict, and neglect.
But slowly, the bell began to fade.
Teachers started leaving. Some went months without salaries; others feared insecurity on the long roads to school. Classrooms that were once full became quiet, with broken desks and torn books. When rains failed and hunger spread, many children stayed home to help their families survive, while some girls were married off too early, their dreams folded away like unused exercise books.
Amina, once the top student in her class, now sat under an acacia tree selling tea. Her school had closed after the headteacher transferred and no replacement came. Each time she heard a radio announce exam results from other regions, her heart tightened—not from jealousy, but from loss.
Community elders tried their best. They held meetings, repaired walls with their own hands, and begged leaders to remember them. Yet promises came like clouds that never rained. Education offices were far away, and the region felt forgotten.
Still, hope refused to die completely. One evening, Amina gathered younger children and began teaching them letters in the sand. Others joined her. It was small, fragile, but real.
And in that quiet act, the north-east whispered a truth to the nation: when education declines, a region bleeds silently—but when people rise to protect it, even the weakest bell can ring again.

Residential proximity to nuclear power plants and cancer incidence in Massachusetts, USA (2000–2018) – Harvard University

Abstract 
Purpose To investigate the associations between residential proximity to nuclear power plants and ZIP code–level cancer incidence among Massachusetts residents. 

Methods 
We assessed proximity of Massachusetts ZIP codes to nuclear power plants using an inverse-distance weighted metric. We obtained cancer incidence data (2000–2018) from the Massachusetts Cancer Registry. We applied two approaches: (1) longitudinal Generalized Estimating Equation (GEE) Poisson regression to evaluate yearly incidences for all cancers combined, and (2) cross-sectional log-linear Poisson regression for site-specific cancers. We adjusted models for PM2.5, demographic, socioeconomic, environmental, and healthcare covariates, and stratified analyses by sex and four age groups (45–54, 55–64, 65–74, 75 +). 

Results 
Proximity to plants significantly increased cancer incidence, with risk declining by distance. At 2 km, females showed RRs of 1.52 (95% CI: 1.20–1.94) for ages 55–64, 2.00 (1.59–2.52) for 65–74, and 2.53 (1.98–3.22) for 75 +. Males showed RRs of 1.97 (1.57–2.48), 1.75 (1.42–2.16), and 1.63 (1.29–2.06), respectively. Cancer site-specific analyses showed significant associations for lung, prostate, breast, colorectal, bladder, melanoma, leukemia, thyroid, uterine, kidney, laryngeal, pancreatic, oral, esophageal, and Hodgkin lymphoma, with variation by sex and age. We estimated 10,815 female and 9,803 male cancer cases attributable to proximity, corresponding to attributable fractions of 4.1% (95% CI: 2.4–5.7%) and 3.5% (95% CI: 1.8–5.2%). 

Conclusions 
Residential proximity to nuclear plants in Massachusetts is associated with elevated cancer risks, particularly among older adults, underscoring the need for continued epidemiologic monitoring amid renewed interest in nuclear energy.

At fourteen, she flirted with Nazi officers. Then she led them into the woods and shot them.

May 1940. Nazi tanks rolled into the Netherlands, and for most Dutch teenagers, childhood ended overnight.

For Freddie Oversteegen, it ended with a question.

She was in eighth grade, living in Haarlem with her mother—a communist who had spent years secretly hiding Jewish refugees in their home. When a resistance commander named Frans van der Wiel knocked on their door in 1941, he wasn’t looking for men.

He was looking for girls.

Because Nazi soldiers never suspected teenage girls.

Van der Wiel needed fighters—young ones who could pass checkpoints, laugh with guards, and vanish into crowds. He asked Freddie’s mother if her daughters could join the resistance.

Freddie was fourteen. Her sister Truus was sixteen.

Their mother answered without pause: “Yes. They’re ready.”

Freddie wasn’t sure she was ready. But she knew what silence meant. Jewish neighbors were disappearing. Collaborators were thriving. The Nazis were winning.

So she agreed.

Her early missions were small—delivering illegal newspapers, helping families hide, cutting phone lines. Then the assignments changed.

Van der Wiel asked if she could kill someone.

The method was brutally simple. Freddie dressed like any Dutch girl—bows in her hair, a bicycle beside her. She approached Nazi officers or collaborators in public spaces. She smiled. She flirted. Just enough.

“Would you like to take a walk in the woods?”

Most said yes. A young girl posed no threat.

Freddie led them into the forest. Sometimes her sister Truus waited there with a gun. Sometimes their friend Hannie Schaft—a red-haired woman who dyed her hair dark—stood hidden among the trees.

Sometimes Freddie fired the shot herself.

“I shot him at close range,” she said in a 2014 interview, nearly seventy years later. “I don’t want to say more than that.”

Between missions, Freddie returned home and did homework. She helped with chores. She tried to behave like a normal schoolgirl—studying verbs in the afternoon after luring men to their deaths that morning.

The mental divide was crushing. But she believed it was unavoidable.

“It was them or the people we loved,” she said.

The operations intensified. Bridges were sabotaged. Weapon convoys ambushed. Prisoners freed in daylight, guards shot as resistance members vanished into crowds before reinforcements arrived.

The Nazis protected their officers with care—but never imagined teenage girls were the danger. That blind spot cost them lives.

In 1945, Hannie Schaft was captured. The Gestapo tortured her. She gave nothing away. Three weeks before liberation, she was executed in the dunes outside Haarlem.

She was twenty-four.

Freddie and Truus survived—barely. They were hunted, nearly captured again and again, forced to watch friends die brutally.

When liberation came in May 1945, Freddie was nineteen. She had spent nearly a third of her life as an assassin.

Then came silence.

After the war, Europe preferred heroic male narratives and quiet forgetting. Women fighters were sidelined. Killing Nazis was noble for men—but unsettling when done by teenage girls.

Freddie returned to civilian life. She married. Had children. Took ordinary jobs. For decades, she told no one what she had done.

Not from shame—but because who could understand?

How do you tell your children that their mother once smiled to gain trust, then killed?

The nightmares never stopped. The faces never vanished. Freddie did not regret her actions—she believed they were necessary—but she carried every death with her.

“People ask if we felt like murderers,” she said. “We didn’t. But we weren’t heroes either. We did what had to be done.”

In the 1980s, historians began recording women’s resistance stories before they were lost. Freddie spoke—not to celebrate violence, but to explain what resistance truly demanded.

Not just bravery. Violence.

Not just risk. Moral compromise.

Not just heroism—but the willingness to do terrible things for reasons that mattered.

Her story asks an uncomfortable question: what would you do?

It’s easy to claim you’d resist fascism. Harder to accept what resistance actually requires. At fourteen, Freddie should have been thinking about dances. Instead, she calculated routes and escape angles.

At sixteen, she should have been falling in love. Instead, she learned the sound of a gunshot at close range.

The Dutch resistance succeeded partly because of people like her—young, female, underestimated. The Nazis never saw them coming.

But survival came at a cost. Freddie lived to ninety-two, but only the first fourteen years were innocent.

When Freddie Oversteegen died in 2018, obituaries called her a hero, an icon, a symbol of courage.

She rejected those words.

“We weren’t heroes,” she said until the end. “We were girls who saw what was happening and refused to look away.”

But “that’s all” meant carrying a gun. Smiling at men she would kill. Living with nightmares for seventy years. Giving up childhood, innocence, and peace for something larger than herself.

At fourteen, Freddie Oversteegen learned that courage sometimes looks like violence.

And that the most moral option available can be the unthinkable one.

When asked if she would do it again, her answer never changed:

Yes.

Because silence—safety bought with other people’s lives—was worse than anything the war took from her.

She was just a girl with ribbons in her hair and a bicycle.

The Nazis never suspected her.

That was their fatal mistake.

Royal Commissions Must Be Above Suspicion — Process Matters

By Michael Kennedy

Royal Commissions do not exist merely to uncover facts. They exist to restore public confidence when trust has been shaken. That is why perception matters almost as much as integrity itself.

The appointment of former High Court Justice Virginia Bell AC to lead the Royal Commission into the Bondi terror attack and the broader issue of antisemitism has prompted legitimate public debate. Not because of any allegation of bias or impropriety — there is none — but because of relationships, optics, and process.

Let’s be clear at the outset: Virginia Bell is a distinguished jurist. She served on the High Court of Australia from 2009 to 2021, was previously a judge of the NSW Supreme Court, and has been entrusted with sensitive inquiries before, including the investigation into former Prime Minister Scott Morrison’s secret ministerial appointments. Her legal credentials are not in dispute.

However, Royal Commissions are not ordinary inquiries. They operate in politically charged environments, often intersecting with national security, social cohesion, and government accountability. In such circumstances, confidence in independence must be unquestionable.

Ms Bell was appointed to the High Court by a Labor government under Kevin Rudd in 2009. She was formally recognised under another Labor government in 2012 for her service to the law and public policy. She has now been appointed by the Albanese government to lead one of the most sensitive Royal Commissions in recent years.

None of this establishes bias. Appointment by governments of the day is standard constitutional practice. But it does establish proximity, and proximity creates perception — especially when the appointing government is itself a stakeholder in the outcomes, policy responses, and narrative framing of the inquiry.

That perception risk is heightened by the Prime Minister’s public insistence that Ms Bell is “the most qualified person” for the role. This claim is unnecessary and unconvincing. Australia has no shortage of eminent, independent, and nationally respected figures capable of leading such an inquiry.

Among those widely regarded as equally qualified are:

Robert French, former Chief Justice of the High Court

James Allsop, former Chief Justice of the Federal Court

Dennis Richardson and Duncan Lewis, former national security chiefs with deep counterterrorism expertise

Justice Michael Lee, a Federal Court judge respected across communities, including within parts of the Jewish community

The existence of multiple credible candidates does not diminish Ms Bell — but it does raise an important question: why was there no transparent or consultative selection process?

In other Westminster democracies, appointments to inquiries of this sensitivity often involve parliamentary consultation or confirmation mechanisms. In Australia, the executive alone decides. That may be lawful, but it is no longer sufficient in an era of declining trust.

A Senate-based or bipartisan selection process would not weaken Royal Commissions — it would strengthen them. It would shield commissioners from politicised attacks, reassure affected communities, and protect findings from claims of narrative management or institutional self-interest.

Some critics have mocked concerns about perception as “politicisation.” In fact, the opposite is true. Ignoring perception is what politicises an inquiry. Transparency disarms suspicion; secrecy feeds it.

This debate is not about Virginia Bell’s integrity. It is about process integrity.

If Royal Commissions are to retain their authority in a divided and sceptical society, governments must accept a simple principle: being independent is not enough — independence must be seen to be beyond question.

That is not an attack on the commissioner. It is a call to modernise how Australia appoints those entrusted with its most serious national inquiries.

PRESS STATEMENT
NCIC SUMMONS HON. RIGATHI GACHAGUA OVER TRIBAL AND DIVISIVE REMARKS
The National Cohesion and Integration Commission (NCIC) has noted with grave concern recent public remarks attributed to Hon. Rigathi Gachagua, former Deputy President of the Republic of Kenya, which are perceived to be divisive and ethnically charged, contrary to the National Cohesion and Integration Act, 2008, particularly Sections 13(1)(a) and 62.
Of specific concern to the Commission are the following:
1. Remarks on National and Extra-County Secondary Schools
Statements suggesting that access to national and extra-county secondary schools should be influenced by regional or ethnic considerations. The Commission notes that national schools are constitutionally established to promote integration, equality, and interaction among learners from diverse backgrounds, and any discourse implying regional entitlement undermines this objective.
2. Remarks Concerning the Somali Community
Statements allegedly linking Kenyan businesses and members of the Somali community to a fraud-related incident in Minnesota, USA. The Commission is concerned that such remarks may amount to ethnic profiling and stigmatization, and risk unfairly associating an entire community with alleged criminal activity.
Following a preliminary assessment and in line with its mandate, the NCIC has summoned Hon. Rigathi Gachagua to appear before the Commission at NCIC Headquarters, Britam Towers, Upper Hill, Nairobi, to provide clarification and assist in ongoing investigations.
A WARNING TO ALL LEADERS
The Commission reminds all public leaders that their words carry responsibility. Rhetoric that stereotypes, profiles, or divides communities threatens national cohesion and will attract firm and lawful action.
Rev. Dr. Samuel Kobia, CBS
Commission Chairman

🆘 NO ONE SHOULD BE INVISIBLE. PLEASE HELP THE CIEZA 26. 🆘

Our hearts are breaking for 26 forgotten souls. Located in the Cieza kennels, these dogs are living a life of silence. Most have been there for years with zero adoption prospects. Because they are a distance away from our usual volunteer routes, they virtually never get visitors.

They spend their mornings watching the gate, waiting for someone who never comes. No walks, no treats, no soft voices—just the bars of a kennel.

At our rescue, we believe that ALL dogs matter. No matter how old they are, how long they’ve been waiting, or how far away they are. We are pleading with our community to help us change their story.
