The Gambia Ranks 4th Most Peaceful Country in Africa in 2025 Global Peace Index

The Gambia has been ranked the 4th most peaceful country in Africa and 55th globally in the 2025 Global Peace Index (GPI), marking a notable improvement in the country’s international standing on peace, stability, and security.

The ranking, published by the Institute for Economics and Peace (IEP), assesses 163 countries worldwide using 23 qualitative and quantitative indicators, including levels of societal safety and security, ongoing domestic and international conflict, and the degree of militarisation.

According to the index, The Gambia’s upward movement reflects sustained political stability, low levels of violent conflict, and continued efforts to strengthen democratic governance and national cohesion in the post-transition period. Analysts note that improvements in civil liberties, institutional trust, and security sector reforms have contributed to the country’s improved peace profile.

Within Africa, The Gambia now ranks alongside some of the continent’s most stable states. The top five African countries in the 2025 Global Peace Index are Mauritius, Botswana, Namibia, The Gambia, and Sierra Leone, countries widely recognised for relatively strong governance frameworks and low conflict exposure.

Officials and observers have described the ranking as an encouraging signal for investment confidence, tourism growth, and regional cooperation, as peace and stability remain critical foundations for sustainable development. While challenges remain, the index suggests that The Gambia’s trajectory continues to move toward greater social harmony and institutional resilience.

The Global Peace Index is widely regarded as one of the world’s leading measurements of national and regional peacefulness, and its findings are frequently used by policymakers, development partners, and investors to assess risk and long-term stability.

"Pain doesn't make you smaller it stretches you." A rape survivor told her this. Years later, she would prove those words prophetic in ways neither could imagine.
A woman in Congo spoke those words to Ashley Judd during a humanitarian mission. Ashley was there to listen, to witness, to support survivors of unspeakable violence.
But those words would become Ashley's own story too.
Because Ashley Judd has spent her life being stretched by pain and refusing to let it break her.
Born in 1968 in Granada Hills, California, Ashley Tyler Ciminella grew up in chaos. Her mother, Naomi Judd, would become a country music legend alongside Ashley's sister Wynonna. But during childhood, there was no glamour—only instability, poverty, and constant upheaval.
Her parents divorced when she was young. The family moved endlessly, struggling financially. Ashley attended thirteen different schools before graduating high school. And she experienced sexual abuse as a child—trauma that would haunt her for decades.
"I was a very hurt little girl," Ashley later revealed. "And I carried that hurt into adulthood."
But Ashley was brilliant. She enrolled at the University of Kentucky, majoring in French with minors in anthropology, art history, theater, and women's studies. She was accepted into the Peace Corps. Her path seemed destined for academia or humanitarian work.
Then she decided to try acting.
In the early 1990s, Ashley moved to Los Angeles with no formal training, no connections, and almost no money. She lived in a tiny guesthouse and worked odd jobs while auditioning.
Casting directors didn't know what to do with her. She was too intense. Too intelligent. Too strong. They wanted her softer, quieter, more "likable."
Ashley refused to shrink.In 1993, she landed the lead in an indie film called Ruby in Paradise. Shot on a shoestring budget in Florida, Ashley played a young woman escaping abuse and searching for independence.
It was raw, honest, devastating. Ashley won the Independent Spirit Award for Best Actress. Critics called her a revelation.
But Hollywood still didn't know what to do with her fierce intelligence.
Throughout the 1990s, Ashley chose roles that refused the victim narrative. In Kiss the Girls opposite Morgan Freeman, in Double Jeopardy playing a woman framed for murder who fights back—these weren't typical female roles. They were complex, intelligent, determined women who took control.
Just like Ashley herself.
Behind the scenes, though, she was struggling. In 2006, she checked into treatment—not for addiction, as tabloids speculated, but for depression stemming from childhood trauma.
She wrote about it openly in her memoir, All That Is Bitter & Sweet, discussing the abuse she endured, the pain she carried, and the grueling work required to heal.
"I had to learn that my worth wasn't tied to what others thought of me," she wrote.
Ashley also became a dedicated humanitarian. She traveled to some of the world's most dangerous places—Rwanda, Congo, Kenya—working with survivors of sexual violence and exploitation.
She didn't just write checks. She went there. She sat with survivors. She listened to their stories. She bore witness to their pain.
It was in Congo that a rape survivor told her: "Pain doesn't make you smaller. It stretches you."
Those words would prove prophetic.
In 2017, Ashley Judd became one of the first women to publicly accuse Harvey Weinstein of sexual harassment. She detailed how he harassed her in a hotel room in 1997 when she was a rising star, appearing in a bathrobe and making unwanted advances.
She knew speaking out could destroy her career.
And for a while, it did.
Weinstein used his power to blacklist her, telling directors she was "a nightmare to work with." Roles vanished. Opportunities disappeared.
But Ashley didn't stop. She became a leading voice of the #MeToo movement, advocating for survivors and demanding systemic change. She wasn't seeking revenge—she was seeking justice.
And she inspired millions of women to speak their truths.
Then in 2021, while on a humanitarian mission in the rainforests of Congo, Ashley suffered a catastrophic accident. She tripped over a fallen tree in darkness and shattered her leg in four places.
She lay on the forest floor for hours in excruciating pain, waiting for rescue. Local villagers carried her on a makeshift stretcher for hours through the jungle. A man named Dieumerci held her shattered leg completely still for five hours without moving. Another man had to reset her broken bones while she bit down on a stick and screamed.
She was finally airlifted to South Africa for emergency surgery. Doctors said she was fortunate to survive. Fortunate to keep her leg. The nerve damage was so severe they couldn't promise her foot would ever move again.
Ashley spent months in agonizing recovery, relearning to walk.
And then, as soon as she could, she returned to hiking.
Because that's who Ashley Judd is. She gets knocked down—and she stands back up, stronger than before.
Today, Ashley continues her humanitarian work. She speaks out for survivors. She advocates for policy change. She refuses to be silenced by those who tried to punish her for speaking truth.
Hollywood may have blacklisted her. But Ashley never needed Hollywood's approval. She has something far more valuable: her integrity, her voice, and her absolute refusal to let pain make her smaller.Here's what Ashley Judd's life teaches us:
She grew up surviving trauma that would mark her for decades. She moved to Los Angeles with nothing but determination while casting directors told her she was "too much." She won critical acclaim for Ruby in Paradise and starred in films playing women who refused victimhood. She sought treatment for childhood wounds and wrote openly about her healing journey. She traveled to war zones supporting survivors of violence. In 2017, she spoke out against Harvey Weinstein, knowing it would likely end her career—and it did, but she kept fighting. In 2021, she shattered her leg in Congo, nearly died, and spent months unable to walk.
She proved everyone wrong and returned to the work she loves.
Because Ashley Judd understands something essential: pain doesn't diminish us. It expands us. It stretches our capacity for courage, compassion, and resilience.
The Congolese woman who told her "pain doesn't make you smaller, it stretches you" was describing her own survival.
But she was also predicting Ashley's future.
Every time life tried to break Ashley Judd, she grew stronger. Every time someone told her to be quiet, to be smaller, to give up—she stood taller.
Ashley Judd shows us what it means to transform pain into power. To turn trauma into advocacy. To let hardship stretch us toward our fullest, most courageous selves.
She proves that the strongest steel is forged in the hottest fire—and that sometimes, the greatest heroism is simply refusing to let pain make you smaller

InfoCheck Emerges as a Pillar of Information Integrity in The Gambia’s Digital Age

As misinformation and digital manipulation increasingly shape public discourse across Africa, 
The Gambia’s InfoCheck has emerged as a key institutional response to the growing challenge of information disorder, positioning itself at the center of national efforts to safeguard truth, accountability, and democratic stability.
Formerly known as the Fact-Check Centre The Gambia, the organization officially rebranded as InfoCheck in October 2025, alongside the launch of its 2026–2030 Strategic Plan, signaling a shift from ad-hoc fact-checking toward a more structured, nationwide information integrity framework.

Founded in 2021 and headquartered in Brusubi, InfoCheck was established amid rising concerns over the impact of false information on elections, social cohesion, and public trust. Its evolution comes at a critical moment, as The Gambia prepares for future electoral cycles in an era marked by rapid social media growth, artificial intelligence driven content, and declining trust in traditional information gatekeepers.

Since its inception, InfoCheck has produced over 100 verified fact-checks, addressing misleading claims on governance, public policy, and social issues. According to the organization, it has also trained more than 600 young people and students in fact-checking and media literacy skills, an intervention experts describe as vital in a country where digital consumption is outpacing critical media awareness.

Speaking at the strategic plan launch, Executive Director Omar Saibou Camara emphasized that misinformation is no longer a marginal issue but a structural threat to democratic participation. He noted that the organisation’s work is grounded in the principles of truth, transparency, and accountability, with a focus on empowering citizens to independently verify information.

Regionally, InfoCheck is increasingly compared to established African fact-checking platforms such as Africa Check (South Africa), Dubawa (Nigeria and Ghana), and PesaCheck (East Africa), which have played measurable roles in correcting public narratives, supporting election observation efforts, and influencing media standards. Analysts say InfoCheck’s expansion places The Gambia firmly within this continental ecosystem of democratic resilience.

Beyond content production, InfoCheck’s 2026–2030 Strategic Plan prioritises the expansion of media and information literacy (MIL) programmes, with targets to train 2,500 community members, establish 10 regional media literacy hubs, and deepen collaboration with institutions such as the Access to Information Commission and the Ministry of Information. The goal is to move fact-checking upstream, preventing misinformation before it spreads.

However, observers caution that challenges remain. Like many civic media organizations across Africa, InfoCheck faces sustainability pressures linked to funding, algorithm-driven misinformation, and uneven digital literacy levels outside urban centers. Addressing these constraints, experts argue, will be critical to scaling impact beyond pilot programmes.

Despite these hurdles, civil society analysts view InfoCheck as an increasingly important actor in The Gambia’s democratic architecture, particularly as the country navigates political transitions, electoral reforms, and heightened online engagement.

As Africa grapples with the consequences of information disorder, from election interference to social polarization, InfoCheck’s trajectory reflects a broader continental shift: from reacting to misinformation, to building permanent institutions that defend the public’s right to verified, credible information.

- 🙏🙏How to offer Food to the Lord🙏🙏

As you walk down the supermarket aisles selecting the foods you will offer to Krishna, you need to know what is offerable and what is not. In the Bhagavad-gita, Lord Krishna states, "If one offers Me with love and devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, I will accept it." From this verse it is understood that we can offer Krishna foods prepared from milk products, vegetables, fruits, nuts, and grains. Meat, fish, and eggs are not offerable. And a few vegetarian items are also forbidden–garlic and onions, for example, which are in the mode of ignorance. (Hing, or asafetida, is a tasty substitute for them in cooking and is available at most Indian groceries.) Nor can you offer to Krishna coffee or tea that contain caffeine. If you like these beverages, purchase caffeine free coffee and herbal teas.

 
While shopping, be aware that you may find meat, fish, and egg products mixed with other foods; so be sure to read labels carefully. For instance, some brands of yogurt and sour cream contain gelatin, a substance made from the horns, hooves, and bones of slaughtered animals. Also, make sure the cheese you buy contains no rennet, an enzyme extracted from the stomach tissues of slaughtered calves. Most hard cheese sold in America contains rennet, so be careful about any cheese you can't verify as rennetless.
 
Also avoid foods cooked by non-devotees. According to the subtle laws of nature, the cook acts upon the food not only physically but mentally as well. Food thus becomes an agent for subtle influences on your conscious. The principle is the same as that at work with a painting: a painting is not simply a collection of strokes on a canvas but an expression of the artist's state of mind, which affects the viewer. So if you eat food cooked by non-devotees-employees working in a factory, for example–then you're sure to absorb a dose of materialism and karma. So as far as possible use only fresh, natural ingredients.
 
In preparing food, cleanliness is the most important principle. Nothing impure should be offered to God; so keep your kitchen very clean. Always wash your hands thoroughly before entering the kitchen. While preparing food, do not taste it, for you are cooking the meal not for yourself but for the pleasure of Krishna. Arrange portions of the food on dinnerware kept especially for this purpose; no one but the Lord should eat from these dishes. The easiest way to offer food is simply to pray, "My dear Lord Krishna, please accept this food," and to chant each of the following prayers three times while ringing a bell:
 
1. Prayer to Srila Prabhupada:
 
nama om vishnu-padaya krishna-preshthaya bhutale 
srimate bhaktivedanta-swamin iti namine 
namas te saraswate deve gaura-vani-pracharine 
nirvishesha shunyavadi pashchatya desha tarine
"I offer my respectful obeisances unto His Divine Grace A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, who is very dear to Lord Krishna, having taken shelter at His lotus feet. Our respectful obeisances are unto you, O spiritual master, servant of Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Gosvami. You are kindly preaching the message of Lord Caitanya deva and delivering the Western countries, which are filled with impersonalism and voidism."
 
2. Prayer to Lord Chaitanya:
 
namo maha-vadanyaya krishna-prema-pradaya te 
krishnaya krishna-chaitanya-namne gaura-twishe namaha
"O most munificent incarnation! You are Krishna Himself appearing as Sri Krishna Caitanya Mahaprabhu. You have assumed the golden color of Srimati Radharani. and You are widely distributing pure love of Krishna. We offer our respectful obeisances unto You."
 
3. Prayer to Lord Krishna:
 
namo brahmanya-devaya go-brahmana-hitaya cha 
jagad-dhitaya krishnaya govindaya namo namaha
"I offer my respectful obeisances unto Lord Krishna, who is the worshipable Deity for all brahmanas the well-wisher of the cows and the brahmanas and the benefactor of the whole world. I offer my repeated obeisances to the Personality of Godhead, known as Krishna and Govinda."
 
Remember that the real purpose of preparing and offering food to the Lord is to show your devotion and gratitude to Him. Krishna accepts your devotion, not the physical offering itself. God is complete in Himself–He doesn't need anything–but out of His immense kindness He allows us to offer food to Him so that we can develop our love for Him.
 
After offering the food to the Lord, wait at least five minutes for Him to partake of the preparations. Then you should transfer the food from the special dinnerware and wash the dishes and utensils you used for the offering. Now you and any guests may eat the prasadam. While you eat, try to appreciate the spiritual value of the food. Remember that because Krishna has accepted it, it is non-different from Him, and therefore by eating it you will become purified.
 
Everything you offer on your altar becomes prasadam, the mercy of the Lord. The flowers, the incense, the water, the food–everything you offer for the Lord's pleasure becomes spiritualized. When we offer the Lord something with genuine love and devotion, He enters into the offering, and thus the remnants are non-different from Him. So you should not only deeply respect the things you've offered, but you should distribute them to others as well.

The Surprising Wonders of Aging
By Sam Yau
 
 
Doorway
 
What if these are not your fading years,
but a season quiet enough
to finally hear your own voice?
 
There is a turning in you,
a slow, sure pivot
from speed to depth,
from proving to simply being.
 
This is not decline.
This is refinement.
The metal is the same;
the fire has only burned away
what was never you.
 
Clarity
 
Your life is a long‑lived house.
You know its halls by heart.
Some rooms glow with laughter,
others still hum with old arguments.

Closets sag with outfits
that no longer fit—
roles, stories, expectations,
kept long after
the occasion has passed.
 
Aging is the courage
to open those doors,
to hold each object to the light,
and ask,
“Do I still need this to be me?”
 
You know more clearly
what really matters.
You can say yes and no
with less doubt.
 
As you see what is irreplaceable—
health, time, meaning, kindness—
your focus sharpens.
You live closer
to what you value.
 
With clarity,
life grows lighter.
 
Presence
 
The mind is a tireless traveler,
looping through yesterday,
sketching tomorrows
on the thin paper of your nerves.
 
But the only ground
it truly touches
is this moment
this breath,
this heartbeat.
 
Aging can free you
from the tyranny of “someday,”
invite you to inhabit “now”
with less demand
and more gratitude,
 
until this moment
becomes enough.
 
Depth
 
When you were young,
you ran your fingers
across many surfaces—
identities, experiences,
places, people, dreams—
searching for something
that felt like home.
 
You have learned to stay:
with grief until it loosens,
with wonder until it ripens,
with your own heart
until it softens.
 
Depth begins
when attention stops wandering
and starts to root.
 
We look beneath appearances,
feel the many layers
inside a single gesture,
a single silence.
 
When life has depth,
it carries an inner richness
no surface can replace.
 
Compassion
 
You have survived more than
you once thought possible—
illnesses, disappointments,
heartbreaks, endings.
 
Every scar has carved out
a little more space inside you,
a room where harshness
no longer fits.
 
You remember the times
you stumbled,
said the wrong thing,
stayed too long,
left too soon,
did not yet know
how to be tender.
 
So when you see someone struggle,
you do not rush to judge.
You think, “Like me,
they are carrying
more than I can see.”
This is compassion.
 
But begin with yourself.
You were doing the best you could
with the tools and fears you had.
You still are.
So are they.
 
Grace
 
Grace is the art of embracing
inevitable change
with acceptance and poise,
like water easing
around the rocks in its way.
 
Grace unfolds as
clarity, presence, and depth ripen.
It is not resignation,
but a willing step
toward each new limit or loss
guided more by curiosity
than bitterness.
 
Nothing in nature
stays in bloom.
Trees do not cling
their leaves back on.
Rivers do not argue
with their currents.
 
Grace turns your attention
from what is missing
to what has always been here.
 
You thank your knees
for every mile they carried.
You forgive your hands
for their trembling.
You wrap your body
in kinder thoughts.
 
Grace is the beauty
that shines through you
when you stop
arguing with time.
 
Solitude
 
Solitude is not emptiness,
but a portal to enter
the deeper recess of
your inner life.
 
It is a space
to hear your thoughts,
to feel your emotions,
to sense your body,
to witness how you construct
an inner world that filters
your experiences with
the outer reality.
 
When you become
an attentive witness,
you discover
your inner world reveals itself
as vast, rich, and wise.
 
You gain the freedom
to respond instead of react to life
in a calmer and wiser way.
 
And when you learn
to enjoy your own company,
you are never truly alone.
 
Joy
 
Joy has changed its costume.
It no longer arrives trumpeting
with bright banners and applause.
 
It slips in quietly now—
the first sip of morning,
a familiar bird at the window,
a hand resting in yours
without needing words.
 
There is joy
being authentic,
living the unique you,
without needing
external validation.
 
You return to passions
you once tucked away
for “someday”—
a song, a sketch, a garden,
a story only you can tell.
 
You discover that joy lives
not in how much you achieve,
but in how faithfully
you inhabit what you love.
 
It is less fireworks now,
more candlelight—
steady, gentle,
enough to see your life clearly
and call it good.
 
9. Peace
 
Peace in aging
is a spacious acceptance
of life as it has been.
 
It does not mean
the absence of fear or regret,
only the softening
of their grip.
 
Peace grows
as you stop insisting
life must match your plans,
let go of the dream
of a perfect unblemished story.
 
You sense a steadiness in you
that outlasts each change
of body and mind.
 
Your mind has weathered
every season—
storms of worry,
hail of what‑ifs,
winds of imagined futures.
 
Slowly, you discover
you are not the storm.
You are the sky
it moves through.
 
Thoughts come and go
like clouds.
Feelings rise and fall
like waves.
You remain—
the spaciousness
that can hold them
without breaking.
 
Even the thought
of your own ending
no longer feels
like an enemy,
but part of the same great rhythm
you have always lived inside.
 
10, Inheritance
 
In the end, it may not matter
how many places you went,
how much you gathered,
how loudly
your name was spoken.
 
What endures is simpler:
the relief people felt
in your presence,
the way you listened,
the way you softened
instead of hardened
as the years went on.
 
Aging, fully lived,
is not a quiet erasing.
It is the final, honest shape
of a life learning, at last,
to be light,
to be kind,
to be here.

EIR Emergency Roundtable: Senior Experts Confer on Plan of Action ‘To Bring the World Back from the Brink’
Jan. 12, 2026 (EIRNS)—Executive Intelligence Review sponsored an Emergency Roundtable Jan. 12, featuring leading political figures from around the world, which convened online under the theme, “It’s Worse Than You Think: The Strategic Implications of the Attack on Venezuela and How To Bring the World Back from the Brink.” Ten experts, from the Americas, Eurasia and Africa, representing long experience and tested judgment in international affairs, met for nearly three hours, with a live-stream audience averaging 1,200 participants, with translation in English, French, German and Spanish.

Helga Zepp-LaRouche, Editor-in-Chief of EIR, and founder and leader of the Schiller Institute, welcomed her 10 fellow panelists, saying: “We have assembled here today not to lament the unprecedented situation which can only be described as a threat to the existence of the entire human civilization, but to discuss, analyze, and catapult an international response to restore international law.”

The stern reports and evaluations that followed provided a powerful expression of the shock and disgust around the world at the violent actions of these past weeks, and the role of the United States government in acting with abandon to discard international law.

However, as one speaker said: “we are not here to become more knowledgeable” about the crises, but to confer on galvanizing action to change the situation. Proposals ranged from a “Declaration” to be issued, to consensus that the priority is to mobilize the forces of the Global Majority to discuss new “configurations” to be supported to restore international law and morality. Many confirmed that the UN General Assembly is still a formation of potential positive international impact. The idea was posed to create a “structured international civil organization.”

Several speakers made the point that the cultural and political situation inside the United States is a priority to transform and upgrade. There is a correspondence between the violence underway inside the United States, and the international lawlessness from Washington. As one senior U.S. diplomat stated, now is the time that “America must introspect.”

Zepp-LaRouche summed up at the conclusion of the discussion that an organizing grouping will be formed to formulate priorities and to move on followup action.

The discussion period allowed for several exchanges on how to make this Roundtable of leading figures the basis for a global movement. The proposals discussed were for a UN General Assembly action to stop the U.S. policy; creating a movement of civil society organizations to intervene globally; activate mass movements along the model of Mohandas Gandhi, Nelson Mandela, and Martin Luther King, Jr.; start a movement for the forgiveness of the unpayable debt; to remind Trump that he campaigned against the “Deep State,” but now appears to be run by that same Deep State.

Terming the event, “extremely productive,” Zepp-LaRouche called for everyone to reach out to good institutions and individuals. She noted—not in a religious, but in a humanitarian way—that Pope Leo XIV has called for a Jubilee (the forgiveness of debts), and called for the “coincidence of opposites” way of thinking based on Nicholas of Cusa (15th century), which provides one path for organizing. The necessary elimination of the debt bubble must be controlled—an uncontrolled collapse could cause chaos. We should get this discussion to world leaders and institutions.  

Extraordinary Panel

The discussants were truly an extraordinary gathering of expertise and morality, amounting to a Council of Elders. The moderator was Dennis Speed of the Schiller Institute. Presentations were made by the following speakers, in the order given, proceeding after the Mrs. Zepp-LaRouche’s opening: 1) Naledi Pandor, former South African Minister of International Relations and Cooperation; 2) Zhang Weiwei, Professor of International Relations at Fudan University in Shanghai; 3) Chas Freeman, former U.S. Ambassador; 4) Dmitri Trenin, Director and Academic Supervisor of the Institute of World Military Economy and Strategy at the HSE University in Moscow ; 5) Donald Ramotar, former President of Guyana; 6) Graf Hans-Christof von Sponeck, former UN Assistant Secretary General; 7) María de los Ángeles Huerta, former Mexican Congresswoman; 6) Namit Verma, Indian author and security analyst; 9) Dennis Small, EIR Ibero-America Editor; and 10) Lt. Col. Ralph Bosshard (ret., Swiss Army), former military adviser to the OSCE secretary general.

Video archive of the Roundtable will be available, and upcoming issues of the weekly EIR will publish selected transcripts. The following are selected highlights.

Zepp-LaRouche pointed to U.S. President Donald Trump’s recent declaration that he is not bound by international law, but only by his own mind, allowing the “might makes right” actions he is following. Trump’s call for increasing the U.S. defense budget from $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion, together with the military buildup across Europe, demonstrates that we are on a path to global nuclear war. She insisted that we are the only species capable of reason, and thus, can and must act to change this disastrous course. She reviewed her own proposal for “Ten Principles of a New International Security and Development Architecture” (https://schillerinstitute.com/blog/2022/11/30/ten-principles-of-a-new-international-security-and-development-architecture/) and noted that these ideas were contained also in the four global Initiatives of Chinese President Xi Jinping (https://scsp222.substack.com/p/xis-four-global-initiatives-chinas).

She called for a return to the principles of the 1648 Peace of Westphalia, placing the concept of “one humanity” above all, as also in the concept of a “coincidence of opposites” presented by Nicholas of Cusa in the 15th century, as a means of resolving differences by reaching a higher, unified vision. We must reach back to all the great thinkers of our different cultures, such as Confucius, Plato, and Leibniz, to restore a true love for humanity through agapē.

Hon. Naledi Pandor addressed the horror expressed around the world at the illegal acts against Venezuela; and she warned that an attack on Cuba would be “a catastrophe.” She is the former South African Minister of International Relations and Cooperation, and Chair of the Nelson Mandela Foundation, who initiated the South Africa’s motion to the International Court of Justice (ICJ) to investigate Israel’s genocide in Gaza. Pandor pointed out that most of the Western nations accept that the West can override the interests of Russia. Developing countries have suffered under colonial rule, which the UN Charter was intended to eliminate, assuring the protection of the vulnerable from the strong. What is occurring now is the “most dangerous abuse of international law since 1948,” she said. The BRICS, the Hague Group (formed by nations of the Global South in January 2025 to defend the ICJ’s investigation of genocide in Palestine), the African Union, and other international organizations “must do more to restore international law,” while civil society organizations must also speak out. The UN must be reformed, so that those who break the rules of the Charter face a court. And individuals, too, must cause “good trouble.”

Prof. Zhang Weiwei expressed his outrage at Trump’s actions in Venezuela, terming it a “dangerous precedent” for the future. He noted that the U.S. had a “long history of reckless invasions,” adding that the new U.S. National Security Strategy granting power to the U.S. over all of the Western Hemisphere is “shortsighted and self-defeating,” which is destroying the country’s “soft power” by carrying out regime-change operations militarily, while using a “value-based humanitarian figleaf.” The U.S. action is destroying the UN Charter, which was “forged by two world wars.” He called for all nations to “unite to save the UN Charter.” He condemned the recent moves in Japan to restore the militaristic policies that had caused such destruction in World War II, insisting that China “will not accept the return of Japanese militarism,” and warned the U.S. and others that the world will not accept the end of the UN Charter.

Chas Freeman, former U.S. Ambassador to Saudi Arabia, expressed support for German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier’s recent denunciation of the U.S. being responsible for a “breakdown of values” and allowing the world to become a “den of thieves.” “My country,” he said, “has followed Israel in the law of the jungle,” acting like a mafia in protection rackets. “We are heading into a New Dark Age,” he warned. The genocide in Gaza, he said, demonstrates that “words won’t fix it” when there are such blatant crimes against humanity. The weather has been quite unpredictable, so to ensure the safety of our volunteers, we decided to reduce the scale of our outreach. Although we considered cancelling, we knew people would be waiting for us, regardless of the weather. As expected, it wasn’t as busy as our usual Sunday night, but 82 people came to us for a meal. This week, we pre-packed meals, including a main course, dessert, and a hot drink. We explained the provisions due to the weather, encouraging people to return to their hostels, tents, or any dry places, and we wanted to get out of the wet and cold as soon as possible. People were incredibly grateful for our support, as we could have easily cancelled. With 11 local volunteers, we managed the queue efficiently, ensuring no one left hungry.

It’s been a busy week as we’ve been helping arrange additional winter beds. We provided furniture and a washing machine for a new ladies’ house and will continue supporting with food donations so they can cook meals. Visiting the house was heartwarming, seeing the excitement on their faces and hearing them talk about their future.

We donated breakfast items to St Anne’s, ensuring our street homeless can access a hot breakfast. Given the wet and cold conditions, we provided shower gels and washing powder so people can enjoy a hot shower at the resource centre and wash their clothes and sleep bags.

We would like to express our gratitude to our local authority for their tireless efforts to get as many of our homeless community into shelters, even if temporary. It’s important that people are off the streets, dry, and warm until the weather improves. We understand resources are limited, but working together for the good of our community is the only way we can make a difference.

Once again, we thank everyone who supports us each week. We are grateful to our selfless volunteers for dedicating their valuable time to make a difference in the lives we touch.

To make a delicious omelette, you need simple ingredients and follow a few easy steps. Here is a step by step guide on how to make an egg omelette: Ingredients Required:2 or 3 large eggs,1 tablespoon water or milk , Salt and pepper to taste,1 tablespoon butter or cooking oil , Optional fillings (grated cheese, chopped ham, sliced ​​mushrooms, diced peppers, chopped onions, spinach, etc.)Tools: small bowl , Wire fork or whisk , Non-stick frying pan (about 8 inches in diameter for 2-3 eggs) , Spatula . Instruction: Prepare the Filling (Optional): If you're using a filling that requires cooking time (such as mushrooms or raw onions), cook it first in a separate skillet or in your omelet pan before proceeding to the next step. Set aside. Beat the Eggs: Crack the eggs into a small bowl. Add water or milk, salt, and pepper. Beat with a fork or wire whisk until the egg whites and yolks are well combined and no white streaks are visible. Do not overbeat until foamy. Heat the Pan: Melt the butter or heat the oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat. Make sure the entire surface of the pan is coated with the butter/oil. Cook the Eggs: Pour the egg mixture into the hot pan. The eggs will begin to cook quickly around the edges. Shape the Omelette: While the eggs are cooking, use a spatula to push the cooked parts of the egg at the edges of the pan toward the center. Tilt the pan so that the uncooked parts of the egg flow into the empty spaces on the hot surface. Repeat this process several times until the top of the egg is mostly solid but still slightly wet or shiny in the center. Add Filling and Cheese: Sprinkle the filling you have prepared and grated cheese on one side of the omelette (half). Fold the Omelet: Using a spatula, fold the omelette in half (into a semicircle) over the filling. Serve: Let the omelet sit in the pan for about another minute to allow the filling to warm and the cheese to melt. Then, carefully slide the omelet from the pan onto a serving plate. SENATOR BARAU JIBRIN CFR AND THE SURVIVAL OF KANO APC: A TIMELY REBUTTAL TO POLITICS OF ENVY AND DESPERATION 

Muazu Ibn Abdallah ✍️ ✍️ ✍️ 

In every political system, there are critical moments that clearly  distinguishes statesmen from political opportunists. Kano State today stands at such a defining crossroads. As political realignments intensify and Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf is widely reported to be considering decamping to the All Progressives Congress (APC), the party must take stock of its true pillars of strength, its strategic stabilisers, and its moral compass. At the heart of this reality stands Senator Barau Jibrin CFR PhD, Deputy President of the Senate and the deputy speaker ECOWAS Parliament, a man whose relevance is neither accidental nor manufactured, but rather earned through consistency, sacrifice, and service delivery.

Regrettably, instead of consolidating around this invaluable asset, some elements within the APC have resorted to smear campaigns, baseless allegations, and desperate attempts to tarnish the image of Senator Barau. These attacks are not rooted in principle or party interest; they are driven by envy and political anxiety, especially by those who believe that destroying Senator Barau’s reputation is the only route through which their political principals can gain relevance.

History, however is stubborn and does not bend to propaganda, also the political history of Kano does not lie. And as Hausa popular saying goes 'mai hali baya fasa halinsa' (persons hardly abandoned his true character), amid these internal squabbles, Senator Jibrin CFR, PhD has consistently proven himself as one of the most formidable political gladiators in contemporary Nigerian politics. Against entrenched interests, hostile alliances, and overwhelming forces, he repeatedly emerged victorious at the polls. His political dexterity and grassroots appeal did not only secure personal victories; they fundamentally redefined Kano North as an APC stronghold, an achievement no fair-minded observer can deny.

While others inherited structures, Senator Barau built political capital through the confidence of the people. Elections after elections, he demonstrated that political legitimacy flows from the masses, not from sponsored narratives or fleeting alliances.

Senator Barau has continues to serve as the strategic backbone of Kano APC, a role he has performed consistently and diligently for quite a very long time and more significantly since the party's 2023 electoral setback. Through legislative excellence, empowerment initiatives, and grassroots connection, he has not only sustained the party but expanded its influence.

Legislative Record and National Influence

.Highest Bill Sponsorship: Senator Barau topped the legislative productivity chart in the Senate, earning the "Highest Development-Driven Bills Award" from the Senate Press Corps.

·North West Development Commission: He championed the establishment of the North West Development Commission (NWDC), which has N585.9 billion proposed for its takeoff in the 2025 budget, aimed at addressing developmental challenges in seven northwestern states.

·Constitutional Review Leadership: As Chairman of the Senate Committee on the Review of the Constitution, he led a significant retreat in Kano, emphasizing alignment with citizens' aspirations.

·International Parliamentary Role: Serving as First Deputy Speaker of the ECOWAS Parliament, he enhanced Nigeria's regional diplomatic engagement and even facilitated the Parliament's relocation to Kano for nearly a week .

Empowerment and Development Initiatives

Senator Barau's commitment extends beyond legislation to direct community impact through multiple channels:

Senator Barau recently announced massive empowerment initiatives Which further demonstrate leadership driven by empathy and foresight.
Beginning Tuesday, 13th January, over 12,000 low-income earners across Kano State will receive ₦20,000 cash grants each, offering timely relief in a period of economic strain. This follows an earlier program targeting 10,000 beneficiaries with similar grant.

Even more striking is his second phase intervention:
₦100,000 monthly support for 100 beneficiaries in each of the 13 local governments of Kano North, for 12 consecutive months starting February.

130 cars to be distributed to beneficiaries across diverse sectors.

1,000 motorcycles for headmasters, teachers, commercial riders, and others.

1,300 grinding machines for widows and vulnerable women.

1,300 sewing machines for women entrepreneurs.

1,300 bicycles for primary and secondary school students.

Sports equipment and jerseys for 1,950 football teams across Kano North.

Notably, Senator Barau has pledged to extend similar empowerment programmes to Kano Central and Kano South, reflecting a pan-Kano vision anchored on fairness and inclusivity.

Apart from these recent empowerment initiatives, senator Barau had previously provided massive employment opportunities for Kano state indigenes.  On January 1, 2026, he distributed 129 federal government employment letters to constituents, a remarkable feat in Nigeria's competitive job market .

· Educational Support: He has sponsors 70 postgraduate students from Kano to study AI, Cybersecurity, and Forensic Science in India, plus thousands more in domestic scholarship programs .

· Agricultural Support: Distributed 69 trucks of fertilizer (41,400 bags) to farmers across all 44 LGAs of Kano State, contributing to reported bumper harvests .

· Transport Infrastructure: Launched the Kano North Transport Service with 107 buses to boost commercial activities .

· Security Enhancement: Facilitated 1,000 motorcycles to the Kano State Police Command to enhance policing across all local government areas .

Strategic Importance in Kano's Political Landscape

As Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf's potential defection from the New Nigeria People's Party (NNPP) to APC creates political uncertainty, Senator Barau's stabilizing role becomes increasingly critical. The governor's anticipated move follows a pattern of defections from NNPP that began in July 2024, which Senator Barau helped facilitate.

Within this volatile context, Senator Barau represents:

· Political Continuity: With experience dating back to the House of Representatives (1999-2003) and various Kano State government roles, he provides institutional memory and stability .

·Electoral Strength: He has transformed Kano North into an APC stronghold through consistent electoral success against formidable opposition.

·Bridge-Building Capacity: His empowerment programs extend across all three Kano senatorial districts, not just his North constituency, demonstrating inclusive leadership.

·National Connection: As Deputy Senate President, he maintains crucial linkages with the federal government and national party structures.

The Economic Impact of Sustained Empowerment

The 129 federal appointments facilitated in January 2026 alone represent more than just jobs, they signify transformative economic opportunities for families across Kano. When combined with the massive cash transfer programs, educational scholarships, agricultural support, and business empowerment initiatives, Senator Barau has created an integrated development ecosystem that addresses multiple dimensions of poverty and underdevelopment simultaneously. This comprehensive approach explains his enduring popularity and the groundswell of grassroots support that makes him politically formidable.

A Call for Party Unity and Forward Focus

Political observers are increasingly drawing attention as the  consultations regarding Kano's evolving political landscape deepened,  this period demands strategic cohesion, not internal fragmentation. Thus, the attacks on Senator Barau appear particularly ill-timed and counterproductive given that various strategic stakeholders across Kano APC have endorsed him for the governorship race while endorsing President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for a second term .

· Resource Stewardship: Senator Barau has shouldered party responsibilities, including providing palliatives and support to stakeholders since the 2023 elections.

· Inclusive Politics: His empowerment programs target widows, students, teachers, farmers, and vulnerable populations across political affiliations.

· Democratic Dividends: Through legislative and executive channels, he has delivered concrete benefits that exemplify what democratic governance should achieve.

The Path Forward for Kano APC

As the APC prepares for a potential "comeback" in Kano politics, the strategic integration of incoming defectors with established performers like Senator Barau will determine the party's success . 

Political competition within parties is natural, but when it escalates to baseless attacks against a proven performer who has expanded the party's stronghold, it crosses from healthy rivalry to strategic self-sabotage. Senator Barau's remarkable legislative productivity, consistently demonstrated electoral strength, and unparalleled commitment to development delivery make him not a threat to be diminished but an asset to be celebrated and supported.

As Kano's political landscape continues to evolve, one truth remains evident: sustainable political relevance derives from consistent service delivery rather than tactical manipulation. Senator Barau Jibrin has mastered this equation, transforming Kano North into an APC fortress while extending development programs across the entire state. For APC members contemplating the party's future in Kano, the path forward lies in recognizing that unifying behind proven performers while welcoming new members creates an unstoppable coalition—one built on achievement rather than allegation, and development rather than denigration.

"“Bandwagon” geopolitics is ending in the Middle East: global actors need to adjust.
 
1. Years back, when I had the opportunity to choose a topic for my master's dissertation, I chose to concentrate on the Middle East. Even though ISIS had emerged in Iraq and Syria, I wanted to explain that in the context.
 
2. I decided to look at the politico-religious rivalry in the region. Led by Saudi Arabia and Iran, the Sunni-Shia “Cold War” between the two powerful states explained many of the dynamics in the region.
 
3. One of the features of the Saudi-Iran rivalry was “bandwagoning”. This is a situation where relatively weaker states or political entities tend to unflinchingly follow stronger ones in the pursuit of their national interest. It is often found in military alliances. While this could prove efficient for weaker parties, it could also be burdensome when the stronger ones make expensive mistakes.
 
4. In the Middle East, (at the time of my research and before) Iran and Saudi Arabia led states and proxies that mostly bandwagon. They had a strong influence on these states and proxies that trusted them to lead geopolitical decisions and security dynamics.
 
5. And so what?
 
6. This meant that the management of peace in the region despite being evasive, had some level of predictability considering that the most influential actors could rein in their proxies and weaker counterparts.
 
7. In recent years, this is changing in ways that need the attention of regional and global actors engaged in the region. Understanding this could change the decades-old template used in approaching the region. Getting Saudi Arabia to agree to an issue will not mean other Sunni-led states are going to follow. More interesting, Iran is increasingly having its proxies and weaker allies acting independently regardless of discomforts in Tehran.
 
8. How?
 
9. When Riyadh resolved to use force to put the legitimate government of Yemen in its “rightful” place, it had the support and participation of some of the Sunni-led states in the region. However, as the war dragged on without any success the UAE and others revised their stance on the matter—they withdrew their forces. Also, when Riyadh refused to join the Abraham Accord, Bahrain the UAE rightly thought they had their peculiar interests and went ahead with it.
 
10. In recent events, Iran is consistently found in an awkward place as its proxies are increasingly taking decisions and acting in ways that suggest that they are increasingly becoming independent of decisions in Tehran. From militias operating in Syria and Iraq to more organized entities like Hezbollah and the Houthis, there appear to be independent stances. Even before Israel and Hamas (which most likely happened without Tehran’s blessing), Hezbollah had some security and economic cooperation with Israel concerning offshore resources. "

THE CAREER ADVICE WE ARE NOT TELLING YOUNG CONSTRUCTION PROFESSIONALS:
CHOOSE PEACE BEFORE LOVE

There is one crucial issue those of us with more life and site experience are not telling the younger generation clearly enough.

We have spoken extensively from the mentorship angle. We have advised you to study hard in school, read widely, research, and understand theory. We have encouraged early practical exposure. Find a mentor. Walk onto construction sites. Attend seminars, conferences, and trainings. Learn relevant software. All of these are correct and necessary.

But there is a critical part we keep avoiding.

Who you choose to marry.

If you are a young man or woman working in construction, understand this clearly. Site work is not easy. It is physically demanding, mentally exhausting, and requires absolute concentration. To execute work properly on site, to follow standards, and to avoid costly mistakes, your brain, energy, and attention must be fully engaged.

Consider a typical site day. Repeatedly climbing stairs in a six-storey building. You cannot even count how many times you go up and down. Supervising artisans, checking levels, inspecting reinforcement, resolving site issues, making decisions under pressure. By the time you get home, you are completely drained.

For a site engineer or project engineer, home must be a place of rest.

If you return home to tension, emotional instability, constant conflict, threats, or pressure, it will destroy you gradually. Red alart you must check : When someone says, “I will make your life unbearable” or “I will make this house hot for you,” that is not love. That is a clear warning sign. That is violence, whether it comes from a man or a woman.

Run.

Choose peace.

Many of us are not saying this loudly enough. Construction work is tedious. Doing things correctly on site is even more demanding. After casting days, after heavy setting-out, after intense supervision, many of us are physically and mentally spent. Sometimes all you can do is eat, pray, and sleep.

Before tools like laser levels simplified certain tasks, think of the stress involved in using builder’s lines, manual measurements, and constant rechecking. The strain was real. Even today, with better tools, site pressure remains high.

So before you choose who to marry, make this your first checklist item.
Will this person give me peace of mind?

PUL Calls for Responsible Journalism and Security Collaboration at Third Media–Security Conference in Ganta

(Ganta, Nimba County, January 13, 2026): The Press Union of Liberia (PUL) has underscored the critical need for a strong and responsible partnership between the Liberian media and the nation’s joint security forces. This call to action was issued on Monday, 12 January 2026, at the opening of the third Media–Security Conference, in Ganta, Nimba County, to foster professionalism, integrity, and mutual respect in electoral processes.

In an address at the conference, PUL President Julius Kanubah emphasized the pivotal roles of journalists and law enforcement in safeguarding Liberia’s democracy and promoting social cohesion. “Constructive engagement between the media and security sector is essential,” Kanubah stated. “Together, we can uphold freedom of expression, a free press, and the rule of law, while ensuring that our conduct reflects the highest professional standards.”

Organized under the auspices of the National Elections Commission (NEC) and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the Ganta conference involves 47 journalists and law enforcement officers from Grand Cape Mount, Margibi, Bong, Lofa, and Nimba Counties. 

The primary focus of the gathering is to review and update the Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) that guide collaboration, cooperation, and coordination between the media and security agencies, particularly during electoral processes.

Representing Joint Security, Deputy Commissioner of Police and Head of the West African Police Information System at the Liberia National Police (LNP), Augustine Browne, stressed the importance of unity in advancing peace and stability. ‘It is imperative for the media and security to work in concert to prevent misunderstandings and foster a peaceful environment’, Browne remarked.

UNDP Programme Officer Roosevelt Zayzay also noted the value of the SOP in reducing potential conflicts and misunderstandings between media professionals and security officers throughout the 2023 General and Presidential Elections. ‘A clear framework ensures that all parties understand their roles and responsibilities, minimizing confrontation and building public trust’, Zayzay said.

Executive Director of the NEC, Anthony Sengbe, urged all stakeholders to maintain the highest levels of professionalism. ‘Our collective commitment will ensure that Liberia’s electoral process remains peaceful and free from violence’, Sengbe stated.

Attorney Christopher Fayiah, Deputy Executive Director of the Liberia Peacebuilding Office, highlighted the need to integrate lessons learned and best practices into the revised SOP. ‘Continuous improvement of the framework is vital to address emerging challenges and to strengthen the role of women in peacebuilding initiatives’, Fayiah said.

The Ganta conference builds on two preceding regional media–security conferences held in Zwedru, Grand Gedeh County, and Buchanan, Grand Bassa County, which collectively engaged media and security representatives from several counties across Liberia. The current review process emphasizes roles and responsibilities, dispute-resolution mechanisms, and the enhancement of women’s participation in peace promotion.

Following the conference on Wednesday, 14 January, a comprehensive working session will collate insights from all three regional gatherings. These findings will inform a validation workshop that will lead to the finalization of the revised SOP.

The SOP review and regional consultations are part of the Liberia Electoral Support Project (LESP), managed by UNDP and generously supported by the European Union and the Governments of Sweden and Ireland.

Islamic Military Counter Terrorism Coalition Signs MOU with Government of Sierra Leone & Launches Strategic Initiative

Freetown, Tuesday, January 13, 2026– Sierra Leone has signed a landmark Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Islamic Military Counter Terrorism Coalition (IMCTC) aimed at boosting the country's counter-terrorism efforts. The historic signing of the MOU and the launch of the IMCTC strategic initiative at the Freetown International Conference Centre (Bintumani) on Tuesday, January 13, 2026, aims to strengthen strategic partnerships. The partnership will focus on training defense forces personnel, who will in turn train religious leaders such as Imams and Pastors on counter-terrorism and extremist ideologies. Additionally, it seeks to develop expertise in anti-money laundering to combat terrorist financing and enhance national security, addressing threats from the volatile Sahel region.

With support from the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the initiative seeks to enhance governance, build capacity, and protect Sierra Leone and West Africa from terrorist expansion. The MOU was signed by the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS), Lieutenant General Amara Idara Bangura on behalf of the Security Sector of Sierra Leone, and Major General Mohammed bin Saeed Al-Moghedi, Secretary-General of the IMCTC.

In his welcome address, National Security Coordinator of the Office of National Security (ONS) in Sierra Leone, Mr. Abdulai Caulker, commended the IMCTC delegates for the initiative to launch the Counter-Terrorism Coalition Strategy in Sierra Leone, highlighting the country's commitment to collective security and global partnership. He emphasized that this milestone event marks a significant step in Sierra Leone's counter-terrorism journey, enhancing intelligence-driven cooperation with IMCTC. Mr. Caulker praised His Excellency President Dr. Julius Maada Bio's leadership in consolidating Sierra Leone's alliance with IMCTC member states, strengthening regional security. He stressed the need for sustained joint action against evolving terrorist threats, leveraging strategic foresight, inter-agency coordination, and capacity building.

The Minister of Internal Affairs, Mr. Morie Lengor, in his keynote address, emphasized that terrorism and extremism remain threats in Sub-Saharan Africa, particularly the Sahel region, and require multilateral cooperation to prevent their spread. He commended the IMCTC for the initiative to train the security sector in Sierra Leone on counter-terrorism, which he said would add professional value to participants.

Major General Mohammed bin Saeed Al-Moghedi, Secretary-General of the IMCTC, commended the Government of Sierra Leone for the hospitality accorded to him and his delegation. He emphasized the importance of integrated partnerships to tackle terrorism in the Sahel region, citing support from Saudi Arabia. "Terrorism is a global phenomenon that requires cross-border cooperation to protect communities," Al-Moghedi stated. He emphasized that countering terrorism demands an integrated partnership, rather than fragmented efforts.

Sierra Leone's Ambassador to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, Mohammed Barrie, provided a brief historical perspective on the formation of the IMCTC, founded in December 2015 by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud. He explained that the coalition aims to counter the misconception of Islam as a terrorist religion, promote unity among Islamic countries, and combat extremism globally. Ambassador Barrie requested the IMCTC for the following:

● capacity building to enhance Sierra Leone security sector readiness.
 
 ● the establishment of a counter-terrorism centre in Freetown

● Research collaboration, information sharing,

● Public diplomacy initiatives to counter extremist narratives.

The Deputy Minister of Defence (DMD) of Sierra Leone, Colonel (Rtd.) Muana Brima Massaquoi, on behalf of the Minister of Defence and Commander in Chief of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Sierra Leone, H.E Brigadier (Rtd.) Julius Maada Bio, expressed deep appreciation to the Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques, King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, and the Crown Prince and Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, for the strategic initiative in establishing the IMCTC. He said the Ministry of Defence remains committed to recognizing terrorism as a transnational threat that demands collective action, shared responsibility, and sustained partnership. On his personal behalf, and on behalf of the President and people of Sierra Leone, the DMD expressed appreciation for the launch and particularly, the three-week training component for the selected members of security forces. 

The three-week training for Sierra Leone's security sector will equip participants with skills to neutralize unexploded ordnance and Improvised Explosive Devices (IEDs), including identification, towing, and safe disposal. The final week focuses on counter-terrorism operations, training participants to search, locate, and respond to explosive threats in realistic scenarios involving persons, vehicles, buildings, and areas.

The Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) of the Sierra Leone, Lieutenant General Amara Idara Bangura, delivered the vote of thanks.

To make a delicious omelette, you need simple ingredients and follow a few easy steps. Here is a step by step guide on how to make an egg omelette: Ingredients Required:2 or 3 large eggs,1 tablespoon water or milk , Salt and pepper to taste,1 tablespoon butter or cooking oil , Optional fillings (grated cheese, chopped ham, sliced ​​mushrooms, diced peppers, chopped onions, spinach, etc.)Tools: small bowl , Wire fork or whisk , Non-stick frying pan (about 8 inches in diameter for 2-3 eggs) , Spatula . Instruction: Prepare the Filling (Optional): If you're using a filling that requires cooking time (such as mushrooms or raw onions), cook it first in a separate skillet or in your omelet pan before proceeding to the next step. Set aside. Beat the Eggs: Crack the eggs into a small bowl. Add water or milk, salt, and pepper. Beat with a fork or wire whisk until the egg whites and yolks are well combined and no white streaks are visible. Do not overbeat until foamy. Heat the Pan: Melt the butter or heat the oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat. Make sure the entire surface of the pan is coated with the butter/oil. Cook the Eggs: Pour the egg mixture into the hot pan. The eggs will begin to cook quickly around the edges. Shape the Omelette: While the eggs are cooking, use a spatula to push the cooked parts of the egg at the edges of the pan toward the center. Tilt the pan so that the uncooked parts of the egg flow into the empty spaces on the hot surface. Repeat this process several times until the top of the egg is mostly solid but still slightly wet or shiny in the center. Add Filling and Cheese: Sprinkle the filling you have prepared and grated cheese on one side of the omelette (half). Fold the Omelet: Using a spatula, fold the omelette in half (into a semicircle) over the filling. Serve: Let the omelet sit in the pan for about another minute to allow the filling to warm and the cheese to melt. Then, carefully slide the omelet from the pan onto a serving plate. ## **Royal Commissions Must Be Beyond Doubt — Process, Perception, and Consequences Matter**

**By Michael Kennedy**

Royal Commissions are not convened simply to gather facts. They are established when confidence has been shaken — when the public needs assurance that truth will be pursued without fear, favour, or political convenience. In those circumstances, *perception matters almost as much as integrity itself*.

The appointment of former High Court Justice **Virginia Bell AC** to lead the Royal Commission into the Bondi terror attack and the broader issue of antisemitism has reignited an important national discussion. Not about allegations of bias or misconduct — there are none — but about **relationships, optics, and the adequacy of process** in appointments to inquiries of exceptional sensitivity.

Let us state the facts clearly. Virginia Bell is an eminent jurist. She served on the High Court of Australia from 2009 to 2021, following appointment by the Rudd Labor government. She was recognised for her service to the law in 2012 under the Gillard Labor government. More recently, she led the inquiry into former Prime Minister Scott Morrison’s secret ministerial appointments. Her legal credentials are not in question.

However, Royal Commissions are not ordinary legal exercises. This inquiry touches terrorism, antisemitism, public protest, policing, intelligence failures, and government response. It sits squarely at the intersection of national security and social cohesion. In such cases, **the threshold for public confidence must be higher than usual**.

Ms Bell’s repeated appointment by Labor governments does not establish bias. But it does establish *institutional proximity*, and proximity creates perception — particularly when the appointing government is itself a stakeholder in the policy, political, and narrative outcomes of the inquiry. That perception is amplified when the Prime Minister publicly insists she is “the most qualified person” for the role.

Australia simply does not lack qualified candidates.

Among those widely regarded as equally capable — and, in some cases, carrying less political baggage — are figures such as **Robert French**, former Chief Justice of the High Court; **James Allsop**, former Chief Justice of the Federal Court; **Susan Kiefel**, former Chief Justice of the High Court; and **Justice Michael Lee**, a Federal Court judge respected across legal and community lines. From a national security perspective, former ASIO Directors-General **Dennis Richardson** and **Duncan Lewis** bring deep operational and counter-terrorism expertise that would have added immediate credibility in an inquiry of this nature.

The existence of multiple credible candidates does not diminish Ms Bell. But it does expose the weakness of the process. The government alone chose the commissioner. There was no parliamentary consultation, no bipartisan shortlisting, and no Senate confirmation. That may be lawful — but in today’s climate, it is no longer sufficient.

Other Westminster democracies routinely involve legislatures in appointing leaders of sensitive national inquiries. Australia does not — by choice, not necessity. A **Senate-based or bipartisan selection process** would not undermine Royal Commissions; it would strengthen them. It would protect commissioners from politicised attacks, reassure affected communities, and inoculate findings against claims of narrative management or institutional self-interest.

An even stronger model would have been a **panel commission**, combining a senior jurist with a national-security expert. Such arrangements are common internationally in terrorism-related inquiries. They balance procedural fairness with operational realism and reduce the risk that any single perspective dominates the inquiry’s direction.

Some critics have dismissed concerns about perception as “politicising” the Royal Commission. That argument gets it backwards. **Ignoring perception is what politicises an inquiry.** Transparency disarms suspicion; opacity feeds it.

There is also a further issue that must be confronted honestly: **should criminal consequences flow from this inquiry?**

Royal Commissions do not lay charges — nor should they. But they absolutely can, and often must, **refer evidence to prosecutors, police, or integrity bodies**. If the inquiry uncovers evidence of criminal negligence, failure to act on intelligence, misuse of public office, breaches of counter-terrorism law, or deliberate suppression of warnings, referrals to the Director of Public Prosecutions or relevant authorities are not optional. They are essential to credibility.

An inquiry that gathers evidence under oath, exposes systemic failures, and then produces recommendations with no pathway to accountability risks becoming a political pressure valve rather than a justice mechanism.

Ultimately, this debate is not about Virginia Bell’s integrity. It is about **process integrity**. Royal Commissions derive their authority not only from the calibre of the individuals who lead them, but from the confidence the public has in how those individuals are chosen — and in whether findings carry real consequences.

If governments want Royal Commissions to retain legitimacy in an era of deep public scepticism, they must accept a simple principle: **being independent is not enough — independence must be seen, structured, and safeguarded**.

That is not an attack. It is a call to modernise how Australia handles its most serious national inquiries — before confidence erodes beyond repair.

📍  Q.: Why do Catholics pray to Mary?

A: For Catholics, there are different types of Marian prayer that reflect different intentions. Reciting the "Magnificat," for example, is a way to praise God as Mary did. By reciting the "Angelus," you commemorate an event in salvation history, one in which Mary had a major role. Such commemorations are also made by the entire Church in the liturgical cycle. At Christmas, for example, the faithful recall Mary's role in the birth of Christ.

Prayers invoking Mary's intercession for your own personal intentions are in a separate class, arousing controversy since the time of the Reformation in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

The practice of invoking saintly people for their intercession before God in union with Jesus has roots in sacred Scripture. In this regard, Matthew 18:19-20 refers to saints on earth, and Revelation 18:20 refers to saints in heaven. In the early centuries of the Church, veneration and invocation was offered to those martyred for Christ. The practice derives from the doctrine that the saints are united with Jesus in one mystical body (Romans 12:5).

The practice of calling on Mary for aid also appears to be very old in the Catholic Church. An ancient testimony of confidence in Mary is the prayer Sub Tuum, which historians place in the second/third century:

♡   We fly to your patronage,
 O holy Mother of God;
 despise not our petitions in our necessities,
 but deliver us always from all dangers,
 O glorious and blessed Virgin.
(Dictionary of Mary, p. 143)

This practice became an area of significant disagreement between Catholics and Protestants. After the crisis of the Reformation, the Catholic Council of Trent repeated traditional Christian teaching on the intercession of the saints, which applies preeminently to Mary:

 The saints who reign together with Christ, offer up their prayers to God for men; ... it is good and useful to invoke them suppliantly and, in order to obtain favors from God through his Son Jesus Christ our Lord who alone is our Redeemer and Saviour, to have recourse to their prayers, assistance and support.
(Theotokos, p. 188)

The Synod of Jerusalem held by the Orthodox Church proclaimed a similar position about a century after Trent. Protestants counter that reliance on Mary and the saints detracts from reliance on Jesus Christ, who is our 'one mediator':

 For there is one God, and one mediator also between God and men, the man, Christ Jesus, who gave Himself as a ransom for all, the testimony borne at the proper time.
(1 Tm 2:2-5 - New American Bible)

A thorough examination of this topic by the Lutheran-Catholic Dialogue Commission may be found in The One Mediator, The Saints and Mary (Augsburg Press, 1992). An excellent contemporary Catholic reflection on the subject is found in chapter 3 of Pope John Paul II's 1987 encyclical, Mother of the Redeemer. A small subsection of paragraph 38 of that chapter is as follows:

 The Church knows and teaches with Saint Paul that there is only one mediator: "For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all." (1 Tm 2:5-6).

 The maternal role of Mary toward people in no way obscures or diminishes the unique mediation of Christ, but rather shows its power [Vatican II Constitution on the Church, # 60]: it is mediation in Christ.

Catholics do not pray to Mary as if she were God. Prayer to Mary is memory of the great mysteries of our faith (Incarnation, Redemption through Christ in the rosary), praise to God for the wonderful things he has done in and through one of his creatures (Hail Mary) and intercession (second half of the Hail Mary). The latter is addressed to Mary not as to a vending machine but a support person helping us to discern the will of God in our lives. Mary is a volunteer, highly recommendable and recommended, but not a mandatory and inescapable passage.

"Remember me, you heirs of God, you brethren of Christ; supplicate the Savior earnestly for me, that I may be freed through Christ from him that fights against me day by day" (The Fear at the End of Life [A.D. 370]).
Ephraim the Syrian

"You victorious martyrs who endured torments gladly for the sake of the God and Savior, you who have boldness of speech toward the Lord himself, you saints, intercede for us who are timid and sinful men, full of sloth, that the grace of Christ may come upon us, and enlighten the hearts of all of us that so we may love him" (Commentary on Mark [A.D. 370]).
The Liturgy of St. Basil

"By the command of your only-begotten Son we communicate with the memory of your saints . . . by whose prayers and supplications have mercy upon us all, and deliver us for the sake of your holy name" (Liturgy of St. Basil [A.D. 373]).
Pectorius

"Aschandius, my father, dearly beloved of my heart, with my sweet mother and my brethren, remember your Pectorius in the peace of the Fish [Christ]" (Epitaph of Pectorius [A.D. 375]).
Gregory Nazianz

"May you [Cyprian] look down from above propitiously upon us, and guide our word and life; and shepherd this sacred flock . . . gladden the Holy Trinity, before which you stand" (Orations 17 [24] [A.D. 380]).
Gregory Nazianz

"Yes, I am well assured that [my father's] intercession is of more avail now than was his instruction in former days, since he is closer to God, now that he has shaken off his bodily fetters, and freed his mind from the clay that obscured it, and holds conversation naked with the nakedness of the prime and purest mind . . . " (ibid., 18:4).
Gregory of Nyssa

"[Ephraim], you who are standing at the divine altar [in heaven] . . . bear us all in remembrance, petitioning for us the remission of sins, and the fruition of an everlasting kingdom" (Sermon on Ephraim the Syrian [A.D. 380]).
John Chrysostom

"He that wears the purple [i.e. a royal man] . . . stands begging of the saints to be his patrons with God, and he that wears a diadem begs the tent-maker [Paul] and the fisherman [Peter] as patrons, even though they be dead" (Homilies on 2 Corinthians 26 [A.D. 392]).
John Chrysostom

"When you perceive that God is chastening you, fly not to his enemies . . . but to his friends, the martyrs, the saints, and those who were pleasing to him, and who have great power [in God]" (Orations 8:6 [A.D. 396]).
Ambrose of Milan

"May Peter, who wept so efficaciously for himself, weep for us and turn towards us Christ's benign countenance" (The Six Days' Work 5:25:90 [A.D. 393]).
Jerome

"You say in your book that while we live we are able to pray for each other, but afterwards when we have died, the prayer of no person for another can be heard . . . But if the apostles and martyrs while still in the body can pray for others, at a time when they ought still be solicitous about themselves, how much more will they do so after their crowns, victories, and triumphs?" (Against Vigilantius 6 [A.D. 406]).
Augustine

"A Christian people celebrates together in religious solemnity the memorials of the martyrs, both to encourage their being imitated and so that it can share in their merits and be aided by their prayers" (Against Faustus the Manichean [A.D. 400]).
Augustine

"There is an ecclesiastical discipline, as the faithful know, when the names of the martyrs are read aloud in that place at the altar of God, where prayer is not offered for them. Prayer, however, is offered for the dead who are remembered. For it is wrong to pray for a martyr, to whose prayers we ought ourselves be commended" (Sermons 159:1 [A.D. 411]).
Augustine

"At the Lord's table we do not commemorate martyrs in the same way that we do others who rest in peace so as to pray for them, but rather that they may pray for us that we may follow in their footsteps" (Homilies on John 84 [A.D. 416]).
Augustine

"Neither are the souls of the pious dead separated from the Church which even now is the kingdom of Christ. Otherwise there would be no remembrance of them at the altar of God in the communication of the Body of Christ" (The City of God 20:9:2 [A.D. 419]).
Sozomen

"Gregory of Nazianz presided over those who maintain the consubstantiality of the Holy Trinity, and assembled them together in a little dwelling, which had been altered into the form of a house of prayer, by those who held the same opinions and had a like form of worship. It subsequently became one of the most conspicuous in the city, and is so now, not only for the beauty and number of its structures, but also for the advantages accruing to it from the visible manifestations of God. For the power of God was there manifested, and was helpful both in waking visions and in dreams, often for the relief of many diseases and for those afflicted by some sudden transmutation in their affairs. The power was accredited to Mary, the Mother of God, the holy virgin, for she does manifest herself in this way" (Church History 7:5 [A.D. 444]).
Pope Leo I

"Let us rejoice, then, dearly beloved, with spiritual joy, and make our boast over the happy end of this illustrious man in the Lord [the martyr Laurentius] . . . By his prayer and intercession we trust at all times to be assisted . . ." (Sermons 85:4 [A.D. 450]).
