POLAND & UK DEEPEN SECURITY PARTNERSHIP — A NEW TRANSATLANTIC MOMENT 

Poland’s President Karol Nawrocki held his first high-level talks with British Prime Minister Keir Starmer in London, marking a major step forward in bilateral cooperation on defense, Ukraine security, and economic ties. The meeting underscored Warsaw and London’s shared commitment to European security at a time of growing regional risk.  ￼

The discussions focused on military coordination amid Ukraine peace efforts, including enhanced defense industry collaboration and the continued presence of British forces stationed in Poland as part of NATO’s eastern deterrence posture. Warsaw also highlighted the UK’s support following past Russian airspace violations and ongoing efforts on Poland’s Miecznik frigate program, demonstrating real industrial and strategic cooperation between the two nations.  ￼

This London visit coincides with broader allied moves: British leaders have affirmed a role in a transnational security framework for Ukraine, with any future peacekeeping troop deployments subject to parliamentary approval and coordinated with the United States. Starmer’s government has been shaping policies that would see British military assets support stability in Ukraine under a Coalition of the Willing model — a framework developed with European partners and backed by U.S. engagement.  ￼

Poland and the United Kingdom are not just reaffirming old alliances — they are actively co-crafting Europe’s defense architecture in response to Russia’s aggression. Their collaboration spans boots, ships, and shared strategic frameworks, reinforcing Poland’s role as a key pillar of transatlantic security.

Fried duck isa popular Indonesian dish of duck meat boiled with spices and then fried until tender inside and crispy skin, served hot with rice, hot chili sauce, and fresh vegetables (such as cucumber, basil)This dish is rich in savory flavor, loved by many, and has regional variations of spices, such as richer spices in Bali or sweet and savory in Madura, making it an iconic Indonesian dish. Main Characteristics: Tender Meat: After being boiled or steamed with spices (garlic, ginger, turmeric, coriander, etc.), duck meat becomes very tender. Crispy Skin: The final frying process makes the skin crispy and appetizing. Serving: Always accompanied by warm white rice, spicy chili sauce (shrimp paste, onions, etc.), and fresh vegetables (cucumber, lettuce, basil leaves).  Regional Variations: Bali: Known for its rich spices. Madura: Has a distinctive sweet and savory taste. Javanese: A simple version with banana leaves, cucumber and spices. Why It's Popular: Unique texture: A combination of soft meat and crispy skin. The savory taste and rich spices typical of Indonesia. This is deeply disturbing and unacceptable. Under the Persons with Disabilities Act, no Person with Disability should ever be denied admission on account of disability. Such an action is unlawful, discriminatory, and a direct violation of the Constitution of Kenya.

The conduct of the Principal must be condemned in the strongest terms possible. Schools are institutions of inclusion, not exclusion.

I commend Makarina Mike for his courage, vigilance, and concern in speaking out. Silence in the face of injustice only normalizes discrimination. As indicated by Makarina,the appropriate course of action is to challenge this matter in a court of law. The Ministry of Education placed the learner in that school, and the school has a legal obligation to admit and accommodate the child.

All Organizations of Persons with Disabilities (OPDs), parents, and allies to stand in solidarity against this injustice. Education is not a favour  it is a fundamental right.

Article 20. Right to Education

(1) Every person with disability has a right to admission to any institution of learning and access to an
inclusive, quality education on an equal basis with others.

(2) No person shall be excluded from the education system on the basis of disability.

(3) The National government shall facilitate participation of persons with disabilities in accessible and
adaptable continuing adult education programmes on an equal basis.

(4) The National and County Governments shall ensure that persons with disabilities have access to
inclusive education, without discrimination and on an equal basis at all levels.

(5) Every child with disability has the right to free and compulsory basic education.

(6) Children with disabilities shall not be excluded from free and compulsory early childhood, primary
or secondary education, on the basis of disability.

(7) Every child with disabilities has a right to equal access to play, recreation and leisure and sporting
activities, including those activities in the school system.

(8) The Council in consultation with relevant Government establishments shall ensure that—

(a) learning institutions take into account the needs of persons with disabilities with respect
to the set entry requirements, pass marks, curriculum, examinations, auxiliary services,
use of school facilities, class schedules, physical education requirements and other similar
considerations;

(b) learning institutions provide individualized support measures, appropriate equipment,
assistive devices, adaptive technologies and other supportive services in environments that
maximize academic and social development, consistent with the goal of full inclusion of
students with disabilities;

(c) the Ministry responsible for education formulates strategies to implement inclusive
education through—

(i) enforcement of recruitment and retention of special education teachers in all schools
and institutions;

(ii) adaptation and structural adjustments of all educational institutions to the needs of
persons with disabilities;

(iii) establishment of specialized institutions that undertake research and development in
education for learners with disabilities;

(iv) establishment of at least one assessment centre in each county to support educational
institutions within the county, by way of teacher trainers, educational aids, equipment
and materials;

(v) promotion of the use of appropriate augmentative and alternative modes, means and
formats of communication, adaptive technologies, including Braille and Kenya Sign
Language; and

(vi) introduction of Kenyan Sign language courses in all learning and training institutions.

(9) The Cabinet Secretary in charge of education shall develop an adaptable examination framework
and award a certificate to children with intellectual disabilities after completion of their education.

(10) Each learner with disability including an intellectual disability has a right to be assessed and be
placed in an appropriate learning institution in accordance with the outcome of the assessment.

(11) Any person who denies a person with disability admission on the basis of disability commits an
offence and is liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding five hundred thousand shillings or to
imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years or both.

(12) In addition to subsection (11) the court may order unconditional admission of the person with
disability.

(13) The Cabinet Secretary responsible for education shall—

(a) facilitate through policies and legislation, the development of persons with disabilities
through their personality, talents and creativity, as well as their mental and physical
abilities, to their fullest potential;

(b) in collaboration with the relevant line ministries shall provide training facilities for speech
therapy, occupational therapy, physiotherapy, guidance and counselling, audio-logical
assessments, habilitation, and aural and oral rehabilitation for children with disabilities; and

(c) together with the County Education Committees in charge of education make policy,
legislation and sustainable financial frameworks in each financial year to achieve full
realization of the right to education for persons with disabilities.

(14) Every Person with Disabilities is entitled to receive the support services required, within the general
education system, to facilitate his or her effective inclusive education.

(15) The Council shall work in consultation with relevant agencies of National and County Governments
to make provisions for an integrated system of special and non-formal schools and institutions,

I recall that Hon. David Ole Sankok The Global GeoPolitician David Ole Sankok  consistently stood firm against such injustices when he was Chairman Board of Directors NCPWD and nominated Member of National Assembly.That same spirit of bold advocacy like this is needed now.

Discrimination has no place in our education system.

This is how I numb out when I'm facing the biggest block.
.
I catch myself, around hour 3, and I ask myself:
"Hold up, am I relaxing right now with my fuzzy blanket, lit candles, and a plate of cheese OR am I numbing my anxiety/ fear because I am experiencing the biggest, most common block?"
.
If it’s the second, most of the time, I force myself to turn off the TV and as Anna said in Frozen II, a version of my future self forces me to “do the next right thing”.
.
So…..
.
Do you want to know what the most common block is?
.
The biggest thing holding us back from creating the lives we feel called to create professionally and personally? 
.
It's *not* your lack of vision, clarity, or even courage.
.
It's your fear of disappointing the people you love most.
.
Here's what I've noticed after coaching hundreds of women:
The biggest block to living out our purpose (both professionally and personally) isn't imposter syndrome or lack of strategy.
It's the terror of hurting feelings or losing respect of those we belong to.
.
Our mothers. Our partners. Our church families. Our best friends.
.
We would rather betray ourselves than risk their disappointment.
We'd rather dim our desires than threaten the version of us they've grown comfortable with.
.
And here's the thing...
This pattern isn't your fault.
.
You were taught (often by well-meaning people who loved you) that your worth is tied to how well you perform for others.
That your desires are selfish.
That good women sacrifice.
That trusting yourself is arrogant.
.
But what if the Gospel of Mary Magdalene was right when it said, "The hidden treasure within the soul is not recognized by all, but seek it for yourself"?
.
What if your desires aren't dangerous...but Divine?
.
What if choosing yourself isn't selfish...but sacred?
.
This is the journey of The Treasure Within.
.
Over 12 weeks, we'll gather on Thursday nights (6:30-8 pm CST, starting THIS Thursday, January 15th) in a sacred circle where we question the inherited narratives that have kept you performing instead of present.
.
You'll learn to:
Reconnect with your body through somatic awareness (because your body has been trying to tell you something)
.
Set boundaries with controlling people using a proven framework (without the guilt spiral)
.
Trust your desires as sacred guidance (not something to apologize for)
.
Integrate your intuitive gifts without shame (yes, you're allowed to know things)
.
Make peace with your faith journey (even if it looks nothing like it used to)
.
Understand your cyclical nature and honor your rhythms (instead of pushing through)
.
Reclaim pleasure and sexuality as holy (this one's big)
.
Lead from wholeness, not performance (the world needs this version of you)
.
We'll be reading my upcoming novel, There, He Holds Her, together as our shared language for processing what emerges.
.
You'll have access to a private community for daily support.
You'll receive curated nonfiction resources, integration exercises, and somatic practices each week.
.
And here's what I know to be true:
When you stop betraying yourself to keep others comfortable, you don't lose the people who truly love you uncondiiontally. 
.
You lose the version of the relationship that was built on your silence.
.
And what emerges in its place?
.
Real intimacy. Honest connection. Relationships built on who you actually are.
.
Not everyone will rise to the occasion of your counteroffer and move toward a win-win in which you both work together at loving well.
.
And that's okay.
.
Because at the end of the day, you (and only you) are in charge of your emotional currency and how you spend it.
.
Your permission slip to choose yourself.
.
Your 12-week refuge from the exhaustion of appeasing and impressing.
.
Only 2 days left to join us.
Only 3 spots remain in this founding cohort.
.
If something in your chest just said "yes," listen to it.
That's not anxiety.
.
That's the treasure within, knocking on the door of your heart.
.
Comment "TREASURE" or DM me and I'll send you the details.

"The courtroom had barely emptied when something unusual happened.
Just moments after handing down the sentence, the judge did not retreat to his chambers. He moved quickly through the back corridors, his black robes still on, his face set with purpose. People who work in courthouses know this almost never happens.
Judge Vance had a reputation across the county. Tough. Fair. Unmoved by excuses. That morning, he sentenced a 19 year old named Tyrell to three years behind bars. The law was clear, and the sentence followed it.
During the hearing, Tyrell tried to hold himself together. He stared straight ahead, jaw tight, hands clenched. He was waiting for one face in the gallery. His mother.
She was supposed to be there. She always was.
She had worked double shifts, sometimes back to back, to pay for his lawyer. She skipped doctor visits and ignored her own chest pains because she believed showing up for her son mattered more than anything. She promised him she would be in that courtroom no matter what.
Her seat stayed empty.
An hour later, in a cold concrete holding cell, Tyrell finally learned why.
His lawyer could barely get the words out. That morning, while getting dressed for court, the stress overtook her. Her heart gave out before the ambulance could help.
The sound that came out of Tyrell was not just crying. It was raw and animal. He collapsed against the wall, convinced he had killed the one person who never gave up on him. Every bad choice, every night she stayed awake worrying, every shift she worked exhausted played over and over in his head.
A veteran bailiff who had seen decades of hardened men break only once walked straight to the judge’s chambers. He told Judge Vance that this was different. This kid was not acting. He was shattered.
Judge Vance sat quietly after the bailiff left. He knew the law had been served. But he also knew something else. If a young man drowned alone in that kind of guilt, prison would not fix him. It would finish him.
So instead of sending a chaplain, instead of calling a counselor, the judge did something no one expected.
He went down to the cell block himself.
Still wearing his robes, he sat on the narrow cot beside Tyrell. No bench. No authority. Just a human being next to another human being at his lowest point.
He gently took Tyrell’s cuffed hands and said, “Look at me.”
Through tears and gasps, Tyrell whispered that everything was his fault. That his mother was gone because of him. That he did not deserve to breathe the same air anymore.
The judge did not raise his voice. He did not lecture. He shook his head and spoke slowly.
“You made a mistake. That is not the end of who you are. You still have choices left.”
Then he did more than offer words.
He promised Tyrell he would personally arrange a temporary release so he could bury his mother. He told him he would come visit him in prison. And if Tyrell stayed focused and did right while inside, the judge would personally review his case for early release.
Not as a favor. As a promise.
For many people over 50 and 60, this story hits hard because it reminds us of something we rarely see anymore. Accountability with compassion. Justice with humanity. A reminder that sometimes the most powerful thing a person in authority can do is sit down, listen, and refuse to let another soul believe they are beyond saving."

Chapter Thirty Nine

Danyaal

Stillness does not last in the palace.
It is noticed. It is interpreted. It acquires witnesses. Even silence becomes a kind of testimony if left unattended.

I leave the balcony before the quiet between Wajiha and I can harden into meaning, before it can be assigned intent by someone trained to extract narratives from posture alone. 

The corridors are empty at this hour, but I am well aware that emptiness here is deceptive. The palace is never unoccupied. It merely pretends to be.

Wajiha does not look back as I step away. I do not expect her to. What passed between us did not require confirmation. That, more than anything, unsettles me.

Most people seek reassurance when answers fail them. She did not. She recalibrated.

‘If I’m the access point…’

The thought does not simply echo. It is a root that I knew from the very beginning . That is the problem.

I have spent years learning how to recognize dangerous intelligence. It announces itself quietly, often disguised as restraint. 
Wajiha did not sound clever. She sounded certain. Certainty, when earned, is volatile.

By the time I reach my office, the palace lights have shifted into their nocturnal configuration. Softer and warmer, designed to encourage rest, like an illusion of safety. 
I do not indulge it.

Before I open a single file, I already know this will not be solved from behind a screen alone. Certain truths survive digitization precisely because no one believes they will ever be sought in person.

I start off with public records, and the files are easily accessible. Too easily. 
That, I note.

The Royal family had already anticipated this direction of inquiry, or perhaps they had simply trusted the public to stay within acceptable parameters. Either way, the permissions are there. Silent and unquestioned.

I do not begin with Prince Zaiden just yet. 
That would be obvious. Obvious lines of inquiry attract attention. Instead, I spend three days circling the absence, by pulling institutional cross references, reviewing legacy access protocols, tracing how royal records are structured rather than what they contain.

I take note of the patterns that emerge slowly. Not in content, but in architecture.
Certain archives are sealed with redundancy. Others rely on tradition. 

Academic records, especially those unrelated to governance, are treated as inert. It's a safety net. They are where people hide without meaning to.

If Wajiha is right, and my instincts tell me she is, then Ammah is a convergence.
And what I know about convergences, is that they require at least two trajectories.

Prince Zaiden is the perspicuous one. Not because he is guilty of anything, but because he is unavoidable. You do not build a myth that large without leaving structural shadows behind.
I begin where it  would be expected for me to.
Prince Zaiden’s records are extensive.
As the Sultana’s firstborn, his life was documented in detail from infancy. Every milestone, tutors, foreign visits, academic progress. The narrative is clean and linear. A prince groomed for leadership, educated in political science and statecraft, prepared for a future he would never inherit.

I skim through it quickly.
This is the version meant to be remembered, the one made for the heart of the public. 
The efficiency with which the archive presents him is almost impressive. 
There is no ambiguity here. No contradiction. Every year accounted for. Every transition smoothed. The palace excels at continuity. It understands that chaos is rarely dangerous yet inconsistency is.

I request supplementary academic records, the kind most people forget to seal because no one thinks to look there.
Attendance logs.
External enrollments.
Correspondence between institutions.
It takes a day longer than expected.
Then two.
Then three.
That alone is not remarkable. 

Administrative delays are common. But this one feels… curated. As though someone needed time to decide which version of completeness would be least provocative.
When the file arrives, it is less informative than I anticipated.
I study the metadata first. Confirm authenticity. No anomalies. No evidence of retroactive modification. Whoever constructed this did not need to falsify anything. They relied instead on omission.

Prince Zaiden completed his political studies.
Graduated with honors.
No surprise there. His aptitude was never in question. Even his detractors conceded his discipline.

Yet… I can't help but notice gaps. 
Not absences.
Gaps.

The significance of this is what I fear holds consequence. 

Absences imply neglect. Gaps imply design.
Weeks where attendance is logged but lecture participation is absent.
Seminars attended remotely before such accommodations were common.
Practical modules completed through alternative credits.

At first glance, it reads like privilege.
On second glance, it reads like avoidance and avoidance is not the same as secrecy. Secrecy hides, but avoidance reroutes.
I cross-reference course schedules against palace travel logs. 

The overlaps are imperfect. Just enough misalignment to suggest intentional decentralization. A prince attending class without being seen to attend class. A presence that registers without occupying space.
I sit with it longer than I should.

Tapping my pen against the desk I envision the prince.. Having everything, the wealth, the legacy and privilege and somehow he managed to pour out his heart onto canvas and paint. 

Then I widen the net.
Foreign academic registries. Independent institutions. Cultural exchange programs that existed on the margins of political relevance.

That is when I see it.
The moment does not announce itself. There is no dramatic shift, no instinctive surge of certainty. Only a subtle tightening in my chest, the sensation of something aligning too cleanly.

A secondary enrollment.
Different institution.
Different name.
Same years.

I do not move.
The room feels narrower, as though the truth has weight and has chosen this moment to settle.
The art school is modest, internationally respected but politically insignificant. Known for classical technique, conservation ethics, historical study.
Prince Zaiden enrolled under a pseudonym.
Not a clever one.
Just… different enough, unremarkable and so common. 
Zaid Abdullah 

This is not illegal. It barely qualifies as subversive. The palace has always tolerated harmless secrecy, provided it does not challenge the narrative. A prince studying art under an assumed name does not threaten governance. If anything, it humanizes him in retrospect.
Still, digital records only tell part of the truth.

But I need to know more. 
I arrange for transport that night.
The private security jet leaves before dawn, unmarked, routine enough not to invite questions. By midmorning, I am walking the corridors of a university that does not know it matters.

The dean receives me without suspicion.
He is old enough to remember when the school mattered less to the world and more to itself. His office is cluttered with framed exhibition posters and fading photographs of graduating classes whose names no one outside these walls would recognize.

“I’m researching institutional culture,” I tell him. It is close enough to the truth to avoid correction. “A specific period. Late eighties . Early nineties."

He smiles faintly at that. Nostalgia is a language administrators rarely resist.

“That was a quieter time,” he says. “Before patronage. Before performance became currency.”

“What kind of students did you have then?” I ask.

He sits forward, arms on his desk, thinking. “Serious ones. People who didn’t expect to be seen. A few… unusual enrollments.”

“Unusual how?”

“Oh.. You know. Older than average. Or younger than they claimed. Some who arrived with no interest in recognition.” He pauses, eyes narrowing slightly, memory rearranging itself. “There were students who treated anonymity like relief.”

I nod, encouraging silence to do its work.

“They studied restoration mostly,” he adds after a moment. “People who understood that preservation is restraint. Knowing when not to touch something.”

“Were they close?” I ask, carefully. “Students from that period.”

He smiles again, softer this time. “Art schools are intimate by nature. You share failures before successes. It creates bonds.” 

A pause. “Some disappear afterward. Others… leave traces.”

“May I stay a while longer? I am fascinated by this academic culture.”

“Of course! You are most welcome, I'll call for a tour guide…”

“Ah! That's generous, but no need. I'll just walk the grounds.”

I thank him as I walked out. He never remembers my name.

The archives smell of dust and solvent. 
Real paper. Real ink. The kind of records no one bothers to sanitize because they assume no one important ever cared enough to be here.
I scroll through faculty rosters.
Course catalogs.
Exhibition archives.

The deeper I go, the quieter the record becomes. This institution does not mythologize its students. It documents them with humility. Names appear and disappear without ceremony. Talent is noted sparingly. Failure is recorded without cruelty.

And then… quietly, devastatingly, I find the overlap.
I close my eyes.
Not because this proves anything.
But because it reframes everything.

Ammah’s name appears in the exact same catalogs. 
Her name is not highlighted.
Not exceptional.

Just present.
A student of restoration theory.
A contributor to a collaborative exhibit.
A scholarship recipient thanked in the acknowledgments of a traveling collection.
There is no photograph of them together.
No letter linking them.
No correspondence archived under either name.

But they were there.
At the same time, the same year, walking the same halls. 
Studying the same discipline.
Learning how to preserve what time tries to destroy.

That detail lands harder than it should.
Restoration is not creation. It is not reinvention. It is the careful study of fracture. The ethics of intervention. Knowing when to leave damage visible because erasure would be a lie.

I can vividly imagine Prince Zaiden in those classrooms, coming across as unremarkable, anonymous, relieved. I imagine the way anonymity must have felt like oxygen. The way art might have offered him something politics never could: stillness.

And I imagine Ammah right beside him.
Not as a plot, not as a villain.

But I strongly believe she sat next to him as a woman who believed she had found something real in a world that traded in appearances.
That is the most dangerous origin of all.

I lean back slowly, allowing the chair to support the gravity of internal weight I did not realize I was holding.
Prince Zaiden lived a divided life.
A public heir.
A private man.
The palace knew the first.
It never questioned the second.

I understand now why no one looked here. This narrative threatens no one unless someone insists on connecting it to something else. And until Wajiha existed, until her presence disrupted the symmetry, there was no reason to.

I do not tell anyone what I’ve found.
Not the Sultana.
Not Wajiha.
Not yet.

Because this is not evidence.
This is context.
And context, wielded incorrectly, destroys the wrong people.
I have seen it happen too many times, women reduced to motives, men absolved by silence, truth rearranged until it serves the least vulnerable. 

I will not be the instrument of that violence.
The balcony was a mistake.
Not only emotionally but strategically too.

Sightlines there are too clean. Too predictable. The palace understands elevation. It watches balconies because balconies suggest intimacy. Gardens, by contrast, are assumed to be ornamental. Distractions. Background.

I activate the secure channel as I stand.
“Elias,” I say.

“Yes, sir.”

“Send a message to Wajiha.”

A pause. He is careful not to ask why.

“Tell her we can’t keep meeting where sightlines are predictable,” I continue. “Suggest the lower gardens. Eastern paths. After dusk.”

“Understood.”

I end the transmission and glance once more at the dimmed screen.
Nothing here condemns anyone.
But everything here has shifted.
The university breathes around me, unaware, or perhaps pretending to be.

But I know the palace gardens are built for misdirection.
And this story, whatever it becomes, will require space to grow.

ENOUGH, BE WISE (1)
(Proverbs 4:7) Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and 
with all thy getting get understanding. 
Many believe that wealth comes simply by working hard, but Scripture 
shows that hard work without wisdom leads to frustration (Ecclesiastes 
10:15). “Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom” (Proverbs 
4:7).
Diligence is powerful, yet it is wisdom, knowledge, and understanding 
that turn effort into results. Many people believe that hard work is the 
only ingredient needed to produce wealth. While diligence is important, 
Scripture teaches us that hard work without wisdom, knowledge, and 
understanding often leads to struggle, frustration, and stagnation. The 
Bible says: “The labor of the foolish wearies every one of them, because 
he knows not how to go to the city” (Ecclesiastes 10:15).
Hard work opens the door, but wisdom, knowledge, and financial insight 
fill the house with abundance. Hard work without wisdom can lead to 
futility. A man can be busy, active, and hardworking, yet unproductive,
simply because he lacks direction. Hard work becomes fruitful when 
guided by insight, strategy, and divine understanding.
The farmer who plants in dry season works hard, but without wisdom. 
The builder who ignores foundation principles sweats, yet wastes effort. 
Hard work alone doesn’t create wealth, wisdom, knowledge, and 
financial insight do. Wisdom turns labour into results. Wisdom is a 
wealth-generating force. The Bible is clear that wealth does not come by 
strength alone. Proverbs 24:3–4 says, “By wisdom a house is built, by 
understanding it is established; by knowledge the rooms are filled with all 
precious and pleasant riches”. 
Hard work may bring income, but wisdom brings increase. Hard work 
may bring wages, but understanding brings wealth. Joseph did not rise in 
Egypt because of sweat alone; he rose because of insight and 
interpretation (Genesis 41:38–40). Solomon didn’t become the wealthiest 
king because he worked the longest hours, he operated by wisdom from 
above (1 Kings 4:29–34). Wisdom is from God alone. “Wisdom belongs 
to God” (Job 12:13). God is the ultimate source (Proverbs 2:6), giving it 
to those who ask (James 1:5). Child of God, true wisdom comes from 
God. It involves applying God's truth, not just knowing it. True wisdom 
starts with fearing the Lord. This year, don’t just work hard, work smart. 
Be diligent and apply wisdom and your result will be outstanding.
Thought for the Day: Hard work produces sweat; wisdom produces wealth.
Prayer: Lord, give me wisdom to work smart, knowledge to make right decisions, 
and insight that multiplies the work of my hands. Let Your blessing guide me into 
increase, abundance, and financial peace. Amen.

SIGNIFICANCE OF GOD’S LEADINGS 

It's crucial to understand that divine direction is rarely a constant, audible voice. Scripture and experience show it comes through a confluence of ways, with the Holy Spirit as the primary Guide (John 16:13):

A. For Relationship (Primary Purpose)
Divine direction is primarily about intimacy, not just information. As seen in Psalm 32:8, God says, "I will counsel you with my eye upon you." The goal is a walking, talking relationship where we learn to discern His heart and character. The journey with Him is as important as the destination.

B. For Identity and Security
Being led by God confirms our identity as His children ("For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God" - Romans 8:14). It provides deep security, knowing we are not subject to random chance or fate, but are under the purposeful care of a loving Father. This frees us from the tyranny of anxiety and the need to control every outcome.

C. For Protection and Provision
God's direction often serves as a protective boundary, leading us away from harm (spiritual, emotional, physical) and toward places of provision and flourishing (the "green pastures" of Psalm 23). It is an aspect of His deliverance.

D. For Purpose and Fruitfulness
God directs us into our created purpose. He guides us to the "good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them" (Ephesians 2:10). His direction aligns our lives with His eternal kingdom purposes, ensuring that our labor is not in vain but bears lasting fruit (John 15:16).

A life visibly guided by God becomes a powerful testimony to His reality and faithfulness. I recently shared a table in a bar. He is fifty five and he told me that he is already feeling the loneliness of being neglected by his three children who moved out and are living their lives out there. “Watoto hawapigi simu hata tu kutuma kitu when I am down with Malaria ni noma mzae,I truly regret making and raising children,I envy your Uncle's lifestyle,I swear.”

That slapped me hard in my face because i am on the line but i keep telling myself,hawa wangu sio kama hao wenu,hawa wangu ni special to me,just to shake off the reality of having children who will be swallowed by the world that did not raise and pay their school fees.

But!

Si ni life?

Învăț să mă iert
Sufletul plânge, nu dorea să mai treacă prin durere.

A venit ca o lovitură finală, pentru a mă îngenunchea.

Am să plâng, am să tac, pentru a mă putea ierta.

În naivitatea mea, încă cred în oamenii din jur.

De fiecare dată spun, am să fiu mai atentă!

Uite că, de fiecare dată, mă neglijez pe mine.

Spun, nu are ce să se întâmple mai rău,

Surprinzător, parcă lovește și mai adânc în inimă.

Mă întreb... cât îmi e dat să mai duc povara?

Acum aleg tăcerea, am să mă adun pe mine.

Nu îmi doresc alt suflet, alt chip, mă accept.

Nu aș putea fi nepăsătoare cu cei din jur.

Mi-e dat să duc durerea, pentru că iert ușor,

În schimb, pe mine nu mă pot ierta pe deplin.

Uneori cred că merită toată suferința ce-mi e dată,

Prin ea simt că-mi mântui sufletul aici.

E un crez ca să pot trece peste durere,

Să mă ridic din propria-mi cenușă.

Copiii îmi aduc bucuria și zâmbetul pe chip,

Adultul m-a rănit la fiecare pas, fără să vrea.

Nu mai cer nimic, doar să mă iert pe mine.

Sufletule, tu nu ai vină că eu mă simt incapabilă de tine.

Tu mă iubești așa cum sunt, fără să mă critici.

Da, am sa mă întorc la mine, în suflet... 

Acolo e cald și bine, asa ma pot ierta pe mine.

13.01.2026

Mihaela Dragne

(Ganta, Nimba County, January 13, 2026): The Press Union of Liberia (PUL) has underscored the critical need for a strong and responsible partnership between the Liberian media and the nation’s joint security forces. In an address at the conference, PUL President Julius Kanubah emphasized the pivotal roles of journalists and law enforcement in safeguarding Liberia’s democracy and promoting social cohesion. “Constructive engagement between the media and security sector is essential,” Kanubah stated. “Together, we can uphold freedom of expression, a free press, and the rule of law, while ensuring that our conduct reflects the highest professional standards.”

Organized under the auspices of the National Elections Commission (NEC) and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the Ganta conference involves 47 journalists and law enforcement officers from Grand Cape Mount, Margibi, Bong, Lofa, and Nimba Counties. 

The primary focus of the gathering is to review and update the Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) that guide collaboration, cooperation, and coordination between the media and security agencies, particularly during electoral processes.

Representing Joint Security, Deputy Commissioner of Police and Head of the West African Police Information System at the Liberia National Police (LNP), Augustine Browne, stressed the importance of unity in advancing peace and stability. ‘It is imperative for the media and security to work in concert to prevent misunderstandings and foster a peaceful environment’, Browne remarked.

UNDP Programme Officer Roosevelt Zayzay also noted the value of the SOP in reducing potential conflicts and misunderstandings between media professionals and security officers throughout the 2023 General and Presidential Elections. ‘A clear framework ensures that all parties understand their roles and responsibilities, minimizing confrontation and building public trust’, Zayzay said.

Executive Director of the NEC, Anthony Sengbe, urged all stakeholders to maintain the highest levels of professionalism. ‘Our collective commitment will ensure that Liberia’s electoral process remains peaceful and free from violence’, Sengbe stated.

Attorney Christopher Fayiah, Deputy Executive Director of the Liberia Peacebuilding Office, highlighted the need to integrate lessons learned and best practices into the revised SOP. ‘Continuous improvement of the framework is vital to address emerging challenges and to strengthen the role of women in peacebuilding initiatives’, Fayiah said.

The Ganta conference builds on two preceding regional media–security conferences held in Zwedru, Grand Gedeh County, and Buchanan, Grand Bassa County, which collectively engaged media and security representatives from several counties across Liberia. The current review process emphasizes roles and responsibilities, dispute-resolution mechanisms, and the enhancement of women’s participation in peace promotion.

Following the conference on Wednesday, 14 January, a comprehensive working session will collate insights from all three regional gatherings. These findings will inform a validation workshop that will lead to the finalization of the revised SOP.

I know many of us, especially as young people are dealing with hurtful words, misunderstood actions, and people who don’t really get us.

Lately, I’ve learned something the hard way…

I can’t control what happens around me.
I can’t control what people think about me.
I can’t control how they talk to me or respond to me.

But one thing?
I have full control over how I react or respond.

Before now, I used to react to everything.
I would get hurt, cry, rage, overthink, let it sit in my heart and eat me up.
And honestly? It drained me.

So I had to learn consciously to respond differently.

Not because it’s easy.
There are days I still want to cry.
There are moments when things hurt so deep.

But I remind myself of one thing:
Anything that steals my peace is too expensive.

And I hate seeing myself in a place of emotional chaos, depression, or unrest.

So now, when words hurt me…
When situations try to break me…
I filter them.

If it’s going to disturb my peace, I say no.
If it’s going to eat me up, I refuse to digest it.

It doesn’t mean I’m weak.
Silence doesn’t mean weakness.
Sometimes it means strength, maturity, and self-control.

You can’t control how people treat you.

But you can control your reaction.

You can choose not to explode.
You can choose not to carry every word into your heart.
You can choose peace over chaos.

Personal growth starts here.
Learning how to control your emotions.
Learning how to respond, not react.

I watch my husband struggling for his life. At that moment, I forgot all the problems between us and was only praying for his life .

Micheal wasn’t a good person, but seeing him in that situation broke me . 

The hospital  needed money for his treatment, but I had no money . He had money in his account, after all he just won 11 million naira from betnaija. But we couldn’t access the money because no one knew his phone password. 

His family and I run around and raised an amount to deposit , and they began the treatment. 

The Doctor warned us not to waste time if not it could be fatal. He needed to be transferred to another hospital as soon as possible but we were unable to access the money for the hospital bill.

I had to put my pride aside and went to his side chick that he was staying before he had that accident to beg her to come open his phone because I knew she knows his phone password.

This girl refused, she insulted me instead. She also stated that she does not care about my husband, that I should leave her house. 

It took a lot of begging for this girl to finally give my husband’s phone password and bank pin .

I was able to transfer money for his treatment and was transferred to another hospital. 

He fell into a coma. The doctor said they don’t know how long . It could be days, weeks, months or even years. 

After my husband was admitted in the hospital and receiving treatment proper, his family returned back to their houses leaving me to care for him. 

I had to leave my other two children with my neighbors and manage with the little one while taking care of my husband.

I stayed, and I hope, prayed that he comes out of the coma soon .

Luckily after 3 weeks he came out of the coma . 

The bad news is, my husband may not be able to walk again, his spinal cord was greatly affected.

I had a good long conversation with him . He he couldn’t even talk back , tears were just running down his face. More like he was sorry for all he had done but my mind was made up already.

I was leaving.

I left and I called his family to go and take care of their son 

The chaos that followed after I left was unexplainable.

Madam Abeni stood behind the counter of her largest shop, arms folded, eyes sharp and restless, surveying the space like a general inspecting a battlefield. The shop was already noisy with morning activity, metal shelves clinking, cartons being dragged across the floor, the faint smell of detergent and spices mixing in the air. Yet nothing seemed to satisfy her.

“Aanu” she barked suddenly.

Aanu, who was crouched near a stack of goods trying to arrange sachets neatly, jolted upright.

“Yes, ma?”

Madam Abeni’s eyes narrowed as she pointed sharply at the shelf.

“Is that how I told you to arrange those items? Are you blind or just slow?”

Aanu's hands trembled as she adjusted the sachets quickly.

“I’m sorry, ma. I’ll fix it.”

“Sorry doesn’t sell goods!” Madam Abeni snapped. “If customers come in and see rubbish arrangement like this, will they buy? Must I do everything myself?”

She turned abruptly, heels clicking against the tiled floor.

“Bisi!” she shouted.

Bisi was at the back, counting change for a customer. In her hurry, a few coins slipped from her hand and scattered on the floor.

“Look at this one,” Madam Abeni scoffed loudly. “Always clumsy. How many times have I warned you to count properly? If money gets missing, will you grow another hand to replace it?”

Bisi bent down quickly, face burning with embarrassment as customers watched.
“I’m sorry, ma. It won’t happen again.”

“You people say that every day,” Madam Abeni replied coldly. “Yet nothing ever changes.”

She marched toward the freezer and yanked it open. Her face darkened instantly.

“Who packed this freezer?” she demanded.

Silence.

“I asked a question!” she thundered.

“I did, ma,” Kemi said softly from the corner.

Madam Abeni slammed the freezer door shut.
“Then come here and explain to me why the drinks are arranged like leftovers after a party. Are you running a shop or a beer parlour?”

Kemi hurried over.
“I thought.....”

“Don’t think!” Madam Abeni cut in. “Thinking is what gets you confused. Do exactly what I say. Is that too much to ask?”

She waved her hand dismissively.
“Remove everything and arrange it again. Now.”

Kemi nodded and rushed to obey.

Madam Abeni turned back toward the counter and spotted a dusty section near the entrance. Her eyes flashed.

“See dirt!” she exclaimed. “Do you people sleep here? Is it so hard to clean before opening?”

She grabbed a rag from the counter and flung it toward Sade.
“Take that and clean everywhere properly. Customers are not goats; they don’t like dirt.”

Sade hurried away, scrubbing furiously.

Madam Abeni exhaled sharply, shaking her head.
“Honestly, if I close my eyes for one second, everything falls apart. Is it because it’s not your shop? If it were your own, would you work like this?”

No one answered. The girls moved faster now, afraid of drawing her attention again.

As a customer walked in, Madam Abeni’s tone changed instantly, sweet, polished.

“Good morning, ma. What can I get for you?”

The customer left a few minutes later. The sweetness vanished just as quickly.

“Aanu, why are you standing like a statue?” Madam Abeni snapped. “Bring out more cartons from the store. Do you think goods arrange themselves?”

“Yes, ma,” Aanu replied, already heading toward the back.

Madam Abeni watched them all with hard eyes, issuing instructions without pause. Her words flew around the shop like sharp stones, driven by impatience and a need for control. The girls obeyed in silence, their movements quick and cautious, each one hoping not to be the next target.

By the time the shop began to settle, Madam Abeni stood at the center again, hands on her waist, nodding slightly, not in satisfaction, but in grim approval.

“This is how a shop should look,” she said. “Next time, I don’t want to shout before you do your work.”

No one replied. The girls simply nodded, breathing quietly, as the shop returned to its uneasy rhythm under Madam Abeni’s watchful eye.

Madam Abeni clapped her hands sharply, the sound slicing through the uneasy quiet of the shop.

“All of you, come here,” she said.

The girls gathered reluctantly, forming a loose line in front of the counter. Madam Abeni paced slowly before them, eyes sweeping over their faces as though weighing each one.

“Let me tell you something very clearly,” she began, her voice low but edged with fire. “Some of you think this shop grew by magic. You think money falls from heaven. But let me warn you, laziness is the fastest way to destroy a business.”

She stopped in front of Aanu.
“You,” she said, pointing. “Always dragging your feet.”

She turned to Bisi.
“And you, careless with money.”

Then Kemi.
“And you, doing things halfway.”

She spread her arms wide.
“Is it that you people have gathered together and decided to run this business down?”

“No, ma,” they chorused quickly.

“Then prove it!” Madam Abeni snapped. “Because I will not sit down and watch anybody destroy what I labored for with my sweat. I suffered to build this place. I didn’t borrow money to come and play shop.”

She leaned forward slightly, eyes blazing.
“If you are tired of working here, say it now. I will not tolerate sabotage disguised as laziness.”

The girls shook their heads, fear written plainly on their faces.

“Good,” she said sharply. “Because from today, I’m watching everyone. Any mistake, I will deal with it accordingly.”

She turned abruptly and walked toward the small office at the back of the shop. As she opened the door, she paused and looked back.

“And don’t think I won’t replace any of you,” she added coldly. “People are outside begging for work.”

The door shut behind her with a firm click.

For a moment, the shop was silent except for the faint hum of the freezer.

Then Bisi released a long breath.
“God help us,” she muttered.

Aanu rubbed her arms slowly.
“My heart is still beating fast,” she said. “The way madam talks to someone, ehn… it’s like we’re not human beings.”

Kemi shook her head.
“Honestly, I don’t even know what to say again. Every day shouting. Every day insults.”

Sade glanced toward the office door to be sure it was closed.
“If not that I need this job, I would have left since.”

Bisi leaned against the shelf.
“She talks to us like we want to destroy her life. As if we don’t work from morning till night.”

Aanu nodded.
“She doesn’t see effort. She only sees mistakes.”

Kemi lowered her voice further.
“But you know the painful thing? Madam is not a bad person completely.”

They all paused.

“What do you mean?” Sade asked.

Kemi shrugged.
“She helps people. Remember the woman whose child was sick? Madam paid the hospital bill.”

“And last Christmas,” Ada added reluctantly, “she shared foodstuffs in the community. Plenty.”

Bisi sighed.
“That’s what confuses me. Outside, people praise her. They say Madam Abeni is kind. But here…” She gestured around the shop. “Here, she turns into fire.”

Sade scoffed softly.
“Philanthropic, yes. But hot-tempered like pepper soup.”

They chuckled quietly, the laughter short-lived.

“I hate the way she talks to us,” Ada said, voice tight. “Sometimes I go home and cry.”

Bisi nodded slowly.
“She makes you feel small. Like you’re nothing.”

Kemi frowned.
“But if we’re being honest,” she said, “she doesn’t joke with her business. That’s why it’s still standing.”

Sade crossed her arms.
“She can be serious without being wicked.”

No one argued with that.

Aanu glanced again toward the office.
“If only she knew that the way she talks kills morale.”

Bisi sighed deeply.
“But will she ever listen?”

Silence answered her.

They returned quietly to their duties, movements slower now, not from laziness, but from the heaviness that comes with working under a temper that burned hotter than it healed.

The silence lingered for a while as they returned to their tasks, but it was the kind of silence that carried thoughts rather than peace. The hum of the freezer and the rustle of nylon bags filled the shop until Sade broke it.

She leaned closer to Aanu, lowering her voice.
“Aanu,” she said, “you sef, you’re the one that goes to church the most among us.”

Aanu stiffened slightly but kept arranging goods.
“So?”

“So why don’t you talk to madam?” Sade continued. “You like Bible. Go and preach Jesus to her.”

Aanu froze.

“Are you mad?” she whispered sharply. “Do you want me to lose my job?”

Bisi looked up, curiosity mixed with mischief.
“Ah, Sade has a point o,” she said. “You’re always quoting scriptures. Maybe madam needs salvation.”

Aanu shook her head vigorously.
“No, no, no. Not me.”

Kemi glanced toward the office door again.
“Why are you afraid? If anyone can talk to her calmly, it’s you.”

Aanu finally turned to face them, eyes wide with fear.
“Please don’t joke with that kind of thing,” she said. “Madam doesn’t joke with correction. Especially not from someone like me.”

Sade frowned.
“But isn’t that what Christianity teaches? To speak truth?”

Aanu laughed nervously.
“Truth that will not send you out of work,” she replied. “I like Jesus, but I also like eating.”

Bisi chuckled softly.
“See honesty.”

Aanu lowered her voice even more.
“You people don’t understand. This is not about faith. Madam will hear ‘God’ and think I’m insulting her.”

Kemi nodded slowly.
“She might say you’re calling her wicked.”

“Exactly!” Aanu exclaimed. “Or that I’m telling her how to run her business.”

Sade folded her arms.
“So we should just continue suffering?”

Aanu sighed.
“It’s not suffering I’m afraid of. It’s disgrace.”

Bisi tilted her head.
“But you always say God changes hearts.”

“Yes,” Aanu replied quickly, “but God didn’t say I should be the sacrifice.”

They stifled a laugh.

Sade pressed on, half serious now.
“But imagine if someone talks to her. Maybe she doesn’t know how harsh she sounds.”

Aanu shook her head again.
“She knows. She just doesn’t care.”

Kemi added quietly,
“Some people think shouting equals leadership.”

Bisi sighed.
“I wish she would talk to us like human beings.”

Aanu’s voice softened.
“Madam is generous, no doubt. But her anger controls her.”

Sade clicked her tongue.
“And anger and Jesus cannot stay in the same room.”

Aanu glanced sharply at her.
“Don’t let her hear you say that.”

They all went quiet again.

After a moment, Bisi spoke, more gently.
“Aanu, nobody is forcing you. But sometimes God uses unlikely people.”

Aanu smiled sadly.
“God can use anybody else. I’m not brave like that.”

Kemi nodded in understanding.
“Not everyone is called to confront Pharaoh.”

Aanu released a small breath of relief.
“Thank you.”

Sade shrugged.
“Well, until then, we endure.”

Aanu returned to her work, hands moving mechanically. Inside her chest, faith and fear wrestled quietly, urging courage, the other reminding her of the thin line between obedience and survival.

THE VENERABLE MARPA OBTAINS THE ORAL TRANSMISSION AND SPREADS THE DOCTRINE IN TIBET 

"When Mar-pa was about to leave once more for India and had collected money for the journey, three girls in heavenly robes appeared to him in a vision. To give his enterprise a good start and to fulfil the intention of Naropa's prophecy they said:

The sky-flower, the Daka riding on the foal
Of a barren mare, the Oral Transmission,
Has scattered the hairs of a tortoise, the ineffable,
And with the stick of a hare's horn, the unoriginated,
Roused Tilopa in the depth of ultimate reality.

Through the mute Tilopa, the ineffable 
resisting all attempts at communication,
The blind Naropa became free 
in seeing Truth which is no seeing.
On the mountain of the Dharmakaya 
which is the ultimate, the deaf Naropa,
The lame Mati (Mar-pa) ran in a radiant light, 
which neither comes nor goes.
The sun and moon and dGyes-pa rdo-rje
Their dancing is one-valueness in many.

The conch-shell has proclaimed 
its fame in all directions,
It has called out to the strenuous, 
who are worthy vessels for instruction.
The focal points, Cakrasamvara-the world
Is the wheel of the Oral Transmission:
Turn it, dear child, without attachment. 

After these words they faded like a rainbow.

As a .result of this vision Mar-pa went to Gro-bo-lun, and since a few days were still available, a ]!aka appeared to the venerable Mi-la-ras-pa and said: 'Through long meditation you have attained Mahamudra, the awakening to Buddhahood and the Six Doctrines, but you do not possess the instruction on transference and resurrection, which is the special means of awakening to Buddhahood by a short meditation.' The venerable Mi-la-ras-pa went to Mar-pa and asked to be taught resurrection. Then Mar-pa said that such a method existed but that he did not seem to have learned it; teacher and disciple went through all the books. Although they found many references to transference, there was not one single text on resurrection. The Mar-pa said: 'This vision of yours points to this purpose, I must depart quickly.'

When he arrived in India he met the novice Prajnasinha who told him: 'You have come late, on last year's new moon he (Naropa) passed away. He said many praiseworthy things about you and, convinced that you would come, he left his Vajra and bell and this painted scroll for you. The Vajra and the bell were stolen. But he
(Naropa) is still alive.' With these words he gave him the painted scroll of Hevajra. Although Mar-pa got this visible sign, in his yearning for his Guru he shed many tears of grief. Like a person who is denied meeting his Guru or whose merits are not up to the mark, he asked the novice whether he had any Oral Transmission
instructions. The latter replied: 'I have not even heard the word "Oral Transmission". But since your devotion is equal to the compassion of the venerable one who sees with the eyes of the Dharma, you will certainly meet him, but you should make offerings with all the gold you have with you.' So Mar-pa made an offering each month in the presence of Lord Maitripa, SriSantibhadra, the Dakini Rus-pa'i rgyan-can (Kankhali-bhusania), the novice Prajnasinha, and Naropa's former co-students Riripa and Kasoripa. The first prophecy he received was: 

The dream that the jewel 
has been placed on the royal banner
While a dancing girl gazed askance into a mirror,
A bird rose and settled on the royal
Banner and a captain steered his ship,
Means that you will meet Naropa.

The second:

The dream that the revered Naropa
With elephantine glance
Spread light o'er Tibet
From his eyes, the sun and moon,
Means that you will meet Naropa.

The third: 

The dream that a conch-shell 
blown upon three mountains
Guided beings from the lower valleys,
And that the light glowing in a lantern
Filled the whole human world
Means that you will meet Naropa.

The fourth:

The dream that the blind have been led
From the desert of the misery of an I,
So that the eyes of ignorance have been opened
And the mirror of mind is seen
Means that you will meet Naropa.

The fifth:

The certain fulfilment of the prayer
Imbued with the power of good
By the spiritual Dharmaraja
Means that you will meet Naropa.

The sixth:

In steadfast Pullahari
(Like) the disk of the full moon
Naropa will display the mirror
Of the Dharmakaya which is spirituality.

Exuberant with joy at these assurances and travelling through jungles and cities in search of his Guru, Mar-pa encountered countless difficulties. For instance he was imprisoned for three months by a tyrannical king. Released from prison he continued his search for another eight months, in the first of which he heard
a voice saying:

Are you not deceived by the bewildering dream
Of two women catching hold of you
While riding on a lion, dancing and singing
On top of the sun and moon?

ln the second month another voice said:

If you spur not on the horse in incessant confidence
And devotion with the whip of strenuousness
Will you not roam in Samsara with its duality
Like a deer caught in the hunter's snare?

In the third month:

If you know not that his tracks are as· hard
To trace as a bird's passage through the sky,
Will you not fall into abysmal senselessness
Like a dog pouncing on the shadow of a bird?

In the fourth:

If by that which never was
The snake's coil of doubt is never loosened
In the spiritual Dharmakaya, which is ultimate reality,
Your endeavour is as useless 
as a needle with two points.

In the fifth month, when he had the vision of meeting his Guru, a voice said:

If you know not that his being
Void of desires, is subtle as a rainbow,
How, like a blind man in a circus,
Will you cognize what it means?

In the sixth month, when he again had the vision of meeting his Guru and offering him a gold mandala, he heard a voice saying:

Since all that is is pure from the beginning,
Unless you offer a mandala of ultimate reality
Will not costly mandalas [offered] with desire
Unite in friendship with all worldly interests?

In the seventh month he saw in a vision his Guru sitting in a ravine and eating the brain of a dead man. When he refused in disgust to eat his share from a bone ladle a voice said:

Since the enjoyment of great bliss has but one value
In the vessel of Great Bliss,
If you partake not of it as great bliss
Great Bliss you win ne'er enjoy.

In the eighth month when he was sitting exhausted after vainly pursuing the vision of his Guru, a voice said :

If the horse of non-action, radiant light, the ultimate,
Does not race and neither comes nor goes, ·
Why, in the desert void of sense do you run
Like a deer chasing a mirage?

Praying in despair and saddened by memories of the great scholar Naropa, in his search he (Marpa) came to the jungle of Ri-mun-bcan. He offered some gold to a shepherd and asked him about Naropa. When he was shown a foot-print by a block of quartz his joy that he would now meet the venerable one was immeasurable. He prayed fervently and said: ‘At last father and son will meet.’

When he saw his Guru he felt as happy as when he attained the first spiritual level, and he began to talk incoherently. He placed his Guru’s feet on his head, embraced him, fainted, and when he had come to, he made all his gold into a mandala and offered it to Naropa. Although he was told ‘I do not want it, he pressed it on his Guru and was saddened when Naropa was about to throw it into the jungle, saying: ‘May it be an offering to the true Jewel of a Guru.’ However, the venerable Naropa handed the gold back and said: ‘I do not need it; all that is here is gold’, and touching the ground with his big toe turned it all into gold.

When Naropa was asked about the instruction on resurrection and the Oral Transmission, he said: ‘You have been brought here by the grace of Tilopa. These promised instructions are in Pullahari.’ When asked about the prophecy, he answered:

In the lamasery of Pullahari
Dispel the darkness of Mati’s ignorance
With the sunlight of supreme awareness, ever free.
Bathe him in the light thereof.

Then he said: ‘Come’ (and both went away).
Marpa, terrified at the thought that his Guru must in time depart, and afraid of Tilopa’s anger at their meeting, circumambulated Naropa and begged for his protection. Naropa prayed:

O Guru, deign to dispel all obstacles
Sent by Mara’s daughters to afflict
The son promised me by you:
The worthy Marpa.

In answer to this prayer Tilopa with a host of wrathful deities, carrying various frightful weapons, removed all obstacles. The Dakas folded their hands in terror and said:

We take refuge in the great terrifying
Body armed with fearful weapons,
In that Body and with terrifying
Speech we will do no harm.

When the moon has risen in full splendor twice
Let him ride the horse of the great carriage.
Venerable Naropa, since the prophecy
Has been fulfilled, live among spiritual beings.

With these words they all disappeared. It is said that at this time Marpa himself saw half of Tilopa in the clouds.

Then Naropa and Marpa went to Pullahari. When Marpa asked for the Oral Transmission and in particular for the teaching on transference and resurrection, Naropa asked him: ‘Did you remember to ask for resurrection, or did you receive a revelation?’ Marpa replied: ‘I did not receive a revelation, nor did I remember it myself; I have a disciple named Milarepa, he had a revelation by a Daka. Then Naropa said: ‘How wonderful, in the dark country of Tibet there is a being, bright like the sun rising over the snow.’ He then lifted his hands to his head and with the words

Salutation to the being 
Thos-pa dga', 
Like the sun rising over the snow
In the dread darkness of the North.

he closed his eyes and nodded thrice towards Tibet. It is said that also the hills and trees of Pullahari nodded thrice towards Tibet and that they all lean that way.

Nearly two months later when he had received the symbolic initiations and instructions in the Oral Transmission, Naropa appeared to him in the sky in the shape of the deity Hevajra with eight goddesses, and asked him whether he made obeisance to him or to the tutelary deity. Marpa answered: ‘To the tutelary deity.” Naropa said:

‘There where there is no Guru
Not even the name of the Buddha is heard.
The Buddhas of a thousand aeons
Depend on the Guru for their appearance.

Reflections on the Life of Dr. Herbert V. Guenther

"On March 11, 2006 Dr. Herbert V. Guenther, one of the most important and respected of the early Eastern scholar/translators, passed away at the age of 88.

Born March 17, 1917 in Bremen, Germany, he was fascinated from a very early age by the cultures of Southeast and Central Asia. His extraordinary talent for languages became apparent early on and when he was only nine years old he studied Chinese under the tutelage of a Chinese engineer, and at the age of ten he was teaching German to Russian sailors in exchange for Russian language lessons. His daughter Edith summarizes his extraordinary talents in the following words:

“He haunted the Asian section of Bremen’s Ethnographic Museum and devoured any books he could find on the exploration and history of those areas….”

He attended the Alte Gymnasium in Bremen; in addition to the regular curriculum of Latin, Greek, and Hebrew, he studied Sanskrit by himself from grammar books someone had given to him. The list of languages would grow exponentially, until it was easier for family members to answer the question, “What languages does he know?” by replying, “That’s more easily answered by listing the ones he doesn’t know.” By the time he began his studies at Munich University he read both Chinese and Sanskrit fluently and had written some papers on Sanskrit topics. For this reason he was allowed to study not only Vedic Sanskrit and Iranian Studies but also Pali, Prakrit, and Sinhalese. 

Between 1943-1950 he taught at Vienna University. Around 1948-49, the “Renazification” in Austria began: old Nazis returned there and political tensions ensued; thus, Europe was in the throes of instability. Dr. Guenther felt unease and restlessness, and he also believed that a good Sanskrit scholar had to go to India and live there for some time, otherwise one simply would not know enough. In short, owing to the political climate and his strong desire to learn, Dr. Guenther and his family ventured out towards the East. 

Dr. Guenther and his family stayed in India for more than twelve years, first at Lucknow University, where he taught Russian (and carried on his research work, including in Tibetan), and from 1958 until 1963 at the Sanskrit University in Benares (Varanasi), where he served as Head of the Department of Comparative Philosophy and Buddhist Studies. In 1962, Dr. Guenther accompanied his wife and two daughters back to Vienna, but Dr. Guenther returned to India later, just before he began a tour around the world. It was at this time that Professor Leddy from Saskatoon contacted him and asked him to become a professor in Saskatoon after his world tour. He arrived at the University of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon, in 1964 where he established the Department of Far Eastern Studies (now dissolved and replaced by the Department of Religious Studies) and served as its Department Head. After twenty-one years of service, Dr. Guenther retired in 1985. 

Among his earliest students were Jim Valby and Leslie Kawamura, and following them many students from Canada and the United States graduated with either their M.A. or Ph.D. degrees. He was able to attract students who wanted to study Buddhism but not necessarily in its traditional interpretation, because Dr. Guenther’s approach to the study of Buddhist texts and principles required not only an accurate understanding of the language in which they were written (i.e., Pali, Sanskrit, Tibetan, Chinese, or Mongolian) but also the ability to interpret the texts so that the author’s intention came alive in the translations and interpretations. Consequently, we can credit Dr. Guenther for introducing into the Buddhist academic world an interpretation of the Buddhadharma that was not necessarily sectarian in interpretation. His publications moved from the traditional literal style that tended to be “dry as dust” (Dr. Guenther’s favorite expression) to one which was dynamic and apropos of the human situation. 

When he taught at the Sanskrit University in Benares, he delivered his lectures in Sanskrit; however, his stay in India did not focus only on Indian Buddhism, but also on Tibetan Buddhism, because at that time there were more than thirty outstanding scholarly lamas, refugees from Tibet, at the Sanskrit University, and he was able to converse and exchange ideas with them. Among the Tibetan and Mongolian lamas who very much influenced him were: His Holiness the Dalai Lama; Trijang Rinpoche (Khri-byang Blo-bzang Ye-shes Rin-po-che), tutor to His Holiness; Kathog-on Tulku (Ka thog ‘on sprul-sku), an incarnate lama; the Abbot of Bodhgaya, Tado Tulku (Dar-mdo sprul-sku); Thubten Lhundrup Lekzang (Thub-bstan lhun-grub legs-bzang); Tarthang Tulku (Dar-thang sprul sku), Head Lama of the Nyingma Meditation Center and Nyingma Institute in Berkeley, California; and many others. It was through encounters, exchanges, and discussion with such learned teachers (mkhan-po) and reincarnate lamas (sprul-sku) that Dr. Guenther gained many insights into the living tradition of Tibetan Buddhism.

But that was not all, because while in India, each spring when the snow on the mountains began to melt, the Guenthers began their annual trek up the Himalayas towards Tibet. The family would join one of the trading caravans that crossed the Rohtang Pass from Manali to Lahaul, and stay either as guests of the local ruler or at Shashur Gompa (monastery). There he hand-copied, word for word, line by line, in exact facsimile, original texts. It was from such a hand-copied text that we produced the book Mind in Buddhist Psychology (1975). I must say that his handwriting of the Tibetan texts was much more legible than his everyday handwriting that stood at the foundation of almost all of his written publications. 

Dr. Guenther’s interest was certainly focused on Buddhism. In the earlier period of his life it was in Pali Studies. It was at that time that he wrote Das Seelenproblem im älteren Buddhismus (The Problem of the Soul in Older Buddhism) (1949) and Der Buddha und seine Lehre (The Buddha and His Teaching) (1956). However, even though he was well-trained in Pali, he was interested in other aspects of the Buddhist tradition, for in 1952 he already had published The Tantric Way of Life, which was certainly one of the earlier texts in Tantric Studies. After the publication of Philosophy and Psychology in the Abhidharma (1957), a book which most novices in Buddhist Studies have read and which reflected much of Dr. Guenther’s expertise as a certified Jungian psychologist, his interest became almost exclusively and totally focused on Tibetan Buddhism, and in particular on the Nyingma school of thought. I stated “almost exclusively and totally” because in spite of that strong interest, Dr. Guenther never lost sight of his favorite forms of humanistic studies: Asian art and poetry. These were never forgotten and in fact they promoted his style of writing found in books such as The Royal Song of Saraha (1969) and in his articles such as “Mind, Space and Aesthetic Awareness.” 

His personal library is filled with sources written in Tibetan, Chinese, Sanskrit, French, German, Mongolian, Japanese, and whatever other languages are used to express Buddhist ideas, and with books on art, science, biology, and any other scientific subjects related to Buddhist studies. The list is impressive, but the most important works are his unpublished research materials on the Tibetan books he had read. Tibetan texts written by great teachers have been copied meticulously and accurately, with page and line references, and these have been collated according to topics. Volumes of Dr. Guenther’s works written by him in minute and dense handwriting, topic by topic, with numerous references to texts under each entry, stand in his study as expressions of the fruits of Dr. Guenther’s years of steadfast concentration on his studies. 

There is much more to be said about this outstanding, kind-hearted, and learned scholar, but it would be a grave oversight if I did not mention something about “being Dr. Guenther’s student.” Dr. Guenther was something like a dynamo that starts out rather slowly and winds up to its top speed. Whenever we studied together, and sometimes it was for some eight hours straight, I would end up being totally exhausted and he would end the session by saying, “… now that we have just warmed up….” This indicated his intense interest in seeing his students through, and perhaps he had to spend so much time with me simply because I was unable to keep pace with his mental energy. I remember clearly when after one of those sessions he handed me a volume of the Peking Tibetan Tripitaka and requested me to find a particular word in the book. It was a Friday, but I figured that if I did not begin reading through the book as soon as I got home, there would be no hope of my meeting him on Monday with the answer. I read, and I read, and I read all weekend, but alas I could not find the word he wanted. Sheepishly I returned to the University on Monday to quietly say, “I could not find it!” He smiled and said, “Of course not, it is not in there!” 

Out of great compassion and with a touch of humor Dr. Guenther gently but firmly urged his students forward on their studies. Many students both within the university context and outside have benefited from his deep and profound knowledge. His innovative approach to the study of Tibetan Buddhist texts has influenced many students and will probably continue to do so even in his absence, because his warmth and mind will stay alive in the words that he has left for us to read—Down and Up Again (the title of his “electronic” publication).

I would like to acknowledge and thank Mrs. Edith Kimbell and Mrs. Dr. Ilse Guenther for their willingness to share much of the information that appears in this article."
